title: The Four Ratios That Reveal the Cookie Jar

formulas.name: Provision Coverage Ratio (PCR)
formulas.formula: PCR = Total Provisions / Gross NPAs × 100

variables.meaning: Cumulative provisions held against loans on the balance sheet, disclosed in notes on loan loss provisions
Total gross non-performing assets, disclosed in quarterly results and annual report asset quality notes

formulas.worked_example: Running PCR on three Indian banks, FY23. HDFC Bank: Total Provisions ₹19,410 crore against Gross NPAs of ₹18,019 crore = PCR of 108 percent. Very high — HDFC holds more provisions than its GNPA balance, signalling conservative recognition with buffer for Stage 2 migration. ICICI Bank: Total Provisions ₹39,230 crore against GNPAs of ₹26,962 crore = PCR of 146 percent. Even more conservative. Yes Bank FY19 (peak distress): Total Provisions ₹3,815 crore against GNPAs of ₹7,882 crore = PCR of 48 percent. Markedly below peer — inadequate coverage of known bad loans. Historical Yes Bank FY18: Total Provisions ₹1,890 crore against GNPAs of ₹2,627 crore = PCR of 72 percent. Below peers but above collapse-period level. The PCR trajectory from 72 percent (FY18) to 48 percent (FY19) to requiring ₹15,000+ crore of fresh provisioning (FY20) shows the jar running empty. The analyst lesson — PCR persistently below peer median (typically 70-80 percent for private banks, 65-75 percent for PSU banks) signals either that reported GNPAs understate actual asset quality issues, or that provisions are under-built relative to known risks. Both interpretations are bearish.
formulas.sensitivity_note: PCR alone is not sufficient — a bank can maintain high PCR while aggressively writing off bad loans (which removes them from both the numerator and denominator). Always check PCR in conjunction with net NPA ratio and provision expense trend.

formulas.name: Provision Expense Ratio (Credit Cost)
formulas.formula: Credit Cost = Provision Expense / Average Advances × 10000 (in basis points)

variables.meaning: Provisions created during the period, flowing through the P&L (not the balance sheet provisions balance)
(Opening Advances + Closing Advances) / 2 for the period

formulas.worked_example: For HDFC Bank FY23: Provision expense ₹11,920 crore against average advances of ₹14,40,000 crore = credit cost of 83 bps. This is consistent with HDFC's historical through-the-cycle credit cost range of 70-100 bps, indicating normal-environment provisioning. For Yes Bank FY17 (the jar-filling years): Provision expense ₹2,085 crore against average advances of ₹1,66,500 crore = 125 bps. For Yes Bank FY19 (jar running empty): Provision expense ₹5,778 crore against average advances of ₹2,35,000 crore = 246 bps. For Yes Bank FY20 (jar empty, reality arriving): Provision expense ₹37,765 crore against average advances of ₹1,70,000 crore = 2,221 bps. Credit cost of 2,221 bps — more than 22 percentage points of the loan book — is among the highest ever reported by an Indian bank outside regulatory write-offs. The pattern reveals the manipulation. Normal private banks operate at 70-120 bps credit cost; Yes Bank operated at 120-250 bps during 2017-2019 (already elevated but smoothed) before the 2,221 bps blowout in FY20. The cumulative credit cost across FY15-FY20 for Yes Bank was substantially higher than what reported quarterly numbers would have suggested — the reality was accumulating; the reporting was smoothing.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Credit cost volatility matters as much as absolute level. A bank reporting 100 bps credit cost every year for 5 years is implausibly stable — real credit cycles produce natural volatility. Smoothness of credit cost across economic cycles is itself a cookie-jar signal.

formulas.name: Stage Migration Ratio (Ind AS 109)
formulas.formula: Stage 2 + Stage 3 Ratio = (Stage 2 Assets + Stage 3 Assets) / Total Loan Book × 100

variables.meaning: Loans classified as showing significant increase in credit risk, requiring lifetime ECL provisioning
Loans classified as credit-impaired, requiring full lifetime ECL provisioning at account-specific level
Gross advances including all stages

formulas.worked_example: Under Ind AS 109, banks must disclose stage-wise loan classification. For HDFC Bank FY23: Stage 2 assets 1.8 percent of book, Stage 3 assets 1.1 percent, total Stage 2+3 ratio 2.9 percent. For Kotak Mahindra Bank FY23: Stage 2 at 2.1 percent, Stage 3 at 1.7 percent, total 3.8 percent. These represent a healthy acknowledgment of stressed-but-not-defaulted assets. For a hypothetical mid-cap bank reporting Stage 2 at 0.5 percent and Stage 3 at 0.8 percent, total 1.3 percent, in the same economic environment — the anomaly is the unusually low Stage 2 classification. Stage 2 is the 'watchlist' — loans showing early stress that may migrate to default. A bank reporting very low Stage 2 in an environment where peers report 2-3 percent is either genuinely cleaner or systematically delaying stage migration. The delayed migration is the cookie-jar mechanism — keeping provisioning low today by classifying genuinely stressed loans as Stage 1. Detection: compare Stage 2 ratios across banks operating in similar segments and geographies. Material outliers deserve scrutiny. Cross-check against the bank's disclosure of SMA-1 and SMA-2 (Special Mention Accounts — RBI classification) if available.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Stage 2 classification is highly judgement-dependent. The standard requires 'significant' credit risk increase without defining significant. Two banks with identical loan books can report very different Stage 2 ratios based solely on management philosophy. Always pair Stage 2 analysis with actual default experience over the following 2-3 years.

formulas.name: Specific vs General Provision Mix
formulas.formula: General Provision Ratio = General Provisions / Total Provisions × 100

variables.meaning: Provisions not tied to specific identified losses — includes macro-prudential, counter-cyclical, and contingency provisions
All provisions held on the balance sheet, specific plus general

formulas.worked_example: For HDFC Bank FY23: General provisions roughly ₹8,200 crore out of total provisions ₹19,410 crore = 42 percent general. ICICI Bank: general provisions ₹15,600 crore of ₹39,230 crore = 40 percent. These are conservative buffer levels built during profitable periods to provide flexibility in weaker periods. For Yes Bank FY18: general provisions ₹240 crore of ₹1,890 crore = 13 percent. Dramatically below peer — the bank was not building general buffer during its high-growth phase, meaning it had no cushion when specific losses materialised. The historical pattern reveals the manipulation philosophy: peer banks were building jars during good times (conservative and defensible); Yes Bank was not building any jar, relying on continuing profitability to avoid specific provisioning requirements. When the environment turned, peers had buffers to absorb shocks; Yes Bank did not. Detection: low general provision ratio during high-growth, high-profit periods signals management unwilling to build prudential buffers — a risk management red flag even separate from cookie-jar analysis.
formulas.sensitivity_note: General provisions can also be manipulated in the opposite direction — building very large general buffers during profitable periods and releasing them selectively in weak quarters to smooth earnings. Both extremes (too low and too high) relative to peers warrant investigation.

title: Unit Economics & Operating Leverage Formulas

formulas.name: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
formulas.formula: CAC = Total Sales & Marketing Spend / Number of New Customers Acquired

worked_example.insight: The question: does each customer eventually generate more than ₹2,000 in profit? If yes, model works. If no, buying growth at a loss.
worked_example.problem: Zomato spends ₹800 crore on S&M, acquires 40 lakh new customers.

formulas.name: Customer Lifetime Value (CLTV)
formulas.formula: CLTV = (ARPU × Gross Margin) / Churn Rate

variables.ARPU: Average Revenue Per User per period
variables.CLTV: Total profit a customer generates over entire relationship
variables.Churn Rate: % of customers who stop using the product per period

benchmarks.1x_to_3x: Marginal. Need to reduce CAC or improve retention/margins.
benchmarks.above_3x: Healthy unit economics. Business model works.
benchmarks.below_1x: Broken. Every new customer destroys value.

formulas.sensitivity: If churn increases from 8% to 12%, CLTV drops to ₹5,833 and ratio falls to 2.9x — borderline. Churn is the silent killer of unit economics.

worked_example.problem: Zomato: 8 orders/month × ₹350 AOV = ₹2,800 ARPU. Gross margin 25%. Monthly churn 8%.

formulas.name: Contribution Margin
formulas.formula: Contribution Margin = Revenue - Variable Costs
formulas.why_it_matters: How much each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs and generating profit. If negative, every additional sale makes the company poorer.

worked_example.insight: Each passenger contributes ₹2,300 toward fixed costs. IndiGo's genius: fixed costs per seat among lowest in world (single aircraft type A320, high seat density, fast turnaround).
worked_example.problem: IndiGo Airlines: ticket ₹5,500. Variable costs: fuel ₹2,200, airport ₹600, food ₹100, other ₹300 = ₹3,200.

formulas.name: Operating Leverage (DOL)
formulas.formula: DOL = % Change in Operating Profit / % Change in Revenue
formulas.flip_side: Works in reverse: if revenue falls 20%, profit could fall 40%. Why high-operating-leverage businesses (airlines, hotels, steel, software) are more volatile and often have higher betas.

worked_example.insight: 20% revenue increase → 40% profit increase. Fixed cost base doesn't grow, so incremental revenue flows to profit.
worked_example.problem: Zoho: Y1 Revenue ₹5,000cr, Op Profit ₹1,500cr. Y2 Revenue ₹6,000cr (+20%), Op Profit ₹2,100cr (+40%).

title: The Three Integrity Check Formulas — Your Model's Alarm System

formulas.name: Balance Sheet Integrity Check
formulas.formula: =ROUND(Total_Assets - Total_Liabilities - Total_Equity, 2)

variables.meaning: Reference to the Total Assets cell on the Balance Sheet, typically the subtotal row
Reference to Total Liabilities cell on the BS
Reference to Total Equity cell on the BS
Rounds to 2 decimal places to ignore floating-point noise below ₹0.01 cr

formulas.worked_example: Placed in cell B1 of the Balance Sheet tab (before you even enter any data), formula = ROUND(B45 - B62 - B75, 2) where B45 is Total Assets, B62 is Total Liabilities, B75 is Total Equity. Today the cell shows 0 (all values are empty, which Excel treats as zero). As you populate historicals and forecasts, this cell must remain 0. Conditional formatting rule: if value = 0 then fill green, else fill red. Repeat the formula across all years — if year FY27 suddenly turns red, you know exactly which year has the error.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The ROUND wrapper is critical. Without it, you'll see tiny values like 0.000001 from floating-point arithmetic and panic. With ROUND to 2 decimals, the cell shows 0 whenever the imbalance is less than ₹0.01 cr — which is effectively zero for any reasonable model.

formulas.name: Cash Reconciliation Check
formulas.formula: =ROUND(CFS_Closing_Cash - BS_Cash, 2)

variables.meaning: The closing cash cell at the bottom of the Cash Flow Statement, after adding Opening Cash + CFO + CFI + CFF
The Cash & Cash Equivalents line on the current-year Balance Sheet

formulas.worked_example: Placed in cell B2 of the Cash Flow Statement tab. Formula = ROUND(CFS!B58 - BS!B12, 2). For FY24 Titan: CFS closing cash = ₹1,800 cr. BS cash = ₹1,800 cr. Difference = 0. ✓. Repeat across all years. If any year turns red, the CFS is either missing a line or has a sign error. This check catches roughly 80% of modelling errors in the forecast period.
formulas.sensitivity_note: This check will fire before the BS integrity check does, because a cash tie-out failure propagates into an imbalanced BS. So: fix cash tie-out FIRST, then BS integrity usually resolves itself.

formulas.name: Retained Earnings Roll Check
formulas.formula: =ROUND(RE_Closing - (RE_Opening + Net_Income - Dividends), 2)

variables.meaning: Current-year closing retained earnings on the BS
Prior-year closing retained earnings (i.e. opening for current year)
Current-year Net Income from the IS bottom line
Dividends paid in the current year (from CFF on the CFS)

formulas.worked_example: Placed in cell B3 of the Balance Sheet tab. Formula = ROUND(BS!F75 - (BS!E75 + IS!F45 - CFS!F52), 2). For FY24 Titan: Closing RE ₹9,086 cr = Opening RE ₹7,100 cr + NI ₹3,496 cr − Dividends ₹1,510 cr. 9,086 − (7,100 + 3,496 − 1,510) = 0. ✓. If this check fires, it's usually because Net Income is linked to the wrong year, or dividends from CFF aren't being reflected in RE.
formulas.sensitivity_note: This is the sneakiest check because when it fails, BS integrity also fails — and beginners fix BS integrity with a plug without realising the RE roll was the underlying cause. Always check RE roll before touching anything else.

title: The Efficiency Formula Arsenal (With Indian Worked Examples)

formulas.name: Asset Turnover
formulas.formula: Asset Turnover = Revenue / Average Total Assets

variables.meaning: Net sales / turnover for the period
(Opening Total Assets + Closing Total Assets) / 2

formulas.worked_example: DMart FY23: Revenue = ₹42,840 Cr, Opening Assets = ₹9,800 Cr, Closing Assets = ₹11,300 Cr. Average Assets = ₹10,550 Cr. Asset Turnover = 42,840 / 10,550 = 4.06x. Every rupee of DMart's assets generates ₹4.06 of revenue per year — exceptional retail efficiency. Compare Tata Steel FY23: Revenue ₹2,43,000 Cr, Average Assets ₹2,60,000 Cr. Asset Turnover = 0.94x — each rupee of steel plant generates less than one rupee of revenue annually because steel is brutally asset-heavy. Same metric, completely different business characteristics. The ratio tells you immediately whether you're analysing a capital-light business (retail, IT services, consumer) or a capital-heavy one (steel, power, cement, infrastructure).
formulas.sensitivity_note: Asset Turnover is the single biggest driver of DuPont's turnover lever. A 0.5x improvement in Asset Turnover (say from 1.5x to 2.0x) translates to 33% improvement in ROCE, holding margins constant. That's why asset-light businesses command premium valuations.

formulas.name: Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO)
formulas.formula: DIO = (Average Inventory / Cost of Goods Sold) × 365

variables.meaning: (Opening Inventory + Closing Inventory) / 2
Cost of Goods Sold — raw materials + direct labour + manufacturing overhead

formulas.worked_example: DMart FY23: Average Inventory ≈ ₹2,850 Cr, COGS ≈ ₹36,420 Cr. DIO = (2,850 / 36,420) × 365 = 28.5 days. DMart sells its inventory every ~4 weeks — extraordinary for a 330+ store retailer. Compare Maruti Suzuki FY23: Average Inventory ≈ ₹4,500 Cr, COGS ≈ ₹95,000 Cr. DIO = (4,500 / 95,000) × 365 = 17.3 days. Maruti's JIT system is even faster. Contrast with a capital goods firm like Thermax: Inventory ≈ ₹1,400 Cr, COGS ≈ ₹3,800 Cr. DIO = 135 days — projects take months of WIP build-up. Each industry has its natural DIO range.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Rising DIO trend is one of the earliest warning signs of channel stuffing or declining demand. A company showing DIO rising from 45 to 70 days over 3 years has either inventory obsolescence risk or is pushing stock to dealers to book revenue — both are yellow flags.

formulas.name: Days Sales Outstanding (DSO)
formulas.formula: DSO = (Average Trade Receivables / Revenue) × 365

variables.meaning: (Opening Trade Receivables + Closing Trade Receivables) / 2
Net sales

formulas.worked_example: HUL FY23: Average Receivables ≈ ₹2,300 Cr, Revenue = ₹58,154 Cr. DSO = (2,300 / 58,154) × 365 = 14.4 days. Consumers buy groceries at the till — HUL collects almost immediately. Compare to L&T FY23: Average Receivables ≈ ₹41,000 Cr, Revenue ≈ ₹1,84,000 Cr. DSO = 81.4 days — L&T serves large government infrastructure clients with long payment cycles. Industry norms: B2C retail 0-5 days, FMCG 10-20 days, B2B manufacturing 45-75 days, infrastructure 90-150 days, government-heavy businesses >150 days.
formulas.sensitivity_note: DSO expansion is the single most reliable early warning of revenue quality issues. If DSO jumps from 45 to 75 days while revenue grows, the company is likely booking aggressive revenue that customers haven't paid for. Always validate revenue growth against DSO trend.

formulas.name: Days Payable Outstanding (DPO)
formulas.formula: DPO = (Average Trade Payables / Cost of Goods Sold) × 365

variables.meaning: (Opening Trade Payables + Closing Trade Payables) / 2
Cost of Goods Sold

formulas.worked_example: DMart FY23: Average Payables ≈ ₹5,400 Cr, COGS ≈ ₹36,420 Cr. DPO = (5,400 / 36,420) × 365 = 54.1 days. DMart takes about 8 weeks to pay suppliers. HUL FY23: Average Payables ≈ ₹8,500 Cr, COGS ≈ ₹27,742 Cr. DPO = 111.8 days — HUL enjoys ~4 months of supplier credit, one of the strongest DPO profiles in Indian industry. Compare to a commoditised manufacturer: Payables ₹800 Cr, COGS ₹6,000 Cr. DPO = 48.7 days — no pricing power with suppliers.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Rising DPO that's voluntary (driven by scale/bargaining power like HUL) is a strength. Rising DPO that's involuntary (company stretching payments because cash is tight) is a distress signal. Cross-check DPO expansion with cash flow trends to distinguish the two.

formulas.name: Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC)
formulas.formula: CCC = DIO + DSO - DPO

variables.meaning: Days Inventory Outstanding
Days Sales Outstanding
Days Payable Outstanding

formulas.worked_example: DMart FY23: DIO = 28.5 + DSO = 2.5 (cash retail) - DPO = 54.1 = -23.1 days. NEGATIVE CCC — suppliers fund DMart's operations for 23 days on average. Every rupee of revenue DMart generates sits as working capital cushion. HUL FY23: DIO = 35 + DSO = 14 - DPO = 112 = -63 days. Extraordinary — HUL runs 2 months of supplier-funded operations. Asian Paints FY23: DIO = 55 + DSO = 15 - DPO = 45 = +25 days. Positive but tight — paints business has dealer inventory. A stressed mid-cap: DIO = 110 + DSO = 85 - DPO = 55 = +140 days. The company needs 4+ months of cash tied up in working capital — a massive capital drag.
formulas.sensitivity_note: A CCC improvement of 10 days on a ₹10,000 Cr revenue business frees up ~₹270 Cr of working capital — cash that can fund growth or pay down debt. This is why CFOs obsess over working capital management. And it's why investors prize businesses with durable negative CCC — those companies compound without needing external capital.

formulas.name: Fixed Asset Turnover
formulas.formula: Fixed Asset Turnover = Revenue / Average Net Fixed Assets

variables.meaning: Net sales
Property, Plant & Equipment (net of accumulated depreciation) + Capital Work-in-Progress

formulas.worked_example: Infosys FY23: Revenue = ₹1,46,767 Cr, Net Fixed Assets ≈ ₹13,500 Cr. Fixed Asset Turnover = 10.87x — each rupee of office buildings and IT infrastructure generates ₹10.87 of revenue. That's what 'asset-light' really means. Compare NTPC FY23: Revenue ₹1,75,000 Cr, Net Fixed Assets ≈ ₹2,85,000 Cr. Fixed Asset Turnover = 0.61x — each rupee of power plant generates only ₹0.61 of revenue. Contrast reveals business model fundamentally. Also reveals why power sector needs long-dated debt and low-cost capital to earn adequate returns.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Fixed Asset Turnover is particularly revealing when comparing companies within the same industry. If two cement manufacturers both run at Fixed Asset Turnover of 1.2x while a third runs at 0.8x, the third has either underutilised capacity, overpaid capex, or older/less efficient assets — all concerning for ROCE trajectory.

title: The TVM Formula Family — Five Equations That Power Every DCF

formulas.name: Present Value of a Single Future Cash Flow
formulas.formula: PV = FV / (1 + r)^n

variables.meaning: Present value — what the future cash flow is worth today
Future value — the cash flow at the future date
Discount rate (decimal form, e.g., 0.10 for 10%)
Number of periods (typically years) until the cash flow occurs

formulas.worked_example: You expect HDFC Bank to pay you a dividend of ₹50 per share five years from now. Your discount rate is 11%. The present value is ₹50 / (1.11)^5 = ₹50 / 1.6851 = ₹29.67. So that ₹50 future dividend is worth about ₹29.67 to you today. The other ₹20.33 is the cost of waiting five years to receive it.
formulas.sensitivity_note: PV is highly sensitive to both r and n. At r = 10%, ₹100 in Year 10 is worth ₹38.55 today. Bump r to 12% and it falls to ₹32.20 (a 16% drop in PV from a 2 percentage point change in rate). Push n out to Year 20 at r = 10% and ₹100 is worth only ₹14.86. This is why long-duration cash flows are extremely sensitive to the discount rate — and why terminal value assumptions in a DCF deserve so much scrutiny.

formulas.name: Future Value of a Single Present Cash Flow
formulas.formula: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n

variables.meaning: Present value — the amount you have today
Future value — what it will grow to
Compounding rate per period
Number of compounding periods

formulas.worked_example: You invest ₹1,00,000 in a Nifty 50 index fund and assume a 12% CAGR over 15 years. Future value = 1,00,000 × (1.12)^15 = 1,00,000 × 5.4736 = ₹5,47,360. This is also why your senior keeps repeating that compounding is the eighth wonder of the world — that initial ₹1 lakh grew 5.5x over 15 years without you adding a single rupee.
formulas.sensitivity_note: FV is especially sensitive to time horizon. The same ₹1 lakh at 12% becomes ₹3.11 lakh in 10 years, ₹5.47 lakh in 15 years, ₹9.65 lakh in 20 years, and ₹17.0 lakh in 25 years. Each additional 5 years adds dramatically more value than the last — that is the geometric magic of compounding.

formulas.name: Present Value of an Ordinary Annuity

variables.meaning: Equal periodic payment
Discount rate per period
Number of periods

formulas.worked_example: Going back to the KBC opener — your uncle gets ₹15 lakh per year for 10 years at a 10% discount rate. PV = 15,00,000 × [(1 - (1.10)^-10) / 0.10] = 15,00,000 × 6.1446 = ₹92.17 lakh. The ₹1.5 crore headline number was actually worth ₹92 lakh in present-value terms — less than the ₹1 crore lump sum he turned down.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For any annuity, the present value is bounded above by PMT/r (the perpetuity value). At r = 10% and PMT = ₹15 lakh, even an infinite annuity would only be worth ₹1.5 crore today — so a 10-year annuity at ₹92 lakh has captured about 61% of the perpetuity value. The longer the annuity, the more it asymptotes to the perpetuity, but the gains from extending get smaller and smaller.

formulas.name: Present Value of a Perpetuity
formulas.formula: PV = PMT / r

variables.meaning: Constant cash flow per period, forever
Discount rate per period

formulas.worked_example: A government bond pays ₹100 per year forever (the British Consol bond was structured this way). At a discount rate of 8%, its present value is ₹100 / 0.08 = ₹1,250. No matter how far out you extend, you cannot value an infinite cash flow stream above this number when discounted at 8%.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Perpetuity values are extraordinarily sensitive to small changes in r — at PMT = ₹100, PV at 8% is ₹1,250; at 6% it jumps to ₹1,667 (33% higher); at 4% it doubles to ₹2,500. This is why interest rate movements have such dramatic effects on long-duration assets, and why equity markets often correct violently when central banks raise rates.

formulas.name: Present Value of a Growing Perpetuity (Gordon Growth Model)
formulas.formula: PV = CF₁ / (r - g)

variables.meaning: Cash flow in the first period (one year from now)
Discount rate
Constant growth rate, forever (must be less than r)

formulas.worked_example: You expect TCS to generate ₹50,000 cr of free cash flow next year, growing at 5% forever. At a WACC of 11%, the value of TCS's cash flows from now to infinity is 50,000 / (0.11 - 0.05) = 50,000 / 0.06 = ₹8,33,333 cr. This is the workhorse formula for terminal value in every DCF on Earth.
formulas.sensitivity_note: This formula is mathematically explosive as g approaches r. At r = 11%, g = 5% gives PV multiplier of 16.7x; bump g to 6% and the multiplier becomes 20x; push g to 7% and it shoots to 25x. Tiny changes in g move the answer enormously. This is why the perpetuity growth rate is the single most-debated assumption in any DCF.

title: The Valuation Multiple Formula Arsenal

formulas.name: P/E Ratio
formulas.formula: P/E = Market Price per Share / Earnings per Share = Market Cap / Net Profit

variables.meaning: Current trading price of one share
Earnings Per Share = Net Profit / Number of Outstanding Shares

formulas.worked_example: Nestle India FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹2,20,000 Cr. Net Profit ≈ ₹2,390 Cr. P/E = 2,20,000 / 2,390 = 92x (approximately). Nestle is one of the most expensive stocks in India on P/E basis. Compare Coal India FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹2,30,000 Cr. Net Profit ≈ ₹36,500 Cr. P/E = 2,30,000 / 36,500 = 6.3x. Coal India is one of the cheapest large-caps in India on P/E basis. Same absolute market cap, radically different multiples — because the market prices growth (Nestle's 10-12% CAGR), stability (consumer staples survive recessions), and moat (brand premium) very differently from cyclicality (coal prices), policy risk (government regulation), and structural disruption (renewables replacing coal).
formulas.sensitivity_note: P/E is the most intuitive multiple but also the most dangerous. It breaks for loss-making companies (division by near-zero), for banks (provisioning distorts earnings year-to-year), for companies with heavy one-off items, and for comparisons across companies with different capital structures. Use with care and always cross-check with EV-based multiples.

formulas.name: P/B Ratio
formulas.formula: P/B = Market Price / Book Value per Share = Market Cap / Shareholders' Equity

variables.meaning: Current market value of all outstanding equity
Book Value = Share Capital + Reserves & Surplus

formulas.worked_example: HDFC Bank FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹8,70,000 Cr. Shareholders' Equity ≈ ₹2,80,000 Cr. P/B = 8,70,000 / 2,80,000 = 3.1x. HDFC Bank is the gold standard of Indian private banking, trading at over 3 times book — a premium to the sector median of ~2x and well above PSU banks (many of which trade at below 1x). State Bank of India FY23: P/B ≈ 1.3x. IndusInd Bank FY23: P/B ≈ 1.6x. Kotak Mahindra Bank FY23: P/B ≈ 3.5x. PSU banks (Bank of Baroda, Canara Bank): P/B 0.7-1.0x. The P/B differential across Indian banks exactly reflects the market's view of return quality (ROE), asset quality (NPAs), and growth potential.
formulas.sensitivity_note: P/B is the right lens for banks because banks' 'earnings' fluctuate with provisioning cycles, but their book value — the actual net assets — is a stable anchor. For non-financial businesses, P/B is less useful because book value doesn't capture brand, technology, or goodwill. An Infosys or TCS trading at 15x P/B doesn't mean they're expensive — their book value simply doesn't reflect the economic value of their human capital and client relationships.

formulas.name: Enterprise Value (EV)
formulas.formula: EV = Market Cap + Total Debt + Preferred Equity + Minority Interest - Cash and Cash Equivalents

variables.meaning: Current market value of common equity
Short-term debt + Long-term debt + Current portion of long-term debt
Cash + Cash equivalents + Liquid investments

formulas.worked_example: Reliance Industries FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹17,00,000 Cr. Total Debt ≈ ₹3,10,000 Cr. Cash ≈ ₹85,000 Cr. Minority Interest ≈ ₹1,30,000 Cr. EV = 17,00,000 + 3,10,000 + 1,30,000 - 85,000 = ₹20,55,000 Cr. So while the market cap is ₹17 lakh crore, the full enterprise value — what it would cost to acquire all of Reliance's capital claims — is ₹20.55 lakh crore. This is especially important for valuation comparisons because a company with less debt would have a lower EV relative to its market cap, making direct EV/EBITDA comparisons meaningful.
formulas.sensitivity_note: EV is the 'true cost of acquiring the business' because if you bought the company, you would inherit its debt (added to cost) and could use its cash (subtracted from cost). This makes EV far more accurate than Market Cap for cross-company comparisons. Forgetting to subtract cash or add debt is the most common valuation error beginners make.

formulas.name: EV/EBITDA
formulas.formula: EV/EBITDA = Enterprise Value / EBITDA

variables.meaning: Enterprise Value as defined above
Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation

formulas.worked_example: Asian Paints FY23: EV ≈ ₹2,90,000 Cr. EBITDA ≈ ₹6,800 Cr. EV/EBITDA = 42.6x. Extraordinarily rich — reflects the market's confidence in Asian Paints' 30%+ ROCE moat and durable growth. Compare Tata Steel FY23: EV ≈ ₹2,50,000 Cr. EBITDA ≈ ₹28,000 Cr. EV/EBITDA = 8.9x. Classic cyclical valuation — the market refuses to pay a premium for commodity earnings because steel prices can collapse at any cycle turn. Rule of thumb benchmarks: cyclical commodity businesses 5-10x, stable manufacturing 10-14x, consumer staples 25-45x, luxury consumer and premium brands 40-60x, software/tech 25-50x depending on growth.
formulas.sensitivity_note: EV/EBITDA is the professional's default because it is capital-structure neutral and ignores non-cash depreciation. It works well for cross-company comparison. However, it understates the true cost of capex-heavy businesses (where depreciation is real economic cost). For capex-heavy industries, also look at EV/EBIT.

formulas.name: PEG Ratio
formulas.formula: PEG = P/E Ratio / Expected Earnings Growth Rate (%)

variables.meaning: Current or forward P/E ratio
Expected annual EPS growth rate, usually 2-3 year CAGR

formulas.worked_example: A growth company with P/E of 30 and expected earnings growth of 25% per year: PEG = 30/25 = 1.2. Mildly expensive but close to fair for a growth stock. Peter Lynch's rule: PEG below 1 is potentially cheap, PEG above 2 is expensive. Compare Coal India: P/E of 6, expected growth of 5%: PEG = 6/5 = 1.2. Technically the same PEG as the growth company — illustrating why PEG must be interpreted alongside business quality. A growth business at PEG 1.2 is attractive; a cyclical commodity business at PEG 1.2 is not, because the growth is unreliable.
formulas.sensitivity_note: PEG works beautifully for growth stocks with predictable earnings trajectories but breaks down for cyclicals, turnarounds, or businesses with unreliable forward estimates. Always use multi-year (3-year+) growth estimates rather than single-year growth to avoid being fooled by one-off spikes.

formulas.name: P/S Ratio (Price-to-Sales)
formulas.formula: P/S = Market Cap / Revenue

variables.meaning: Current equity value
Trailing 12-month or forward annual revenue

formulas.worked_example: Zomato FY23 (at listing): Market Cap at IPO ≈ ₹64,000 Cr. Revenue ≈ ₹4,200 Cr. P/S = 64,000 / 4,200 = 15x. Compare Amazon historical P/S during early growth years: 4-6x. Zomato at 15x P/S meant the market was assigning significant growth optionality to future food delivery expansion — partially realised, partially not. P/S is the go-to multiple for loss-making growth companies where P/E is meaningless.
formulas.sensitivity_note: P/S ignores margin differences — a company with 30% operating margin and one with 5% margin can trade at similar P/S but have vastly different intrinsic values. Use P/S only as a starting point for loss-making companies; always overlay margin expectations before concluding.

title: The Three Liquidity Formulas (With Worked Indian Examples)

formulas.name: Current Ratio
formulas.formula: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities

variables.meaning: Cash + Receivables + Inventory + Short-term Investments + Other Current Assets
Trade Payables + Short-term Debt + Current Portion of Long-term Debt + Accrued Expenses + Taxes Payable

formulas.worked_example: Asian Paints FY23 (approximate): Current Assets = ₹9,200 Cr (Cash ₹5,100 Cr + Receivables ₹1,400 Cr + Inventory ₹2,400 Cr + Others ₹300 Cr). Current Liabilities = ₹5,800 Cr (Trade Payables ₹3,800 Cr + Short-term Debt ₹900 Cr + Others ₹1,100 Cr). Current Ratio = 9,200 / 5,800 = 1.59x. Healthy. Asian Paints generates enough current assets to cover short-term obligations 1.6 times over, with room to spare. Compare to Tata Motors FY20 at peak stress: Current Assets ₹52,000 Cr, Current Liabilities ₹75,000 Cr → Current Ratio = 0.69x. A ratio below 1.0x is a red flag — short-term obligations exceed short-term resources.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Current Ratio is highly sensitive to inventory valuation and receivable aging policy. A company that ages receivables longer (booking them as current instead of writing them off) inflates the ratio artificially. Always check inventory days and DSO alongside Current Ratio to validate.

formulas.name: Quick Ratio (Acid Test)
formulas.formula: Quick Ratio = (Current Assets - Inventory) / Current Liabilities

variables.meaning: Total short-term assets as defined in Current Ratio
Raw materials + Work-in-progress + Finished goods + Stock-in-trade
Same as Current Ratio

formulas.worked_example: Asian Paints FY23: Quick Ratio = (9,200 - 2,400) / 5,800 = 1.17x. Still comfortable. Asian Paints can cover its short-term obligations even if every last tin of paint sat unsold. Now compare to Mahindra & Mahindra at the peak of the auto slowdown in FY20: Current Assets ₹42,000 Cr including ₹8,000 Cr of dealer inventory; Current Liabilities ₹38,000 Cr. Current Ratio = 1.11x (looks tight but acceptable). Quick Ratio = (42,000 - 8,000) / 38,000 = 0.89x — below 1.0x. If auto demand stayed weak and dealers couldn't move inventory, M&M would be short on liquidity. The Quick Ratio revealed a stress that the Current Ratio hid.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Quick Ratio is the most widely-used liquidity metric in credit analysis because inventory quality varies enormously by industry. For inventory-heavy businesses (auto, capital goods, retail), the gap between Current Ratio and Quick Ratio is often the real liquidity story. For asset-light businesses (IT, services), the two are nearly identical.

formulas.name: Cash Ratio
formulas.formula: Cash Ratio = (Cash + Cash Equivalents) / Current Liabilities

variables.meaning: Cash in hand + Balances with banks in current/savings accounts
Liquid investments maturing within 90 days — T-bills, money market funds, liquid mutual fund units
Same as above

formulas.worked_example: Infosys FY23: Cash + Cash Equivalents + Liquid Investments ≈ ₹22,000 Cr. Current Liabilities ≈ ₹19,000 Cr. Cash Ratio = 22,000 / 19,000 = 1.16x. Extraordinarily conservative — Infosys can pay every short-term obligation using just cash on hand. This is the profile of a cash-rich IT giant with no debt and no working capital stress. Compare to Vodafone Idea circa FY22: Cash ≈ ₹500 Cr, Current Liabilities ≈ ₹55,000 Cr. Cash Ratio = 500 / 55,000 = 0.009x. Less than 1% coverage — an existential liquidity crisis that no operational improvement could fix without massive equity infusion.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Cash Ratio is the stress-test metric. For companies in cyclical industries (steel, auto, real estate) or facing sector distress, Cash Ratio becomes the primary liquidity measure. A rule of thumb: Cash Ratio below 0.05 for a company with material short-term debt is a screaming red flag — default risk is imminent.

title: The Return Formula Stack and the DuPont Decomposition

formulas.name: Return on Capital Employed (ROCE)
formulas.formula: ROCE = EBIT / Average Capital Employed\nWhere Capital Employed = Shareholders' Equity + Total Debt (Long-term + Short-term)\nOR equivalently: Total Assets − Non-Interest-Bearing Current Liabilities

variables.meaning: Earnings Before Interest and Tax from the P&L. Represents operating profit available to all capital providers before financing and tax decisions.
The total capital invested in operations — equity capital plus interest-bearing debt. Average of opening and closing balances for the period.

formulas.worked_example:
Asian Paints FY24:
EBIT: ₹6,880 cr
Shareholders' Equity (avg): ₹18,620 cr
Total Debt (avg): ₹2,850 cr
Capital Employed (avg): ₹21,470 cr

ROCE = 6,880 / 21,470 = 32.0%

Interpretation: Asian Paints generates ₹32 of pre-tax operating profit for every ₹100 of capital invested in operations. This is among the highest ROCE levels in Indian equity markets, driven by: (a) strong brand-driven pricing power (gross margin 38-42%), (b) efficient working capital management (slightly negative to modestly positive CCC), (c) asset-light manufacturing (shared facilities, outsourced packaging), (d) distribution scale economies (40,000+ dealers).

Peer context (FY24):
• Asian Paints: 32%
• Berger Paints: 18%
• Kansai Nerolac: 15%
• Indigo Paints: 17%

The 14-17 percentage point gap versus peers is the quantitative measure of Asian Paints' franchise strength. Over 10 years, compounding at 30% ROCE versus 15% means total capital earns double the returns — which is why Asian Paints has delivered approximately 25% total-return CAGR over multiple decades.
formulas.sensitivity_note: A 200 bps deterioration in ROCE (30% to 28%) on a ₹21,470 cr capital base represents ₹430 cr of foregone annual earnings — nearly 10% of current EBIT. ROCE deterioration is therefore both a leading indicator of business quality change AND a direct driver of earnings impact.

formulas.name: The DuPont Decomposition of ROE
formulas.formula: ROE = Net Profit Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier\nROE = (Net Income / Revenue) × (Revenue / Average Assets) × (Average Assets / Average Equity)

variables.meaning: Net Income divided by Revenue — measures profitability
Revenue divided by Average Total Assets — measures asset efficiency (how much revenue is generated per rupee of assets)
Average Total Assets divided by Average Equity — measures leverage (how much total assets are supported by each rupee of equity)

formulas.worked_example:
HUL FY24 DuPont Decomposition:
Net Profit Margin: 10,280 / 60,980 = 16.9%
Asset Turnover: 60,980 / 34,580 = 1.76x
Equity Multiplier: 34,580 / 12,050 = 2.87x

ROE = 16.9% × 1.76 × 2.87 = 85.3%

Check: ROE = 10,280 / 12,050 = 85.3% ✓

TCS FY24 DuPont Decomposition:
Net Profit Margin: 46,099 / 240,893 = 19.1%
Asset Turnover: 240,893 / 1,28,200 = 1.88x
Equity Multiplier: 1,28,200 / 98,340 = 1.30x

ROE = 19.1% × 1.88 × 1.30 = 46.7%

INSIGHT: HUL and TCS have similar net profit margins (16.9% vs 19.1%) and similar asset turnover (1.76 vs 1.88). The massive ROE difference (85% vs 47%) is almost entirely explained by the equity multiplier — HUL operates with 2.87x assets to equity (high operating leverage through payables and consumer goods financing), TCS operates with only 1.30x (cash-rich, low-debt IT services structure). This is a leverage-driven ROE difference, not an operational difference. DuPont reveals this clearly where raw ROE comparison misleads.
formulas.sensitivity_note: DuPont decomposition is the most useful tool for understanding WHY two companies have different ROE. Without it, comparing ROE across leverage-different companies is analytically meaningless.

formulas.name: ROIC vs WACC — The Value Creation Test
formulas.formula:
Value Creation = (ROIC − WACC) × Invested Capital
ROIC = NOPAT / Invested Capital
NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − Effective Tax Rate)
WACC = [E/(E+D)] × Cost of Equity + [D/(E+D)] × Cost of Debt × (1 − Tax)

variables.meaning: Net Operating Profit After Tax — operating profit adjusted for tax, excluding interest effects
Equity + Interest-bearing Debt − Excess Cash. Represents the capital actually invested in operations.
The blended cost of capital — typically 11-13% for Indian corporates

formulas.worked_example:
TCS FY24 Value Creation Analysis:
EBIT: ₹55,000 cr
Effective Tax Rate: 25.17%
NOPAT = 55,000 × (1 − 0.2517) = ₹41,157 cr
Equity: ₹98,340 cr
Debt: ₹3,750 cr
Excess Cash: ~₹35,000 cr (TCS is cash-rich)
Invested Capital = 98,340 + 3,750 − 35,000 = ₹67,090 cr
ROIC = 41,157 / 67,090 = 61.3%

WACC for TCS (assume): ~10% (low-risk cash-rich services business)

Value Creation Spread: ROIC − WACC = 61.3% − 10.0% = 51.3 percentage points

Interpretation: TCS earns 51 percentage points above its cost of capital. Over a year, this represents (51.3% × 67,090 cr) = ₹34,400 cr of economic value added. This is why TCS trades at premium multiples — the compounding of 51% spread over WACC creates enormous long-term shareholder value.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Value creation is fundamentally about the spread (ROIC − WACC), not the absolute ROIC. A company earning 15% ROIC vs 12% WACC (3 pp spread) creates more value than a company earning 25% ROIC vs 30% WACC (−5 pp spread). The spread times Invested Capital = economic value added annually.

title: The Budget Math Every Analyst Must Know

formulas.name: Fiscal Deficit Calculation
formulas.formula: Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure - (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts)

variables.meaning: Sum of revenue expenditure and capital expenditure
Tax revenue + non-tax revenue (dividends, fees, interest receipts)
Disinvestment proceeds, recovery of loans (excludes borrowings)

formulas.worked_example:
FY25 Budget Estimates (₹ lakh crore):
Total Expenditure = 48.21
Revenue Receipts = 31.30 (Tax: 25.83, Non-tax: 5.47)
Non-debt Capital Receipts = 0.78 (Disinvestment 0.50, Loan recovery 0.28)

Fiscal Deficit = 48.21 - (31.30 + 0.78) = 48.21 - 32.08 = ₹16.13 lakh crore

Fiscal Deficit % of GDP = 16.13 / 326.4 (nominal GDP) × 100 = 4.94% ≈ 4.9% (matches BE)

This is the lowest fiscal deficit ratio since FY15, signaling the government is committed to its glide path toward 3% over time.
formulas.sensitivity_note: A 50 bps fiscal deficit slippage (from 4.9% to 5.4% of GDP) would represent ₹1.6 lakh crore of additional borrowing. This typically pushes 10Y G-Sec yields up 15-25 bps and weakens INR by 50-80 paise. Equity multiples compress 1-2% across the board.

formulas.name: Capital Expenditure Multiplier
formulas.formula: GDP Impact = Capex Spending × Multiplier

variables.meaning: Government''s capital expenditure that creates assets
How much GDP increases per rupee of capex. Empirical estimates: 2.5x-3.5x for Indian capex over 2-3 years

formulas.worked_example:
FY25 Budget Capex = ₹11.11 lakh crore (an 11% increase from FY24 RE)

Incremental capex YoY = ₹11.11 - 10.00 = ₹1.11 lakh crore additional capex

GDP Impact (over 2-3 years) = ₹1.11 × 3.0 multiplier = ₹3.33 lakh crore additional GDP

As % of GDP = 3.33 / 326.4 × 100 = 1.02% additional GDP growth

This means the FY25 capex push alone could add 30-40 bps to annual GDP growth over 2-3 years, before accounting for crowding-in of private investment.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Capex multipliers vary significantly by type. Infrastructure capex (roads, railways, ports) has the highest multiplier of 3-3.5x. Defence and PSU equity have lower multipliers of 1.5-2x. Quality of capex matters — productive capex compounds; unproductive capex (vanity projects) does not.

formulas.name: Tax Revenue Buoyancy
formulas.formula: Tax Buoyancy = (% Change in Tax Revenue) / (% Change in Nominal GDP)

variables.meaning: Year-on-year growth in total tax collections
Year-on-year growth in nominal GDP

formulas.worked_example:
FY24 → FY25 (Budget Estimates):
Tax Revenue: ₹23.30 lakh crore → ₹25.83 lakh crore (10.85% growth)
Nominal GDP: ₹295 → ₹326.4 lakh crore (10.66% growth)

Tax Buoyancy = 10.85 / 10.66 = 1.018

A buoyancy of 1.0 means tax revenues grow at the same rate as the economy. Above 1.0 means tax revenues are outgrowing GDP (tax base widening). Below 1.0 means tax base shrinking relative to GDP.

India has historically aimed for buoyancy above 1.0, with formalisation, GST integration, and digital tracking driving structural improvement. FY25 buoyancy near 1.0 is healthy but not aggressive.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Tax buoyancy is a direct measure of fiscal health and tax administration efficiency. Buoyancy below 0.9 for 2+ years signals fiscal stress (revenue not keeping pace). Buoyancy above 1.2 sustained signals exceptional formalisation/digitisation gains.

formulas.name: Government Borrowing Impact on Yields
formulas.formula: Δ 10Y G-Sec Yield (bps) ≈ -1.5 × (Δ Net Borrowing / Demand) + Term Premium Adjustment

variables.meaning: Change in net market borrowing vs prior year (in ₹ lakh crore)
Captive demand from banks (SLR), insurance (regulatory holdings), pension funds. Roughly ₹15-18 lakh crore annually in absorptive capacity
Compensation for inflation/policy uncertainty

formulas.worked_example:
FY25 Net Borrowing: ₹11.63 lakh crore (vs FY24 RE: ₹11.05 lakh crore)
Increase YoY: +₹0.58 lakh crore (modest)

Demand absorption capacity: ~₹16 lakh crore annually
Net borrowing as % of demand: 11.63 / 16 × 100 = 73%
This is well within demand capacity, hence yields stable

If instead borrowing had jumped to ₹14 lakh crore (an 87% absorption ratio approaching capacity limits), we''d expect 25-40 bps yield rise.

FY24 Budget reaction: Markets actually rallied because borrowing came in lower than feared, a positive surprise vs market expectations of higher numbers.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Markets react to surprise vs expectations, not absolute levels. If borrowing is announced ₹50,000 crore higher than economist consensus, yields can spike 10-20 bps even in absolute terms. Track the surprise component, not just absolute borrowing.

formulas.name: Sector EPS Impact from Specific Capex Allocation
formulas.formula: Sector EPS Uplift = (Allocated Capex × Capture Rate) / Sector Aggregate PAT × Sector Margin × Asset Turnover

variables.meaning: Government''s allocation to a specific sector
% of capex flowing to listed companies (vs unlisted/PSU/imports)
Combined net profit of listed companies in the sector
Net profit margin of listed companies in the sector
Revenue / Assets ratio for the sector

formulas.worked_example:
Railway Sector Example (FY25 Budget):
Railway Capex Allocation = ₹2.55 lakh crore
Capture Rate (listed cos. like RVNL, IRCON, KEC) = 25% = ₹63,750 crore
Sector Aggregate Revenue (listed railway co''s) = ₹85,000 crore
Sector Margin = 8% (railway capex companies blended)
Incremental Revenue = ₹63,750 crore
Incremental Net Profit = ₹63,750 × 8% = ₹5,100 crore

Sector Aggregate PAT (current) = ₹6,500 crore
Incremental PAT % = 5,100 / 6,500 = 78% theoretical uplift over 2-3 years

In practice, capture rates and execution lags reduce this. Realistic expectation: 25-35% sector PAT uplift over 2-3 years from railway capex allocation. This is why railway stocks (RVNL, IRCON) re-rated 5-10x in 2023-24.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Capture rates are critical and often overestimated. PSU-heavy sectors (railways) have low capture rates because most spending stays internal. Private-heavy sectors (capital goods like L&T) have higher capture. Always check the listed-company capture ratio for any sector before sizing the trade.

title: The Banking Analyst's Formula Toolkit — Every Calculation You Need

formulas.name: Net Interest Margin (NIM)
formulas.formula: NIM = Net Interest Income / Average Interest-Earning Assets

variables.meaning: Interest earned on loans, investments, and cash, minus interest paid on deposits and borrowings (annual figure)
Average of opening and closing balance of advances + investments + cash with RBI + interbank loans (excluding fixed assets and non-earning items)

formulas.worked_example: HDFC Bank FY24: NII = 1,08,532 crore. Average Interest-Earning Assets = roughly 26,00,000 crore (averaging FY23 close and FY24 close). NIM = 1,08,532 / 26,00,000 = 4.18%. Compare to SBI FY24: NII = 1,59,876 crore. Average Interest-Earning Assets = roughly 51,80,000 crore. NIM = 1,59,876 / 51,80,000 = 3.09%. The 109 basis point gap (4.18% vs 3.09%) is the single biggest reason HDFC Bank trades at 2.7x P/BV while SBI trades at 1.5x P/BV — higher NIM mechanically translates to higher RoA, higher RoE, and higher multiple.
formulas.sensitivity_note: NIM is highly sensitive to interest rate cycles. When RBI raises rates, banks with high CASA see NIM expand because deposit costs rise slowly while loan yields rise quickly. When rates fall, the dynamic reverses. NIM also depends on asset mix — retail unsecured loans (credit cards, personal loans) yield 14-18% while large corporate loans yield 8-9%. A bank shifting toward retail expands NIM structurally. Always look at NIM trend over 4-8 quarters, not just point-in-time.

formulas.name: Slippage Ratio (Annualised)
formulas.formula: Slippage Ratio = (Fresh Slippages during the period × 4) / Opening Standard Advances

variables.meaning: Loans that became NPA during the quarter (disclosed in concall and investor presentation). Quarterly figure; multiply by 4 for annualised view
Total advances at start of period MINUS opening GNPA (i.e., the loan book that was still standard at the start)

formulas.worked_example: Bank ABC Q4FY24 disclosure: Fresh slippages = 800 crore. Opening standard advances = 4,00,000 crore. Quarterly slippage ratio = 800/4,00,000 = 0.2%. Annualised = 0.2% × 4 = 0.8%. This is excellent — well below the 1.5% threshold for healthy banks. Compare to Yes Bank FY19: Fresh slippages of around 25,000 crore against opening standard advances of around 2,40,000 crore. Annual slippage ratio = 25,000/2,40,000 = 10.4%. This was a flashing red signal a full year before the moratorium — slippage at 10% means roughly 10% of the loan book is going bad each year, which is mathematically incompatible with bank survival.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Slippage is the leading indicator. GNPA is the lagging indicator. If you wait for GNPA to spike before forming a view, you are 6-9 months behind the curve. Track slippage every quarter from concall transcripts and investor presentations. A bank with stable 1% slippage for 8 consecutive quarters is structurally clean; a bank where slippage rises from 1.5% to 3% to 5% across 3 quarters is in early-stage stress regardless of headline GNPA.

formulas.name: Return on Assets (RoA) and Return on Equity (RoE) Decomposition
formulas.formula: RoA = Net Profit / Average Total Assets    |    RoE = RoA × Leverage    |    Leverage = Average Total Assets / Average Equity

variables.meaning: Universal banking profitability metric — comparable across banks regardless of size
Times equity multiplied. Indian banks operate at 8-12x leverage typically (regulatory limits via Capital Adequacy Ratio)
Shareholder return metric. RoE = RoA × Leverage. A bank improving RoE through higher leverage (vs higher RoA) is increasing risk, not improving fundamentals

formulas.worked_example: HDFC Bank FY24: Net Profit = 60,812 crore. Average Total Assets = approximately 32,00,000 crore. Average Equity = approximately 3,50,000 crore. RoA = 60,812/32,00,000 = 1.90%. Leverage = 32,00,000/3,50,000 = 9.14x. RoE = 1.90% × 9.14 = 17.4%. Compare to SBI FY24: Net Profit = 61,077 crore. Average Total Assets = approximately 60,00,000 crore. Average Equity = approximately 3,50,000 crore (similar absolute equity to HDFC despite being twice the size). RoA = 61,077/60,00,000 = 1.02%. Leverage = 60,00,000/3,50,000 = 17.1x. RoE = 1.02% × 17.1 = 17.5%. Same RoE, very different quality. HDFC achieves it through high RoA and conservative leverage; SBI achieves it through low RoA and high leverage. The HDFC profile is structurally safer and supports higher P/BV multiples.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Always decompose RoE into RoA × Leverage. Two banks with identical 17% RoE can have completely different risk profiles. The bank with 2% RoA and 8.5x leverage is much safer than the bank with 0.7% RoA and 24x leverage, even though headline RoE is the same. Yes Bank in 2018 reported RoE of 17% — but RoA was 1.6% and leverage was 10.6x. The RoE looked fine; the breakdown showed nothing alarming. The actual problem was hidden in slippage and NNPA, not in RoE decomposition. This is why no single metric works — you need the four pillars together.

formulas.name: Price-to-Book Value (P/BV) — The Primary Banking Multiple
formulas.formula: P/BV = Market Cap / Book Value of Equity   OR   Per share: Stock Price / Book Value Per Share

variables.meaning: Net worth from balance sheet — share capital + reserves and surplus. Excludes intangibles for adjusted book value if needed
Book value minus net NPAs (NNPA) and minus any unrecognised stress (restructured loans, SMA-2 accounts). Used for stressed banks where reported book overstates economic value

formulas.worked_example: HDFC Bank Jan 2025: Stock price approximately 1,650. Book Value Per Share approximately 615. P/BV = 1,650/615 = 2.7x. SBI Jan 2025: Stock price approximately 770. Book Value Per Share approximately 510. P/BV = 770/510 = 1.5x. ICICI Bank Jan 2025: P/BV approximately 3.0x. Bandhan Bank Jan 2025: P/BV approximately 1.2x. Indian private banks historically range 2.0-4.0x P/BV; PSU banks historically range 0.7-1.8x. The wide range exists because P/BV directly reflects expected RoE — a bank with 18% sustainable RoE deserves a higher P/BV than a bank with 12%, mathematically. Rule of thumb: justified P/BV ≈ (RoE − Cost of Equity) / (Cost of Equity − Growth) — the Gordon growth model applied to banks.
formulas.sensitivity_note: P/BV is the primary multiple but use it with care. For banks with deteriorating asset quality, ALWAYS calculate adjusted book value by subtracting NNPA and any obviously under-provisioned exposures. Yes Bank in 2019 traded at 0.8x reported P/BV which looked cheap, but adjusted P/BV after writing down stressed loans was 1.5-2x — actually expensive. Always cross-check P/BV against RoE — a bank trading at 2x P/BV with 12% RoE is expensive; the same bank at 2x with 18% RoE is reasonable. The justified P/BV must align with the sustainable RoE.

title: The Cash Flow Formula Arsenal

formulas.name: OCF / Net Profit Ratio
formulas.formula: OCF / Net Profit Ratio = Operating Cash Flow / Net Profit

variables.meaning: Cash from operations, reported on the cash flow statement
Profit after tax attributable to shareholders, reported on the income statement

formulas.worked_example: HUL FY23: OCF = ₹10,400 Cr, Net Profit = ₹9,962 Cr. OCF/NP = 10,400/9,962 = 1.04x or 104%. Exceptional earnings quality — every rupee of reported profit converts to slightly more than a rupee of cash. Classic signature of a high-quality consumer staple. Compare Asian Paints FY23: OCF ≈ ₹5,200 Cr, Net Profit = ₹4,106 Cr. OCF/NP = 126%. Even better — Asian Paints generates 26% more cash than it reports as profit due to negative working capital dynamics. Now contrast with a stressed mid-cap: OCF = ₹140 Cr, Net Profit = ₹350 Cr. OCF/NP = 40%. Only 40% of reported profit is cash-backed — the rest sits in receivables, inventory, or elsewhere on the balance sheet. This is the earnings quality warning that no margin analysis would reveal.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The benchmark is multi-year average, not single year. A high-quality business maintains OCF/NP of 90-110% over 5 years. Single-year aberrations can happen from working capital swings or one-off items. Multi-year patterns reveal the truth. Any business with OCF/NP consistently below 70% across 3 consecutive years should be treated as having suspect earnings quality until proven otherwise.

formulas.name: Free Cash Flow (FCF)
formulas.formula: Free Cash Flow = Operating Cash Flow - Capital Expenditure

variables.meaning: OCF from cash flow statement
Cash spent on acquiring or upgrading property, plant, equipment, intangibles

formulas.worked_example: TCS FY23: OCF = ₹42,500 Cr, Capex = ₹2,200 Cr. FCF = 42,500 - 2,200 = ₹40,300 Cr. An extraordinary FCF profile — TCS generates ₹40,300 crore of completely unrestricted cash annually, which it uses for buybacks, dividends, and strategic investments. Compare to a capital-intensive business like a power utility: OCF = ₹5,000 Cr, Capex = ₹4,200 Cr. FCF = ₹800 Cr. The business generates cash but most of it goes back into the asset base — leaving only ₹800 Cr for shareholders and debt service. Same revenue scale, radically different FCF profiles due to capex intensity.
formulas.sensitivity_note: FCF can be split into 'maintenance capex' (required to keep the business running) and 'growth capex' (optional, for expansion). Sophisticated analysts estimate maintenance FCF separately — this is the 'truly' free cash flow available after essential reinvestment, even if growth is paused. For the TCS example, maintenance capex might be ₹1,500 Cr vs total capex of ₹2,200 Cr, making maintenance FCF = ₹41,000 Cr.

formulas.name: Cash Conversion Ratio
formulas.formula: Cash Conversion Ratio = Free Cash Flow / Net Profit

variables.meaning: OCF - Capex
Reported net profit attributable to shareholders

formulas.worked_example: HUL FY23: FCF = ₹9,100 Cr (OCF 10,400 - Capex 1,300), Net Profit = ₹9,962 Cr. Cash Conversion = 9,100/9,962 = 91%. Strong cash conversion typical of FMCG. Asian Paints FY23: FCF = ₹4,600 Cr, Net Profit = ₹4,106 Cr. Cash Conversion = 112%. The golden signature — FCF exceeding net profit, showing that accounting earnings understate true cash-generating capacity. Compare a capex-heavy business: FCF = ₹300 Cr, Net Profit = ₹1,500 Cr. Cash Conversion = 20%. The business reports ₹1,500 Cr of profit but only ₹300 Cr is truly free — most earnings are consumed by ongoing capex.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Cash Conversion above 80% for 5+ years is the signature of genuinely high-quality compounders. Below 40% consistently indicates capex-heavy or capital-destructive businesses. Use the 5-year rolling average to smooth out investment cycles.

formulas.name: FCF Yield
formulas.formula: FCF Yield = Free Cash Flow / Market Cap (or FCF / Enterprise Value for leverage-adjusted view)

variables.meaning: OCF - Capex for the most recent 12 months
Current market value of equity

formulas.worked_example: TCS FY23: FCF = ₹40,300 Cr, Market Cap = ₹13,80,000 Cr. FCF Yield = 40,300/13,80,000 = 2.9%. Low absolute yield reflecting premium valuation, but stable and growing. HDFC Bank (adjusting for financial services): Net Income + Non-cash adjustments, FCF ≈ ₹45,000 Cr, Market Cap ₹8,70,000 Cr. FCF Yield ≈ 5.2%. Higher yield on a more cyclical business. A mid-cap manufacturing business: FCF = ₹800 Cr, Market Cap = ₹8,000 Cr. FCF Yield = 10%. High yield — often a value opportunity if the business quality is intact. Global benchmark: Indian large-caps typically 2-6% FCF Yield; global mature value stocks 6-10%; high-growth tech 1-3%.
formulas.sensitivity_note: FCF Yield is the cash-based equivalent of earnings yield (inverse of P/E). It's generally more reliable for valuation because cash is less manipulable than earnings. A business with both attractive FCF Yield and growing FCF is often the best long-term investment — high current yield plus compounding.

formulas.name: Capex Intensity
formulas.formula: Capex Intensity = Capital Expenditure / Revenue

variables.meaning: Annual capex from cash flow statement
Net sales for the same period

formulas.worked_example: HUL FY23: Capex = ₹1,300 Cr, Revenue = ₹58,154 Cr. Capex Intensity = 2.2%. Extremely low — FMCG is asset-light, most cash reinvested in brand marketing rather than plants. NTPC FY23: Capex ≈ ₹22,000 Cr, Revenue ≈ ₹1,75,000 Cr. Capex Intensity = 12.6%. Power sector is intensely capex-heavy because every megawatt of capacity needs hundreds of crores. L&T FY23: Capex ≈ ₹8,000 Cr, Revenue ≈ ₹1,84,000 Cr. Capex Intensity = 4.3%. Capital goods are moderate capex — own facilities plus project equipment. Industry benchmarks: FMCG/IT 2-4%, Auto 4-6%, Capital Goods 4-6%, Cement 6-10%, Power/Utilities 10-15%+.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Capex Intensity should be viewed as rolling 3-5 year average to smooth investment cycles. A company with 3% capex in FY22 but 8% in FY23 may be mid-capex cycle, not permanently changed. Consistent high capex intensity limits FCF generation and caps shareholder returns over time.

title: The IT Analyst's Calculation Toolkit — From Constant Currency to Margin Walk

formulas.name: USD Revenue Growth in Constant Currency
formulas.formula: CC Growth = ((Current Period USD Revenue × Prior Period FX Rates) / Prior Period USD Revenue) − 1

variables.meaning: Reported revenue for the current quarter or year, restated using prior period exchange rates for non-USD billings (EUR, GBP, AUD, etc.)
Exchange rates that prevailed during the same period one year ago — used to neutralise cross-currency movement
The difference between reported USD growth and constant currency growth. Positive when USD weakened against EUR/GBP; negative when USD strengthened

formulas.worked_example: Infosys Q4FY24: Reported USD revenue 4,564 million USD, up 1.3% YoY in reported USD. However, the EUR strengthened roughly 2% against USD over the year, and the company derives roughly 25% of revenue from European billings. Cross-currency tailwind = approximately 0.5%. Therefore, Constant Currency Growth = 1.3% − 0.5% = 0.8% YoY. This is the genuine operating growth — the rest was cross-currency movement. Compare to TCS Q4FY24: Reported USD revenue 7,196 million USD, up 3.5% YoY reported USD, up 2.2% YoY in constant currency. Always use CC growth for true comparison — reported USD numbers can be misleading when EUR or GBP moves significantly. The five tier-1 Indian IT companies (TCS, Infosys, HCL Tech, Wipro, LTIMindtree) all disclose CC growth in their investor presentations and concall.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Constant currency growth is the single most important number in any IT services concall. When EUR/USD moved from 1.05 to 1.10 over FY24, it added roughly 50-70 basis points of cross-currency tailwind to reported USD growth for European-exposed Indian IT companies. The opposite happens when USD strengthens. The market consistently rewards companies that explain CC growth clearly and punishes those that hide behind reported numbers. As an analyst, always normalise your peer comparison to CC.

formulas.name: Book-to-Bill Ratio (TTM)
formulas.formula: Book-to-Bill (TTM) = TTM Total Contract Value Signed / TTM Revenue Recognised

variables.meaning: Sum of total contract values for new and renewed contracts won over the trailing twelve months. Disclosed by some companies (HCL Tech, LTIMindtree); estimated from quarterly disclosures for others
Total revenue recognised over the trailing twelve months — the denominator that contextualises whether new wins are growing relative to the existing run-rate

formulas.worked_example: HCL Tech Q1FY25 disclosure: TTM TCV signed = 9,500 million USD. TTM Revenue = 13,700 million USD. Book-to-Bill = 9,500 / 13,700 = 0.69x. This is below the historical healthy threshold of 0.9-1.1x. Interpretation: HCL Tech is winning new business but not at a pace fast enough to support continued strong growth — a leading indicator of growth deceleration in subsequent quarters. Compare to Infosys: TTM TCV approximately 17,300 million USD, TTM Revenue approximately 18,600 million USD, Book-to-Bill = 0.93x — closer to the healthy zone. Tier-1 IT companies typically disclose 'Large Deal TCV' (deals above 50 million USD) which is the most-watched subset. A Book-to-Bill of 1.0x or above for two consecutive quarters is a positive growth signal; below 0.8x for two consecutive quarters is a negative growth signal.
formulas.sensitivity_note: TCV is a leading indicator with a 6-12 month conversion lag — most contracts win-to-revenue takes 2-3 quarters before showing up in the P&L. So a strong TCV quarter today predicts strong revenue 6-12 months out. Conversely, a weak TCV quarter does NOT immediately hurt revenue (existing contracts continue running off) but it forecasts revenue weakness 2-3 quarters later. This is why TCV trends often diverge from current revenue trends. Read both in tandem.

formulas.name: Margin Walk Decomposition
formulas.formula: ΔEBIT Margin = ΔUtilisation + ΔPyramid + ΔPricing + ΔCurrency + ΔSG&A leverage + ΔSub-contractor costs + Other

variables.meaning: Change in billable utilisation. Each 1% of utilisation typically adds/removes ~25-30 bps to EBIT margin
Shift in junior:senior mix. Junior-heavy expansion is margin-accretive (lower fully-loaded cost per billable hour)
Change in realised hourly billing rate. Strong demand allows price hikes; weak demand forces concessions
Net impact of forex on rupee-denominated costs vs USD-denominated revenue. INR depreciation typically adds margin
Operating leverage on fixed costs as revenue scales. Each 5% revenue growth on flat SG&A adds ~30-40 bps margin
Costs of bench staff and external contractors brought in to fill capacity gaps. Higher sub-contractor mix is margin-dilutive

formulas.worked_example: TCS FY24 EBIT Margin = 24.6%, FY23 EBIT Margin = 24.1% — a 50 basis point expansion. Margin walk decomposition disclosed in concall: Utilisation +60 bps (driven by tighter bench management), Pyramid -20 bps (slight senior skew due to wage hikes), Currency +40 bps (INR depreciation against USD), Sub-contractor costs +30 bps (reduced sub-contractor reliance), Pricing -50 bps (some discounting on renewals), SG&A leverage -10 bps. Sum = 60-20+40+30-50-10 = +50 bps — matches the actual margin expansion. The walk reveals what is driving margin and whether the drivers are sustainable. Currency and pyramid mix shifts are usually one-time; pricing and sub-contractor mix can be repeated.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The margin walk is the most useful diagnostic tool in IT services analysis. Analysts who memorise margin numbers without decomposing them into drivers miss the underlying story. A 50 bps margin expansion can be 'good' (utilisation, leverage, pricing) or 'cosmetic' (one-time currency tailwind that will reverse). Always read the margin walk in concall slides and ask: which drivers are repeatable next quarter, and which are not?

title: The Four Driver Frameworks — Formulas You Will Use for Every Company You Ever Model

formulas.name: Framework 1 — Store-Based (Retail)
formulas.formula: Revenue = Store_Count × Revenue_per_Store × (1 + SSSG)

variables.meaning: Total operational stores at the END of the forecast period (not opening). Forecast via: Opening Stores + Net Adds. Net Adds = Gross Adds − Closures.
Average annual revenue per store — serves as the base to which SSSG is applied. Note: this should be average across the base that existed in the prior year, not mixed.
Same-Store-Sales Growth — the year-on-year growth of stores that existed in BOTH years. Disclosed by most Indian retailers in investor presentations and concalls.

formulas.worked_example: Titan Jewellery FY25E forecast. FY24 Actual: 2,450 stores, Jewellery revenue ₹41,280 cr → Revenue per store ≈ ₹16.85 cr. Management guidance: 175 net store adds in FY25, with 8% SSSG. FY25E Store Count = 2,450 + 175 = 2,625. FY25E Revenue = 2,625 × 16.85 × 1.08 = ₹47,772 cr. Growth rate = 47,772/41,280 − 1 = 15.7%. Decomposing: store count growth contributes 7.1% (175/2,450), SSSG contributes 8.0%, slight mix effect contributes the rest. Any investor can challenge 'are you sure about 8% SSSG?' and you can respond with concall guidance or peer benchmarks. That is defensibility.
formulas.sensitivity_note: SSSG is the most investor-scrutinised driver in Indian retail. A 100 bps miss on SSSG (8% assumed vs 7% actual) directly reduces revenue by ~1% in that year. For companies where margins are sensitive to fixed-cost leverage (most retailers), a 1% revenue miss can translate to a 3-5% EBITDA miss. In Session 12's DCF, a persistent 100 bps SSSG cut can remove 8-12% from target price for retail names.

formulas.name: Framework 2 — Volume-Price (Manufacturing, Commodities, Autos)
formulas.formula: Revenue = Volume_Units × Average_Realisation_per_Unit

variables.meaning: Physical units sold — cars, tonnes of steel, smartphones, etc. Forecasted via capacity × utilisation × sales efficiency.
Price per unit AFTER discounts, rebates, and returns. For companies with product mix, this is a weighted average — low-end ASP × share + high-end ASP × share.

formulas.worked_example: Maruti Suzuki FY25E forecast. FY24 Actual: 2.14 million units sold, average realisation ₹5.25 lakh/unit, revenue ₹1,12,430 cr. Management guidance: 8% volume growth (export push + domestic SUV expansion), 2% realisation growth (mix shift toward Brezza/Grand Vitara + price hike pass-through). FY25E Volume = 2.14 × 1.08 = 2.31 million units. FY25E Realisation = 5.25 × 1.02 = ₹5.36 lakh. FY25E Revenue = 2.31 × 5.36 × 10^5/10^7 = ₹1,23,720 cr. Growth = 10.0% (1.08 × 1.02 = 1.1016). Now I can argue: 'I'm forecasting 8% volume based on Suzuki's Manesar capacity expansion coming online Q2 FY25, plus the Kharkhoda plant adding 250,000 units annualised. Realisation growth of 2% reflects a 300 bps shift in mix toward SUVs, which have 18% higher ASP than compacts.' That is a concrete forecast.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For cyclicals (autos, metals, cement), realisation is often the dominant driver. A 5% price hike drops straight to the top line with no additional cost — a pure margin gain. Understanding whether a revenue forecast is volume-led or price-led is critical because price-led revenue growth often compresses margins on the next cycle turn. Always decompose and communicate the split.

formulas.name: Framework 3 — Unit Economics (Internet, Platforms, Fintech)
formulas.formula: Revenue = MTU × Orders_per_MTU × Average_Order_Value × Take_Rate

variables.meaning: Monthly Transacting Users — users who placed at least one paid transaction in the month. Sometimes disclosed as MAU (Monthly Active Users) — MTU is a stricter, more monetisable definition.
Frequency of ordering — how many orders an average MTU places per month. Drives engagement economics.
The average spend per order in rupees. Includes mix of delivery fees, discounts netted, service fees.
The percentage of Gross Order Value (GOV) that the platform keeps as revenue. For food delivery typically 20-25%; for quick commerce higher; for marketplace lower.

formulas.worked_example: Zomato Food Delivery FY25E. FY24 Actual: 18.5 million MTUs, 3.7 orders/MTU/month, ₹430 AOV, 21% take rate. GOV = 18.5 × 3.7 × 12 × 430 / 10^4 = ₹35,305 cr. Revenue = 35,305 × 21% = ₹7,414 cr. FY25E assumptions: MTU grows 12% to 20.7 million (disciplined customer acquisition), Orders/MTU flat at 3.7 (engagement mature), AOV grows 5% to ₹451 (menu premiumisation), Take Rate expands to 22% (platform fee scaling). FY25E Revenue = 20.7 × 3.7 × 12 × 451 × 22% / 10^4 = ₹9,110 cr. Growth of 22.9% — but now I can defend each component: MTU growth is disciplined, AOV growth is premiumisation, take rate expansion reflects platform fee strategy.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The Unit Economics framework is extremely powerful because it reveals which driver is the 'LEVER' vs which is saturating. For mature internet businesses, MTU growth is typically slowing (single-digit) but AOV and take rate still have runway. Distinguishing 'growth from volume' from 'growth from monetisation' is how PMs assess sustainability. Zomato bulls argue take rate has 400 bps more room; bears argue MTU saturation kills the flywheel.

formulas.name: Framework 4 — Utilisation-Billing (IT Services, Professional Services)
formulas.formula: Revenue = Employees × Utilisation × Billing_Rate_per_Hour × Annual_Hours

variables.meaning: Billable headcount (excludes support, admin, bench). For IT services, disclosed as 'software professionals' or 'delivery headcount.'
Percentage of billable hours actually billed. For Indian IT majors typically 82-87%. Key operational metric.
Realised rate per billable hour, after discounts. Driven by onsite/offshore mix, digital mix, and geographical mix.
Standard working hours per year — typically 2,080 (52 weeks × 40 hours) minus leave/holidays, so effective ~2,000.

formulas.worked_example: Infosys FY25E. FY24 Actual: 317,000 employees (of which ~250,000 billable), 83.5% utilisation, ~$32.50 effective billing rate, revenue $18.6 bn. Check: 250,000 × 83.5% × 32.5 × 2000 = $13.6 bn — but this is on a pure hourly basis; Infosys also has fixed-price projects that distort the pure formula. In practice, the framework is: Headcount × Revenue per Employee. FY24 Revenue per employee = $18.6 bn / 317K = $58,700. FY25E: Headcount growth slows to 3% (317K → 327K), but revenue per employee grows 4% (pricing + vertical mix shift). FY25E Revenue = 327K × $58,700 × 1.04 / 10^9 = $20.0 bn. Implied growth: 7.5%. Defensibility: 'I'm assuming modest headcount growth because hiring has slowed industry-wide; revenue per employee growth of 4% reflects improved utilisation (~100 bps) plus digital mix improving realisation.'
formulas.sensitivity_note: For IT services, the pure utilisation-billing framework often breaks down because of fixed-price deals and managed services. A simpler and more common framework is 'Revenue per Employee × Headcount.' Revenue per Employee is the composite KPI that captures utilisation, billing rate, and mix — all in one number. Track it over 5 years and forecast its trajectory — that's Motilal Oswal's, Kotak's, and Nomura's standard approach for IT coverage.

title: The Accrual Adjustment Equations

formulas.name: Revenue Recognition Under Accrual
formulas.formula: Revenue Recognised = Goods/Services Delivered × Price (regardless of cash received)

variables.meaning: The unit of value transferred to the customer in the period
The agreed sale price

formulas.worked_example: TCS signs a 3-year IT contract worth ₹120 Cr in April 2024. Cash will be received in 36 equal monthly instalments of ₹3.33 Cr. In FY24 income statement (April-March), TCS recognises revenue ONLY for the months work is delivered — not the full ₹120 Cr. If 12 months of services are delivered in FY24, revenue recognised = ₹40 Cr (12 × ₹3.33 Cr). The remaining ₹80 Cr stays on the balance sheet as Deferred Revenue or Unearned Revenue (a liability) until services are delivered.
formulas.sensitivity_note: If you confuse cash received (₹40 Cr in year 1) with revenue recognised (₹40 Cr in year 1), you might get the answer right — but if the contract had upfront billing of ₹120 Cr, cash would be ₹120 Cr while revenue is still only ₹40 Cr. Always check timing of delivery vs. billing.

formulas.name: Matching Principle for Expenses
formulas.formula: Expense for the Period = Cost of Resources Consumed in Generating That Period's Revenue

variables.meaning: Materials, labour, depreciation, rent, and other inputs used to produce this period's output

formulas.worked_example: Britannia buys ₹100 Cr of wheat flour in March 2024. By March 31, only ₹70 Cr of flour has been used to make biscuits that were sold. The remaining ₹30 Cr sits in the warehouse. Under matching, only ₹70 Cr is recorded as Cost of Goods Sold (expense) for FY24. The ₹30 Cr stays on the balance sheet as Inventory (asset) and becomes an expense only when those biscuits are eventually sold.
formulas.sensitivity_note: When sales drop suddenly, inventory swells on the balance sheet. If a company expenses everything immediately (violating matching), profit looks volatile. If it incorrectly capitalises consumed inventory, profit looks artificially smooth — a common red flag.

formulas.name: Cash-to-Accrual Reconciliation (Simplified)
formulas.formula: Net Profit (Accrual) = Cash from Operations − Increase in Receivables − Increase in Inventory + Increase in Payables + Non-Cash Expenses (Depreciation/Amortisation)

variables.meaning: Sales booked but not yet collected — reduces cash but not profit
Purchases not yet sold — reduces cash but not profit
Expenses booked but not yet paid — reduces profit but not cash
Non-cash expense — reduces profit but not cash

formulas.worked_example: Hypothetical mid-cap: Cash from Ops = ₹500 Cr. Receivables increased by ₹150 Cr. Inventory increased by ₹80 Cr. Payables increased by ₹60 Cr. Depreciation = ₹100 Cr. Working backward to derive Net Profit: Net Profit = ₹500 + ₹150 + ₹80 − ₹60 − ₹100 = ₹570 Cr. The point: profit and cash diverge by exactly the size of non-cash and working capital items. The bigger the gap, the more aggressive the accruals.
formulas.sensitivity_note: If receivables grow faster than revenue year after year, the company is recognising sales it cannot collect. This is the single most common forensic red flag in Indian small-caps — we will see it again in Module 8.
