title: Segment Metrics and Cross-Segment Comparisons

formulas.name: Segment EBITDA Margin
formulas.formula: Segment EBITDA Margin = Segment EBITDA / Segment Revenue × 100

variables.meaning: Segment operating profit (results) plus segment depreciation and amortisation. For companies that disclose segment EBITDA directly, use the disclosed figure. For those disclosing only EBIT, add back segment depreciation.
External revenue attributable to the segment. Exclude inter-segment revenue unless analysing vertical integration.

formulas.worked_example:
Reliance Industries FY24 Segment EBITDA Margins:
Oil-to-Chemicals: Revenue ₹5,61,500 cr | EBITDA ₹62,400 cr | Margin 11.1%
Jio (Digital Services): Revenue ₹1,19,800 cr | EBITDA ₹51,500 cr | Margin 43.0%
Retail: Revenue ₹3,06,500 cr | EBITDA ₹25,100 cr | Margin 8.2%
Oil & Gas: Revenue ₹24,200 cr | EBITDA ₹15,800 cr | Margin 65.3%

Insight: The four segments have wildly different margin profiles. Jio at 43% is telecom/platform economics. Retail at 8.2% is discount-retail economics (DMart-like thin margins, high turnover). Oil-to-Chemicals at 11.1% is commodity-cyclical economics. Oil & Gas at 65% is legacy upstream economics with depleting reserves. Consolidated EBITDA margin of ~16% is a meaningless average — it matches none of the underlying businesses.
formulas.sensitivity_note: A 100 bps margin shift in Jio (the highest-margin segment) moves consolidated EBITDA by approximately ₹1,200 cr. A 100 bps margin shift in Oil-to-Chemicals (largest revenue) moves consolidated EBITDA by approximately ₹5,600 cr. Analysts forecasting consolidated margins without segment context systematically err on both size and direction of margin movements.

formulas.name: Segment ROCE
formulas.formula: Segment ROCE = Segment EBIT / Segment Capital Employed

variables.meaning: Segment operating profit (results) before centrally-allocated costs. Some companies disclose segment PBT; for ROCE comparison, use EBIT (before centrally-allocated finance costs).

Segment Assets minus Segment Non-interest-bearing Liabilities. Or equivalently, Segment Equity plus allocated Debt. For many Indian companies, segment ROCE requires analyst-level estimation as full capital allocation isn't disclosed.

formulas.worked_example:
ITC Ltd FY24 Segment ROCE:
FMCG-Cigarettes: Capital Employed ₹11,500 cr | EBIT ₹21,800 cr | ROCE ≈ 190% (near-infinite due to low capital intensity of cigarette manufacturing)
FMCG-Others: Capital Employed ₹6,800 cr | EBIT ₹1,090 cr | ROCE ≈ 16% (scaling consumer business)
Hotels: Capital Employed ₹6,200 cr | EBITDA ~₹700 cr, EBIT ~₹400 cr | ROCE ≈ 6% (asset-heavy, cyclical)
Paperboards/Paper/Packaging: Capital Employed ₹9,800 cr | EBIT ₹1,850 cr | ROCE ≈ 19%
Agri: Capital Employed ₹4,500 cr | EBIT ₹820 cr | ROCE ≈ 18%

Insight: Cigarettes is the cash cow with absurd ROCE — it throws off capital that can be redeployed. Hotels, at 6% ROCE (below cost of capital ~11-12%), is a capital-destroying segment subsidised by cigarettes. This is ITC's capital allocation challenge — the conglomerate structure hides the fact that Hotels earns below cost of capital while Cigarettes earns far above. In a standalone company, Hotels would face pressure to either improve returns or be exited. Within ITC, it's been patient capital for decades.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Segment-level ROCE below cost of capital is value destructive even if EBITDA is positive. An ITC investor should mentally discount the Hotels segment to ~0.8-1.0x book value despite its earnings contribution, which changes the sum-of-parts valuation meaningfully.

formulas.name: Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) Valuation
formulas.formula: SOTP Enterprise Value = Σ (Segment EBITDA × Segment-appropriate EV/EBITDA multiple) + Centrally-held Net Cash (or minus Net Debt)

variables.meaning: Latest normalised EBITDA for each segment
EV/EBITDA multiple based on the segment's business model, growth, and risk profile. Not the consolidated multiple.
Cash and debt held at the corporate level not directly attributable to segments

formulas.worked_example:
ITC FY24 SOTP Valuation (illustrative, analyst estimates):
FMCG-Cigarettes: EBITDA ~₹22,200 cr × 17x (mature cash cow, regulatory headwinds) = ₹3,77,400 cr
FMCG-Others: EBITDA ~₹2,400 cr × 30x (scaling consumer growth) = ₹72,000 cr
Hotels: EBITDA ~₹700 cr × 20x (recovery cycle, premium brand) = ₹14,000 cr
Paperboards/Paper: EBITDA ~₹2,800 cr × 10x (cyclical industrial) = ₹28,000 cr
Agri: EBITDA ~₹1,100 cr × 12x (agri-related) = ₹13,200 cr
Add: Net Cash ~₹28,000 cr

SOTP Enterprise Value: 377,400 + 72,000 + 14,000 + 28,000 + 13,200 + 28,000 = ₹5,32,600 cr

At FY24 EBITDA, implied blended EV/EBITDA = ₹5,32,600 / ₹29,000 = 18.4x — versus the consolidated multiple the market may be applying. Analysts who value ITC as 'cigarettes company at cigarettes multiple' systematically under-value the scaling FMCG-Others and Hotels recovery opportunity. Analysts who apply single consolidated multiple miss the mix implications.
formulas.sensitivity_note: SOTP valuation is sensitive to segment-appropriate multiple assumptions. Changing FMCG-Others multiple from 30x to 25x reduces SOTP EV by ₹12,000 cr. Changing Cigarettes multiple from 17x to 15x reduces by ₹44,400 cr. Always present SOTP as a sensitivity range, not a point estimate, and disclose the multiple assumptions explicitly.

title: The Working Capital System Formulas

formulas.name: Working Capital
formulas.formula: Working Capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities

variables.meaning: Cash + Marketable Securities + Receivables + Inventory + Other Current Assets
Trade Payables + Short-term Debt + Current Portion of Long-term Debt + Accrued Expenses + Other Current Liabilities

formulas.worked_example: HUL FY23: Current Assets = ₹15,850 Cr (Cash ₹3,500 + Receivables ₹2,300 + Inventory ₹3,550 + Others ₹6,500). Current Liabilities = ₹19,200 Cr (Trade Payables ₹8,500 + Others ₹10,700). Working Capital = 15,850 - 19,200 = -₹3,350 Cr. Negative ₹3,350 crore. Contrast with L&T FY23: CA = ₹1,35,000 Cr, CL = ₹85,000 Cr. Working Capital = +₹50,000 Cr. Same country, same time period, radically different working capital structures — because of radically different business models (FMCG mass distribution vs project-based infrastructure EPC).
formulas.sensitivity_note: The headline number is only meaningful alongside composition analysis. HUL's -₹3,350 Cr is strategic strength (trade payables of ₹8,500 Cr to thousands of happy suppliers). A distressed company's -₹3,350 Cr could reflect stretched supplier payments, short-term debt building up, or accrued liabilities piling. Always decompose.

formulas.name: Operating Working Capital
formulas.formula: Operating Working Capital = Trade Receivables + Inventory - Trade Payables

variables.meaning: Amounts owed by customers for goods/services sold
Raw materials + Work-in-progress + Finished goods + Stock-in-trade
Amounts owed to suppliers — excludes debt, accruals, taxes

formulas.worked_example: DMart FY23: Trade Receivables ≈ ₹290 Cr, Inventory ≈ ₹2,850 Cr, Trade Payables ≈ ₹5,400 Cr. OWC = 290 + 2,850 - 5,400 = -₹2,260 Cr. Pure operational negative working capital — suppliers fund ₹2,260 crore of operations. No debt, no cash trickery — genuine supplier credit enabling the business to grow without external financing. This is the cleanest measure of working capital moat because it strips out cash hoarding and debt-related noise.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Always prefer Operating Working Capital over headline Working Capital for evaluating business quality. The OWC metric isolates how efficiently the business's operational cycle consumes or generates capital, independent of capital structure decisions. A company with huge cash holdings (Infosys, TCS) might show positive Working Capital purely from cash — but its OWC could be low or negative, revealing the true operational efficiency.

formulas.name: Working Capital Intensity
formulas.formula: Working Capital Intensity = Working Capital / Revenue (expressed as %)

variables.meaning: As defined above
Net sales for the period

formulas.worked_example: HUL FY23: WC = -₹3,350 Cr, Revenue = ₹58,154 Cr. WC Intensity = -3,350/58,154 = -5.8%. Meaning for every ₹100 of revenue, HUL has ₹5.8 of negative working capital — supplier-funded operations. Compare L&T FY23: WC = ₹50,000 Cr, Revenue = ₹1,84,000 Cr. WC Intensity = 27.2% — for every ₹100 of revenue, ₹27 is tied up in working capital. Infrastructure EPC requires massive working capital because projects take 2-3 years and payment cycles are long. Cross-industry comparison: FMCG typically -5% to -15%, IT services 15-25%, capital goods 25-40%, infrastructure 30-50%.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Watch the trend. A company's WC Intensity increasing from 15% to 25% over 3 years is a warning — the business is becoming more capital-intensive, often because of deteriorating cash collection or aggressive revenue recognition. Declining WC Intensity (becoming more negative for FMCG, or less positive for others) signals improving working capital management.

formulas.name: Incremental Working Capital
formulas.formula: Incremental WC = ΔWorking Capital / ΔRevenue

variables.meaning: Change in WC year-over-year (WC_Current - WC_Prior)
Change in Revenue year-over-year

formulas.worked_example: Company A grew revenue from ₹5,000 Cr to ₹6,000 Cr (ΔRevenue = ₹1,000 Cr). Working Capital went from ₹800 Cr to ₹1,000 Cr (ΔWC = ₹200 Cr). Incremental WC = 200/1,000 = 20%. Meaning for every additional ₹100 of revenue, the company needs an additional ₹20 of working capital. Now compare Company B which grew revenue from ₹5,000 Cr to ₹6,000 Cr but Working Capital jumped from ₹800 Cr to ₹1,350 Cr. Incremental WC = 550/1,000 = 55%. For every additional ₹100 of revenue, ₹55 of additional capital is consumed — meaning only ₹45 flows to shareholders. Company A is a scalable business; Company B is a capital-heavy growth trap.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Incremental WC is one of the most underrated metrics in Indian equity research. A company with low Incremental WC (below 15-20%) can grow profitably without external financing. A company with high Incremental WC (above 30%) needs debt or equity issuance to fund growth — diluting existing shareholders. Always compute Incremental WC over 3-5 years to spot deterioration patterns.

_session_title: Working Capital Analysis: The Hidden Health Metric

title: The Four Ratios That Quantify Ownership Behaviour Signals

formulas.name: Pledge Intensity Ratio
formulas.formula: Pledge Intensity = Shares Pledged by Promoters / Total Promoter Holding × 100

variables.meaning: Total promoter shares pledged to lenders as collateral, from BSE/NSE pledge disclosures
Total shares held by promoter group including all promoter entities

formulas.worked_example: Running this on Yes Bank across the 2018-2020 timeline. As of September 30, 2018: Pledged shares approximately 8 crore against total promoter holding of 24 crore = Pledge Intensity 33 percent. By December 31, 2018: approximately 15 crore pledged = 63 percent. By March 31, 2019: approximately 19 crore pledged = 79 percent. By September 30, 2019: approximately 22 crore pledged = 92 percent. By February 2020 (just before RBI moratorium): essentially 100 percent of remaining promoter holding pledged. Each quarterly data point was disclosed in BSE and NSE shareholding pattern filings. Any analyst monitoring pledge intensity would have observed the progression from 33 percent to 92 percent over 12 months — an unmistakable forensic signal of escalating promoter financial stress. Interpretation thresholds: Below 20 percent is normal and typically reflects standard promoter financing arrangements. 20-40 percent warrants investigation of the specific promoter financing structure and counterparties. 40-70 percent is high and indicates material promoter financial stress. Above 70 percent is extreme — the promoter has essentially leveraged his entire ownership stake and faces immediate forced-sale risk if stock price declines trigger margin calls. The Yes Bank progression from September 2018 to March 2020 crossed every threshold in the interpretation ladder over an 18-month period visible to any analyst. For mid-cap coverage, Pledge Intensity above 50 percent sustained for multiple quarters is typically a Sell signal. For large-cap coverage where promoters have diversified personal wealth, Pledge Intensity above 40 percent is the warning threshold because even diversified promoters face financial constraints at this level.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Pledge Intensity should be analysed alongside absolute promoter holding percentage. A promoter with 55 percent holding who pledges 40 percent of it retains substantial voting control even if the pledge is invoked. A promoter with 25 percent holding who pledges 40 percent loses effective control if pledge is invoked. Control concentration matters for interpreting pledge implications.

formulas.name: Pledge Velocity Ratio
formulas.formula: Pledge Velocity = (Current Period Pledge Intensity - Prior Period Pledge Intensity) / Number of Months × 100

variables.meaning: Most recent quarterly pledge intensity percentage
Pledge intensity one or more quarters earlier, typically 4 quarters (1 year) prior
Months between current and prior periods, typically 12

formulas.worked_example: Running this on various Indian companies. Reliance Industries historical: Pledge Intensity has remained below 5 percent for 10-plus years, indicating stable low-pledge ownership structure. Velocity near zero. Yes Bank September 2018 to September 2019: Intensity moved from 33 percent to 92 percent = delta of 59 percentage points over 12 months = Velocity of 4.9 percentage points per month. Extreme acceleration. For comparison, a healthy company might have Pledge Velocity of zero or mildly negative (as promoters unpledge shares). A watchlist company might show Velocity of 0.5-1.0 percentage points per month (gradual increase). A distress-stage company shows Velocity above 2.0 percentage points per month. Yes Bank's 4.9 was uniquely extreme. Interpretation thresholds: Velocity below 0.5 (including negative) is healthy. 0.5-1.5 is watchlist — promoter financing is increasing but not at alarming rate. 1.5-3.0 is material concern — substantial new pledging indicates emerging promoter stress. Above 3.0 is extreme — the promoter is rapidly deploying shares as collateral, consistent with acute financial distress or cascade-pledging patterns. The Velocity metric captures trajectory in ways that Intensity alone cannot. A company at 40 percent Intensity with Velocity near zero (stable at 40 percent for years) has different risk profile than a company at 40 percent Intensity with Velocity of 2.5 (rapidly increasing). Both warrant investigation but the Velocity metric identifies acute escalation patterns.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Velocity should be computed using publicly disclosed pledge data from BSE/NSE portals. For companies without substantial promoter pledging history, Velocity is near zero and the metric provides no signal. For companies with meaningful pledge activity, Velocity is the specific metric that catches acute escalation patterns like Yes Bank 2018-2019.

formulas.name: Insider Trading Signal Ratio
formulas.formula: Insider Net Activity = (Value of Insider Purchases - Value of Insider Sales) / Total Designated Persons' Existing Holdings × 100

variables.meaning: Aggregate rupee value of all insider purchases across designated persons during the measurement window, from SEBI PIT disclosures
Aggregate rupee value of all insider sales during the same window
Aggregate value of shares held by all designated persons at the start of the measurement window

formulas.worked_example: Running this on two Indian companies. Company A (clean large-cap): Over trailing 12 months, insider purchases ₹45 crore, insider sales ₹12 crore, net ₹33 crore positive against total designated holdings of ₹280 crore = Net Activity of positive 11.8 percent. Signals insider confidence — designated persons are increasing exposure to the company. Company B (deteriorating promoter-led): Over trailing 12 months, insider purchases ₹8 crore, insider sales ₹145 crore (concentrated in Q3 before weak Q4 results), net negative ₹137 crore against holdings of ₹450 crore = Net Activity of negative 30 percent. Signals insider concern — designated persons are substantially reducing exposure, particularly concentrated before negative earnings. Cross-reference with the timing of sales is important — sales concentrated 60-90 days before negative results or corporate events suggest information-advantage trading that may trigger SEBI scrutiny. Interpretation thresholds: Net Activity above positive 5 percent is positive signal (insider buying). Between negative 5 percent and positive 5 percent is neutral. Negative 5 to negative 15 percent is watchlist — material insider selling that warrants investigation of timing and context. Negative 15 to negative 30 percent is concerning — substantial insider selling indicates concerns among designated persons. Negative 30 percent and beyond is severe — effectively a vote of no confidence from insiders, particularly when concentrated in timing before negative events.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Insider Trading Signal must be interpreted in context. Large sales might reflect legitimate diversification by specific individuals rather than collective concern. The aggregation across multiple designated persons matters. Also consider exercise of ESOPs separately from purchases — ESOP exercises are compensation-related rather than information-based trades. The cleanest signal is when multiple designated persons are aggressively buying (positive) or selling (negative) in concentrated windows.

formulas.name: Buyback Value Test
formulas.formula: Buyback Yield = (Buyback Price - Current Market Price) / Current Market Price × 100; Buyback P/E = Buyback Price / EPS for TTM period

variables.meaning: Price per share at which the company is repurchasing shares, from buyback announcement
Stock price in secondary market at time of buyback announcement
Earnings per share for trailing twelve months

formulas.worked_example: Running this on two Indian buybacks. TCS December 2023 buyback announcement: Buyback price ₹3,500 per share against market price at announcement of ₹3,270 = Buyback Yield of 7.0 percent. EPS TTM at ₹115 gives Buyback P/E of 30.4x. Historical TCS P/E range 20-35x. The buyback was priced toward the upper end of historical multiples, suggesting management confidence in continued strong performance and willingness to pay premium for share concentration. Whether value-creating depends on forward earnings trajectory. Infosys September 2022 buyback: Buyback price ₹1,850 against market of ₹1,470 at announcement = Buyback Yield 25.9 percent. EPS TTM at ₹52 gives Buyback P/E of 35.6x. Aggressive premium but with substantial return to participating shareholders who tendered. For participating shareholders, value creation was clear (25 percent premium over market). For non-participating shareholders, value creation depends on whether forward earnings justify the P/E paid. Indian IT buybacks have generally been value-creating for participating shareholders through tender offer structure. Interpretation framework: Buyback Yield below 5 percent is unusual and may indicate open market buyback without clear return intent. 5-15 percent is reasonable premium for tender offer. 15-30 percent is aggressive but can be justified by management confidence. Above 30 percent is exceptional and typically signals specific capital-return strategy. Buyback P/E above historical P/E ceiling suggests management is paying premium for share concentration — appropriate if forward earnings are expected to justify, problematic if buyback is EPS-engineering without forward-earnings support. Always compute buyback economics from both participating shareholder perspective and continuing shareholder perspective.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Buyback analysis requires context-dependent interpretation. For cash-rich companies with limited organic reinvestment opportunities (Indian IT services), buybacks at reasonable premiums are typically value-creating. For capital-constrained companies where cash could be used for debt reduction or growth capex, buybacks at any premium warrant scrutiny. Sector context matters.

title: The Top-Down Allocator's Toolkit — From Macro To Sector Conviction

formulas.name: Macro-to-Sector Mapping Framework
formulas.formula: Sector Conviction Score = Macro Driver Score × Sector Sensitivity × Cycle Position Modifier × Valuation Adjustment

variables.meaning: Composite score of relevant macro indicators for the sector (1-10 scale). For capital goods: PMI manufacturing, capex announcements, PLI commitments, IIP capital goods sub-index. For real estate: rural wages, urban income growth, interest rates, RERA-driven consolidation

How responsive the sector is to its key drivers. Cyclical sectors have high sensitivity (1.2-1.5x); defensive sectors have low sensitivity (0.5-0.8x); structural growth sectors (IT services historically) have moderate sensitivity
Where the sector sits in its own sub-cycle. Early-cycle: 1.3x. Mid-cycle: 1.0x. Late-cycle: 0.7x. Trough: 0.9x with recovery optionality. Apply to base score
Sector valuation versus 5-year average. Trading 20%+ below average: +0.3 multiplier. Trading at average: 1.0x. Trading 20%+ above average: -0.2 multiplier. Captures relative attractiveness

formulas.worked_example: Indian Capital Goods sector conviction calculation in late 2024. Macro Driver Score: Manufacturing PMI at 55+ (above 50 expansion line) = 7/10; Capex announcements accelerating from PLI/defence/renewable = 8/10; IIP capital goods sub-index growing 9-10% YoY = 7/10. Average: 7.5. Sector Sensitivity: 1.4x (cyclical with high responsiveness to capex cycles). Cycle Position Modifier: 1.0x (mid-cycle expansion, with multi-year visibility). Valuation Adjustment: -0.1x (trading at premium to historical average given strong cycle). Sector Conviction: 7.5 × 1.4 × 1.0 × (1-0.1) = 9.45 — strong overweight signal. Compare to IT services in late 2024: Macro Driver Score 5.5 (US tech demand still soft), Sensitivity 0.7 (less cyclical than capital goods), Cycle Position 0.9 (recovery from trough), Valuation -0.1 (premium to global peers). Conviction: 5.5 × 0.7 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 3.1 — weak underweight signal. The framework explicitly captures the relative outperformance opportunity. Apply to all major sectors quarterly to refresh portfolio positioning. Compare conviction scores across sectors to identify overweight, neutral, underweight allocations.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The conviction score framework requires honesty about each driver. Avoid confirmation bias — don't inflate macro scores to justify a preferred sector view. Refresh quarterly with updated indicators. Companies and sectors that score consistently high across multiple quarters are durable structural plays. Sectors with declining conviction over multiple quarters signal potential cyclical inflection. The framework is a discipline, not a prediction tool.

formulas.name: Sector Relative Valuation Versus Historical Bands
formulas.formula: Sector Z-Score = (Current Sector P/E − 5-Year Average P/E) ÷ 5-Year Standard Deviation     where Z-Score above 1.0 indicates premium to history; below -1.0 indicates discount

variables.meaning: Forward 12-month P/E of the sector index (Nifty Bank, Nifty Auto, Nifty IT, Nifty Pharma, etc.) or weighted average of major constituents
Mean P/E of the same sector over the past 5 years — captures one full cycle for most sectors
Variability of P/E around the mean — captures the historical range. Higher SD means wider valuation bands
Z-score above +2: strongly overvalued; +1 to +2: moderately overvalued; -1 to +1: fair value; -1 to -2: moderately undervalued; below -2: deeply undervalued

formulas.worked_example: Indian sector relative valuation analysis in late 2024. Nifty Capital Goods Index forward P/E: 65x. 5-year average: 35x. Standard deviation: 12x. Z-Score: (65 - 35) / 12 = +2.5 — strongly overvalued versus history. Implication: cyclical strength reflected in valuation; further multiple expansion is unlikely. Nifty IT Index forward P/E: 28x. 5-year average: 30x. Standard deviation: 5x. Z-Score: (28 - 30) / 5 = -0.4 — fair value. Implication: IT sector at fair valuation following 2022-2024 underperformance; recovery thesis is set up. Nifty Bank forward P/E: 14x. 5-year average: 16x. Standard deviation: 2.5x. Z-Score: (14 - 16) / 2.5 = -0.8 — modestly undervalued. Implication: financial sector reasonable entry point. Combine z-scores with macro conviction scores to form positioning. High macro conviction + reasonable valuation = strong overweight (capital goods despite premium signals continued momentum). Moderate conviction + undervaluation = recovery opportunity (IT, banks). Apply quarterly to all major sectors.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Z-scores are statistical anchors, not absolute targets. A sector trading at +2 standard deviations may continue further if cyclical strength persists; a sector at -1.5 may not mean-revert if structural challenges exist. Combine z-scores with cyclical positioning, macro drivers, and qualitative assessment. Z-scores work best as confirmation rather than primary trigger. Track quarterly evolution — sectors moving from -1 to +1 over 12 months indicate cyclical recovery; from +1 to -1 indicates cyclical normalisation.

formulas.name: Portfolio Construction From Sector Conviction
formulas.formula: Sector Weight in Portfolio ≈ Benchmark Weight × (1 + Conviction Tilt)     where Conviction Tilt = (Sector Conviction Score − Median Conviction) ÷ Maximum Conviction × Maximum Tilt %

variables.meaning: Sector weight in benchmark index (Nifty 50 or Nifty 100). For example, Financials at ~30%, IT at ~14%, Energy at ~10%, FMCG at ~10%, Auto at ~7%, Pharma at ~5%, Capital Goods at ~5%
How much above or below benchmark to position. Strong conviction (score above median + 2): +50% tilt; Moderate conviction: +20% tilt; Neutral: 0% tilt; Underweight: -20% to -50% tilt

Risk-management constraint on how far portfolio deviates from benchmark. Typical institutional portfolios use ±30-50% tilt limits — preventing extreme concentration risk while allowing meaningful active positioning

formulas.worked_example: Sector positioning example based on late 2024 analysis. Capital Goods conviction high (9.5); benchmark weight ~5%; conviction tilt +50% would push portfolio weight to 7.5%. IT services conviction lower (3.1); benchmark weight ~14%; conviction tilt -20% would push portfolio weight to 11.2%. Real Estate conviction moderate-strong (8); benchmark weight ~3% (with selective developers); conviction tilt +30% would push portfolio weight to 4%. Financials conviction moderate (6); benchmark weight ~30%; conviction tilt +10% would push portfolio weight to 33%. Pharma conviction moderate-low (5); benchmark weight ~5%; conviction tilt 0% maintains benchmark. Total active tilt across sectors: +5% in capital goods, -3% in IT, +1% in real estate, +3% in financials. The +6% net cyclical tilt with -3% IT compression captures the sector rotation positioning. The framework explicitly translates conviction scores into portfolio positioning. Refresh quarterly. Monitor performance. The 2022-2024 portfolio with strong cyclical tilt and IT compression captured the multi-bagger opportunity that the benchmark would have missed.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Portfolio construction discipline is what separates a thesis from positioning. Many analysts have correct sector views but fail to translate them into actual portfolio tilts due to risk constraints, peer pressure, or fear of underperformance versus benchmark. Apply the framework explicitly with maximum tilt constraints; communicate the positioning to portfolio managers; track performance. Sectors with consistently high conviction across quarters can sustain larger tilts; sectors with declining conviction signal time to reduce tilt. The framework is the alpha; execution discipline is what captures it.

title: The Quality of Earnings Metrics

formulas.name: Total Accruals Ratio
formulas.formula: Total Accruals Ratio = (Net Income − Cash Flow from Operations) / Average Total Assets

variables.meaning: Profit After Tax from the P&L, excluding discontinued operations
CFO from the Cash Flow Statement (Session 7). For Ind AS, indirect method starting from PBT is standard.
Average of opening and closing total assets for the period

formulas.worked_example:
ABC Industries (hypothetical mid-cap) FY24:
Net Income: ₹420 cr
CFO: ₹285 cr
Opening Total Assets: ₹3,800 cr
Closing Total Assets: ₹4,200 cr
Average Total Assets: ₹4,000 cr

Total Accruals = 420 − 285 = ₹135 cr
Total Accruals Ratio = 135 / 4,000 = 3.4%

THRESHOLDS (from forensic accounting research):
• Below 3% — high earnings quality, earnings mostly cash-backed
• 3-5% — moderate quality, normal operational accruals
• 5-8% — elevated accruals, warrants investigation
• Above 8% — aggressive accruals, major earnings quality red flag
• Persistently above 10% — potential earnings management or fraud

For ABC, 3.4% is in the moderate range — acceptable but at the upper end of normal. The ₹135 cr gap between Net Income and CFO needs explanation — working capital expansion, one-off provisions reversing, tax timing. If the gap is driven by working capital bleed (Sessions 6-7 analysis), it's the kind of pattern that precedes earnings disappointment.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Total Accruals Ratio is the single most diagnostic quality-of-earnings metric. A 10-percentage-point deterioration over 2-3 years (e.g., from 2% to 12%) has preceded every major Indian accounting scandal — Satyam, DHFL, Yes Bank (for specific line items), Manpasand Beverages, and multiple mid-cap stress situations.

formulas.name: Cash Realisation Ratio (CRR)
formulas.formula: Cash Realisation Ratio = Cash Flow from Operations / Net Income, computed over rolling 3-year averages

variables.meaning: Trailing 3-year cumulative CFO
Trailing 3-year cumulative Net Income

formulas.worked_example:
HUL FY22-FY24 (3-year rolling):
Cumulative Net Income: ₹27,180 cr
Cumulative CFO: ₹28,400 cr
CRR = 28,400 / 27,180 = 1.04

TCS FY22-FY24:
Cumulative Net Income: ₹121,800 cr
Cumulative CFO: ₹121,400 cr
CRR = 121,400 / 121,800 = 1.00

Manpasand Beverages FY15-FY17 (pre-collapse):
Cumulative Net Income: ₹268 cr
Cumulative CFO: ₹64 cr
CRR = 64 / 268 = 0.24

INTERPRETATION:
• CRR ≥ 1.0 — exceptional quality, cash generation exceeds reported earnings
• CRR 0.85-1.0 — high quality, tight alignment
• CRR 0.7-0.85 — acceptable, some working capital bleed expected
• CRR 0.5-0.7 — elevated concern, material gap between earnings and cash
• CRR below 0.5 — severe quality issue, reported earnings not translating to cash

HUL and TCS at ~1.0 CRR represent the gold standard. Manpasand's 0.24 preceded its collapse — 76% of reported earnings never materialised as cash.
formulas.sensitivity_note: CRR is particularly powerful because 3-year rolling averages smooth out single-year volatility (e.g., tax timing, large working capital swings). Multi-year CRR tracking catches the 'slow drift' from high-quality to low-quality earnings that is often a multi-year pattern before crisis.

formulas.name: Accrual Decomposition — Working Capital vs Non-Working-Capital
formulas.formula: WC-Driven Accrual = Change in Working Capital (Δ Receivables + Δ Inventory − Δ Payables)\nNon-WC Accrual = Total Accruals − WC-Driven Accrual

variables.meaning: Increase in receivables and inventory, less increase in payables. Direct linkage from Session 6 analysis.
Net Income minus CFO
Accruals from non-working-capital sources — depreciation, provisions, impairment reversals, fair value adjustments, deferred tax

formulas.worked_example:
Example Mid-cap Ltd FY24:
Net Income: ₹850 cr
CFO: ₹620 cr
Total Accruals: ₹230 cr
Δ Receivables: +₹120 cr
Δ Inventory: +₹85 cr
Δ Payables: +₹35 cr
WC-Driven Accrual = 120 + 85 − 35 = ₹170 cr
Non-WC Accrual = 230 − 170 = ₹60 cr

INSIGHT: Of the ₹230 cr total accrual gap, 74% is driven by working capital expansion (CCC deteriorating per Session 6), and 26% is non-working-capital items. The WC-driven portion is concerning because it reflects operational stress — receivables and inventory growing faster than business, payables contracting. The non-WC portion may be normal depreciation and provisions. The decomposition separates operational earnings quality issues from accounting policy issues.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Decomposition reveals WHERE the earnings quality issue is. If total accruals are 5% of assets but almost entirely working capital-driven, the Session 6 framework applies. If they're non-working-capital driven (aggressive provisions, fair value adjustments, deferred tax), they're accounting-choice driven. Different root causes require different analytical responses.

title: The Exceptional Item Normalisation Framework

formulas.name: Adjusted EBITDA (Normalised for Exceptionals)
formulas.formula: Adjusted EBITDA = Reported EBITDA − Exceptional Income + Exceptional Expense

variables.meaning: EBITDA as shown in the annual report, including all exceptional items
One-time gains — e.g., asset sale profit, insurance recovery, litigation win, sale of subsidiary
One-time costs — e.g., product recall, restructuring, impairment, litigation settlement, COVID-related one-offs

formulas.worked_example: Suppose Titan FY23 Reported EBITDA was ₹3,840 cr. The AR notes disclose: (a) a one-time land sale gain of ₹120 cr, and (b) a ₹85 cr loss on fire damage at the Hosur factory (not fully recoverable from insurance). Adjusted EBITDA = 3,840 − 120 + 85 = ₹3,805 cr. The EBITDA MARGIN you use for forecasting must be based on ₹3,805 cr, not ₹3,840 cr — otherwise you're building your forecast on a one-time tailwind that will not repeat. On the IS, you show both: 'Reported EBITDA 3,840' then 'Less: Exceptional Income (120)' then 'Add: Exceptional Expense 85' then 'Adjusted EBITDA 3,805'. Full transparency, zero loss of information.
formulas.sensitivity_note: If Adjusted EBITDA margin is ~50 bps different from Reported, your forecast EPS can shift by 3-5%. The difference between '₹3,805 cr × 12% growth = ₹4,262 cr' and '₹3,840 cr × 12% growth = ₹4,301 cr' compounds over a 5-year forecast into a materially different terminal value. Normalise or pay the price.

formulas.name: Net Debt Reconciliation
formulas.formula: Net Debt = Short-Term Borrowings + Long-Term Borrowings + Current Portion of LT Debt + Lease Liabilities − Cash & Cash Equivalents − Current Investments

variables.meaning: Working capital loans, commercial paper, bank overdrafts — typically Note 22 or 23 in Indian ARs
Term loans, debentures, NCDs — Note 20 or 21 usually
The portion of long-term debt maturing within 12 months — moved from non-current to current on the BS
Post-Ind-AS 116 (FY20), operating leases are capitalised — this is often missed by beginners but is genuine debt-like commitment
Bank balances, fixed deposits under 3 months, cash in hand
Liquid mutual funds, debt funds, treasury bills — often 10x cash itself for Indian cash-rich companies

formulas.worked_example: Titan FY24: Short-term borrowings ₹1,120 cr + Long-term borrowings ₹840 cr + Current portion of LT debt ₹285 cr + Lease liabilities ₹620 cr − Cash ₹1,800 cr − Current investments ₹780 cr = ₹285 cr Net Debt. Note: if you forget lease liabilities, you show 'Net Debt ₹-335 cr (net cash)' which is materially wrong — Titan has real lease obligations on its 3,000+ stores. Post-Ind-AS 116, leases are debt. Every Indian analyst who started before FY20 had to retrain on this.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Enterprise Value = Market Cap + Net Debt. If Net Debt is understated by ₹600 cr (e.g., missed leases), EV is understated by ₹600 cr, EV/EBITDA multiple is understated by ~0.08x, and in a high-multiple stock like Titan (~50x EV/EBITDA), that's a 0.15% error. Small in percentage but real in absolute terms. For a bank or NBFC, where Net Debt is the core KPI, missing leases can mean mis-stating leverage by 200-300 bps.

formulas.name: Working Capital Days (Days-Based Standardisation)
formulas.formula: Receivable Days = (Trade Receivables / Revenue) × 365 | Inventory Days = (Inventory / COGS) × 365 | Payable Days = (Trade Payables / COGS) × 365

variables.meaning: Net of provision for doubtful debts — use the NET number, not gross
Revenue from operations (not total income) — excludes Other Income
Total inventory — raw materials + WIP + finished goods + stores & spares
Cost of goods sold — in Indian ARs this is the sum of 'Cost of materials consumed' + 'Purchases of stock-in-trade' + 'Changes in inventories' (signed correctly)
Amount owed to suppliers — does NOT include statutory dues, employee payables, or other current liabilities

formulas.worked_example: Titan FY24: Receivables ₹620 cr, Revenue ₹47,100 cr → Receivable Days = (620/47,100) × 365 = 4.8 days. Inventory ₹13,200 cr, COGS ₹36,800 cr → Inventory Days = (13,200/36,800) × 365 = 131 days. Payables ₹8,400 cr, COGS ₹36,800 cr → Payable Days = (8,400/36,800) × 365 = 83 days. Cash Conversion Cycle = 4.8 + 131 − 83 = 52.8 days. Titan's cycle is inventory-heavy because jewellery requires holding gold stock — a structural feature, not a red flag.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Days-based standardisation is the foundation for working capital FORECASTING in Session 6. If your historical days are wrong (e.g., you used Total Income instead of Revenue, or Gross Receivables instead of Net), your forecast days are anchored to the wrong base, and your forecast working capital is wrong. Get historical days exactly right or Session 6 suffers.

title: The Volume-Price-Mix Decomposition

formulas.name: Volume-Price-Mix (VPM) Decomposition
formulas.formula: Revenue Growth % ≈ (1 + Volume Growth %) × (1 + Price Growth %) × (1 + Mix Effect %) − 1

variables.meaning: Growth in physical units sold — disclosed in concalls or computed from dispatch data / order fulfilment metrics
Growth in per-unit realisation at constant mix — often disclosed as 'pricing contribution' in FMCG/paints concalls
Residual growth attributable to shift in product/channel composition — often calculated as plug figure after volume and price

formulas.worked_example:
Asian Paints FY23:
Reported Revenue Growth: 16.1%
Volume Growth (disclosed): 2.0%
Price Growth (disclosed): 13.8%
Mix Effect (residual): 16.1% − 2.0% − 13.8% ≈ 0.3%

Insight: 14 out of 16 percentage points of growth came from price — almost entirely pass-through of titanium dioxide and monomer inflation, not genuine demand strength. When TiO2 prices cool in FY24, this 14% reverses, and reported growth collapses to mid-single digits. This is exactly what happened — FY24 revenue grew only 7.5%.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For quick estimation in interviews, use additive approximation: Revenue Growth ≈ Volume + Price + Mix. Multiplicative precision matters only when growth rates exceed 20% — below that, additive is within 50 bps of actual.

formulas.name: Organic vs Inorganic Growth Split
formulas.formula: Organic Growth % = (Current Revenue − Acquisition Revenue − FX Impact) / Prior Period Revenue − 1

variables.meaning: Revenue contribution from companies acquired during the year, annualised if needed for like-for-like
Revenue variation caused by exchange rate movements, computed at constant currency
Base year revenue on which growth is measured

formulas.worked_example:
Infosys FY23:
Reported USD Revenue Growth: 15.4%
USD Constant Currency Growth (stripping FX): 15.4%
INR Reported Revenue Growth: 20.7%
INR Organic Growth after FX adjustment: ~16.0%

Gap: The 20.7% INR headline is flattered by 470 bps of rupee depreciation. The real organic growth is 16%. For cross-company comparison in Indian IT, always anchor to constant currency USD growth or INR organic growth — the reported INR number is inflated by FX in most fiscal years.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For exporters (IT services, pharma, specialty chemicals, textile), FX is the biggest distortion in reported INR revenue growth. Always demand constant-currency disclosures from the company or compute them yourself using period-average USD/INR rates.

formulas.name: Same-Store Sales Growth (SSSG) for Retail/QSR
formulas.formula: SSSG % = (Current Period Sales from Stores Open >12 Months − Prior Period Sales from Same Stores) / Prior Period Sales from Same Stores

variables.meaning: Stores that were operational for the entire comparable period in both years — excludes stores opened in the current year

formulas.worked_example:
Jubilant FoodWorks Q4 FY24:
Total Revenue Growth: 9%
SSSG (Domino's India): −1.5%
New Store Opening Contribution: 10.5%

Insight: All of Jubilant's growth came from opening new stores. Existing stores actually saw a 1.5% sales decline. This is a classic retail red flag — the business is growing by opening outlets faster than it's losing per-store productivity. Eventually new-store additions slow, and the negative SSSG becomes the whole story. This is why SSSG is the single most-watched metric in QSR, retail, and consumer services.
formulas.sensitivity_note: SSSG drives analyst verdicts in retail. Even a 100 bps miss on SSSG guidance can trigger 8–12% stock moves in names like DMart, Trent, Jubilant FoodWorks, and Titan. Watch for 'SSSG ex-inflation' disclosures that separate volume-based traffic from realisation.

title: The Auto Analyst's Calculation Toolkit — From Wholesales to Operating Leverage

formulas.name: Wholesale-Retail Gap and Channel Stuffing Detection
formulas.formula: Channel Stuffing Indicator = Cumulative Wholesales (3M) − Cumulative Retails (3M)     Inventory Days at Dealer = (Dealer Inventory Units × 30) / Monthly Retails

variables.meaning: Sum of OEM dispatches over the trailing three months (from monthly press releases)
Sum of dealer-to-customer sales over the trailing three months (from FADA data)
Number of days of dealer inventory at current retail run-rate. Normal range: 25-35 days. Above 45 days is high; above 60 days is alarming

formulas.worked_example: Maruti Suzuki Q3 FY24 example. Cumulative wholesales over Oct-Dec 2023: 4,98,000 units. Cumulative retails (FADA data) over same period: 4,40,000 units. Wholesale-Retail Gap: +58,000 units in 3 months. Implied dealer inventory increase: roughly 58,000 units. If average monthly retails are 1,46,000 and dealer inventory is 1,80,000 units, Inventory Days = (1,80,000 × 30) / 1,46,000 = 37 days — slightly elevated but within normal range. Compare to a hypothetical channel stuffing scenario: if wholesales over 3M were 5,40,000 vs retails of 4,40,000, the gap of 1,00,000 in 3 months would push inventory days to 55+ days — flashing yellow on channel stuffing. The OEM is dispatching faster than dealers can sell, which historically forces dispatch cuts in subsequent months. This is the leading indicator. When you see persistent wholesale-retail gaps for 3+ months and inventory days above 45, expect dispatch cuts (and earnings disappointments) within 1-2 quarters.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The wholesale-retail gap is the single most important diagnostic in auto cyclical analysis. OEMs control wholesales directly — they can boost dispatches at quarter-end to hit targets. Retails reflect actual consumer demand. The gap is where channel stuffing hides. During the FY18-19 cyclical peak, multiple OEMs ran wholesale-retail gaps for 4-6 months before dispatches collapsed in FY20. Analysts who tracked the gap caught the cyclical turn 2 quarters before consensus. Always read both numbers, never just wholesales.

formulas.name: Operating Leverage in Auto OEMs
formulas.formula: ΔEBITDA Margin (bps) ≈ Volume Growth × Operating Leverage Coefficient ± ASP/Mix Effect ± Raw Material Effect ± Currency Effect

variables.meaning: Year-on-year change in unit volumes (e.g., +15% means 15% more vehicles sold)
Roughly 6-8 bps margin expansion per 1% volume growth for mass-market OEMs (high fixed costs); 3-5 bps for ancillaries (lower fixed cost base)
Margin contribution from price hikes and mix shift to higher-priced models. Premium mix typically adds 30-80 bps margin
Steel, aluminium, copper, rubber prices YoY. Raw materials are 60-70% of OEM cost base. 10% steel price decline can add 80-120 bps margin
USD/INR for OEMs with import content. INR depreciation hurts margins for import-heavy OEMs (e.g., Maruti for components); helps export-tilted OEMs (Eicher Royal Enfield)

formulas.worked_example: Maruti Suzuki FY24: Volume growth +9%, ASP improvement +5% (mix to higher-priced models), raw material costs declining 6% YoY (steel and aluminium deflation). Implied EBITDA margin walk: Operating leverage 9% × 7 bps = +63 bps. Mix improvement +60 bps. Raw material tailwind: 65% of cost × 6% decline = +390 bps gross margin tailwind, of which roughly half captured by OEM = +195 bps. Sum: 63 + 60 + 195 = +318 bps margin expansion implied. Actual FY24 margin moved from 9.3% to 11.4%, a +210 bps expansion — consistent with the framework after accounting for some pass-through to consumers via discounts and competitive pricing pressure. The operating leverage framework explains roughly 70% of margin movement in any given year. The remainder is one-offs (pricing actions, currency, government incentives like SPVs and PLI scheme benefits).
formulas.sensitivity_note: Operating leverage is asymmetric — it expands margins fast on the way up and crushes margins fast on the way down. Maruti's FY18 margin was 15.2% at the cyclical peak; FY20 margin compressed to 8.7% at the trough as volumes fell 16%. The 650 bps margin compression on a 16% volume decline implies operating de-leverage of roughly 40 bps per 1% volume decline. This is why peak earnings should never be extrapolated for cyclical OEMs. Always model through-cycle margins (FY18 to FY24 average) for fair value, not the most recent year's margin.

formulas.name: Ancillary Content Per Vehicle (CPV) and Wallet Share
formulas.formula: Content Per Vehicle = Ancillary Revenue from OEM Customer / OEM Volume Sold     Wallet Share Growth = (CPV Current Year − CPV Prior Year) / CPV Prior Year

variables.meaning: Revenue earned by ancillary from a specific OEM customer (disclosed in customer concentration breakdowns or estimated from segmental data)
Number of vehicles produced by the OEM customer in the same period
(1) New product wins (electronics, advanced safety), (2) Volume mix shift to premium models with higher content, (3) Pricing increases on existing content

formulas.worked_example: Sona BLW Precision Forgings example. Sona supplies powertrain components (gears, differential, BLDC motors) to multiple OEMs including Maruti, Hero, TVS, Stellantis, Hyundai. Estimated CPV with Maruti: FY22: roughly 5,500 INR per vehicle. FY24: roughly 7,200 INR per vehicle. CPV growth: 31% over 2 years, or 14% CAGR. Driver: increasing share of higher-content components (BLDC motors for EVs, advanced gears for premium vehicles). This 14% CPV CAGR is in addition to Maruti's own volume growth (around 9% FY24). So Sona's revenue from Maruti grew approximately 23% in FY24 (volume + CPV growth) versus Maruti's standalone growth of 9%. This wallet share expansion is the structural growth lever for premium ancillaries beyond pure OEM volume cycles. Companies like Sona BLW, Sundram Fasteners, Endurance, and Bharat Forge have grown 12-18% per year over the past 5 years partly through CPV expansion and partly through diversifying customers. The premium ancillaries deserve higher multiples than pure OEMs because they capture both the OEM cycle and the structural CPV growth.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Content Per Vehicle is the most underappreciated metric in Indian auto analysis. Most retail investors track OEM volumes and assume ancillary growth follows. But the strongest ancillaries grow 5-10 percentage points faster than their OEM customers through CPV expansion. This explains why ancillaries like Sona BLW or Endurance compounded at 20-30% over 2018-2023 while OEMs compounded at 8-12%. Always estimate CPV growth for ancillaries — it separates the structural growth stories from cyclical-only plays.

title: The Transmission Mechanism — From Repo to Earnings, Decoded

formulas.name: Bank NIM Sensitivity to Repo Change
formulas.formula: Δ NIM (bps) ≈ Δ Repo (bps) × (Asset Repricing Speed - Liability Repricing Speed) × Net Earning Asset Ratio

variables.meaning: Change in repo rate in basis points
Fraction of loan book that reprices within the measurement window (typically 6-12 months)
Fraction of deposit book that reprices within the measurement window
Net interest-earning assets as % of total assets

formulas.worked_example:
HDFC Bank facing a 25 bps repo cut:
Asset repricing speed (6-month window) = 60% (most loans MCLR-linked or repo-linked)
Liability repricing speed (6-month window) = 35% (CASA share 47% does not reprice; FDs reprice slowly)
Net Earning Asset Ratio = 92%

NIM impact = -25 bps × (0.60 - 0.35) × 0.92 = -25 × 0.25 × 0.92 = -5.75 bps NIM compression

On HDFC Bank''s ₹24 lakh crore loan book, this translates to roughly ₹1,380 crore lower Net Interest Income annually — about 3.5% of FY24 NII. After tax, this is ₹1,034 crore lower PAT, or 2.5% lower EPS. At 19x P/E, that''s ₹38 lower target price.
formulas.sensitivity_note: This is why bank stocks move sharply on rate decisions. The arithmetic is mechanical: faster asset repricing than liability repricing means NIMs follow rates closely. PSU banks with high CASA (40-45%) suffer most from cuts (their cheap deposits do not benefit) and benefit most from hikes. Private banks with lower CASA (35-40%) and higher proportion of EBLR-linked loans see more direct repricing on both sides.

formulas.name: Real Repo Rate (Predictor of Next MPC Move)
formulas.formula: Real Repo Rate (%) = Nominal Repo Rate (%) - CPI Inflation Rate (%)

variables.meaning: Current repo rate set by RBI
Most recent month CPI YoY inflation

formulas.worked_example:
Scenario A (Late 2022): Repo 6.25%, CPI 6.77%, Real Repo = -0.52%. Stimulative policy when economy was hot — clear signal that hikes were coming. RBI delivered 75 more bps in next 4 months.

Scenario B (Mid 2024): Repo 6.50%, CPI 4.83%, Real Repo = 1.67%. Mildly restrictive. Rate cut probability rises but not imminent unless growth slows materially.

Scenario C (Aspirational): Repo 6.50%, CPI 4.0%, Real Repo = 2.50%. Restrictive. RBI under pressure to start cutting.
formulas.sensitivity_note: RBI''s implicit target real repo is 1.0-1.5%. Below 0.5% = hikes incoming. Above 2.0% = cuts incoming. Between 1.0-2.0% = data-dependent. This single ratio predicts MPC direction with 70-75% accuracy across the last decade.

formulas.name: Monetary Transmission Lag (Repo to Lending Rate)
formulas.formula: Effective Lending Rate Change = Repo Change × Transmission Coefficient × (1 - Time Decay Factor)

variables.meaning: Historical pass-through ratio for India: 60-80% in 6-12 months
Fraction of expected change still un-transmitted at time T (decays from 1 to 0 over 6-12 months)

formulas.worked_example:
A 100 bps cumulative repo hike (May 2022 to Feb 2023):
Month 0 (rate decision): Effective lending rate up 0 bps (zero immediate transmission)
Month 3: Up 30 bps (30% transmitted)
Month 6: Up 55 bps (55% transmitted)
Month 12: Up 75-80 bps (full bandwidth)
Month 18: Up 80-85 bps (terminal transmission)

This matches actual data: weighted average lending rate on outstanding loans rose from 8.69% in April 2022 to 9.61% by December 2023 — a 92 bps move on a 250 bps cumulative hike. Roughly 37% transmission over 18 months — lower than ideal because of liquidity surplus and competition.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Transmission has historically been incomplete in India because of CASA-heavy bank funding (cheap deposits do not reprice with policy), fixed-rate loan stock, and competitive pricing pressure. The RBI has been pushing External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR) regime since 2019 to improve transmission, with mixed success.

formulas.name: Sector EPS Sensitivity to 100 bps Rate Move
formulas.formula: Δ Sector EPS = Σ (Δ Interest Cost - Δ Interest Income) ÷ Net Profit

variables.meaning: Change in interest expense from rate move (depends on debt repricing schedule)
Change in interest income (mostly relevant for financials and cash-rich companies)
FY current/forward net profit base

formulas.worked_example:
100 bps rate CUT impact on selected sectors:

Real Estate (DLF, Godrej Properties): Average debt/equity 0.5-0.8x, debt cost 8-9%. EPS uplift: 8-15% (highly leveraged + demand uplift from cheaper home loans).

NBFCs (Bajaj Finance, Cholamandalam): Wholesale funding cost falls 60-70 bps. Lending rates fall slower. Spread expansion of 30-40 bps. EPS uplift: 4-8%.

Auto (Maruti, M&M): Indirect benefit through cheaper auto loans. Volume uplift 3-5%. EPS uplift: 3-6%.

IT (TCS, Infosys): Negligible direct impact. Slight headwind via stronger INR if FII inflows pick up. EPS uplift: -1 to 0%.

PSU Banks (SBI, BoB): Negative for short-term NIM (CASA does not benefit, asset yields fall). EPS impact: -3 to -5% over 6-9 months, then recovers as credit growth picks up.

Real Estate is the highest beta sector to rates — both directly (cost of capital) and indirectly (demand). Always check leverage of your covered companies; rate moves create outsized EPS swings in leveraged businesses.
formulas.sensitivity_note: These sensitivities are first-order. Second-order effects (multiple expansion from lower discount rates, FII flow shifts, currency effects) often double or triple the stock price impact. The 2019 RBI cutting cycle (135 bps cumulative cuts) drove a 22% rally in real estate stocks vs 12% in Nifty.

title: The Universal Ratio Template

formulas.name: The Universal Ratio Formula
formulas.formula: Ratio = Output Metric / Input Metric

variables.meaning: What the business produced — profit, cash flow, revenue, etc.
What the business used to produce it — capital, assets, equity, revenue base, etc.

formulas.worked_example: Take Asian Paints FY23. Revenue = ₹34,488 Cr. Net Profit = ₹4,106 Cr. Total Capital Employed = ₹15,200 Cr. Three ratios, three different stories. Net Margin = 4,106 / 34,488 = 11.9% (every ₹100 of sales yields ₹11.9 of profit). ROCE = (Operating Profit ₹5,500 Cr) / 15,200 = 36.2% (every ₹100 of capital yields ₹36 of operating profit). Asset Turnover = 34,488 / (Total Assets ₹19,000 Cr) = 1.81x (each rupee of assets generates ₹1.81 of revenue). Same company. Three lenses. Three insights. Notice how the 11.9% margin alone tells you nothing — 11.9% is low for software (Infosys runs 25%+) but exceptional for paints. That is why lenses must be interpreted in context.
formulas.sensitivity_note: If the output metric grows faster than the input metric, the ratio improves — that is the signature of a scaling business. If input grows faster than output, the ratio deteriorates — the signature of value destruction.

formulas.name: The Time-Series Delta
formulas.formula: Year-on-Year Change = (Ratio_Current - Ratio_Prior) / Ratio_Prior × 100

variables.meaning: Ratio in the current period
Ratio in the prior period

formulas.worked_example: TCS ROCE moved from 52% in FY22 to 58% in FY23. YoY change = (58 - 52) / 52 × 100 = +11.5%. A double-digit improvement in an already elite ROCE is a massive signal. Always compute the delta — direction matters as much as the level.
formulas.sensitivity_note: A stable ratio in an industry where peers are declining is actually an improvement. Always benchmark the delta, not just the absolute level.

title: The Pharma Analyst's Toolkit — From ANDA Pipeline To Para IV Economics

formulas.name: US Generics Revenue Forecast Framework
formulas.formula: Forward US Generics Revenue ≈ (Existing Run-Rate Revenue × (1 − Price Erosion %)) + (New Launches × Average Per-Product Revenue × Probability of Approval × Time-Adjusted Capture)

variables.meaning: Current quarterly US generics revenue annualised, representing the existing portfolio's contribution
Industry average 8-12% annually; company-specific can be higher in concentrated portfolios. Subtract from existing revenue to get base decline before new launches
ANDAs approved and launched during forecast period. Average per-product revenue 5-15 million USD for plain vanilla generics; 30-100 million USD for complex generics or Para IV first-to-file
Adjustment for FDA approval timing and probability — typical pending ANDA approval probability 60-75% within 24 months of filing
Fraction of full-year revenue captured in the launch period (e.g., a Q4 launch captures only 25% of annualised revenue in current fiscal year)

formulas.worked_example: Sun Pharma US generics example for FY25 forecast. Existing Run-Rate Revenue (FY24): approximately 1.6 billion USD. Price Erosion assumption: 10% annual decline. Existing portfolio contribution to FY25: 1.6 × (1 − 0.10) = 1.44 billion USD. New launch contribution: estimated 8 ANDA approvals × 12 million USD average = 96 million USD, with 75% probability adjustment = 72 million USD. Time-adjusted capture (assume mid-year launches on average, capturing 50% of annualised revenue): 36 million USD. Total FY25 US generics forecast: 1.44 + 0.036 = 1.48 billion USD, implying 7.5% revenue decline YoY. This is the typical pattern for mature US generics businesses — existing portfolio erodes 10% while new launches add 2-4 percentage points back, netting to mid-single-digit decline. The exception is when companies have a major Para IV first-to-file launch, which can add 50-150 million USD of one-time exclusivity revenue. Lupin's gAlbuterol, Lupin gFortamet, Aurobindo's gValsartan — major Para IV launches that drove individual quarters of 30%+ growth.
formulas.sensitivity_note: US generics revenue forecasting is highly sensitive to three variables: (1) base price erosion assumption — using 8% versus 12% changes the existing portfolio outlook by 4 percentage points; (2) new launch counts and timing — FDA approval delays of even 2 quarters can materially change forward earnings; (3) Para IV exclusivity wins — these are binary events that can change a company's outlook by 20%+ in a single year. Always model US generics with explicit price erosion assumptions and a separate line item for major Para IV launches expected. Don't blend them into a single growth number.

formulas.name: India Formulations Growth Decomposition (IPM Tracking)
formulas.formula: Company India Formulations Growth = (Volume Growth × Volume Mix) + (Price Growth × Price Mix) + (New Product Mix Contribution)     where Volume + Price + New Products ≈ Total Revenue Growth

variables.meaning: Year-on-year growth in physical units (tablets, vials, syrups) sold in the Indian Pharmaceutical Market for each company. Tracked monthly by AIOCD-AWACS at company, therapy, and brand level
Year-on-year growth in average realisation per unit, driven by price hikes within NPPA framework (3-5% annually) and mix shift to higher-priced products
Revenue from products launched in the past 12-24 months — a leading indicator of innovation-driven growth
Distribution across therapy areas (anti-diabetic, cardiovascular, anti-infective, derma, etc.) — chronic therapies (diabetes, cardio, respiratory) are higher-quality than acute (anti-infectives)

formulas.worked_example: Cipla India formulations FY24 example. Total India formulations revenue growth: 9% YoY. Decomposition: Volume Growth +3%, Price Growth +4%, New Products contribution +2%. The 9% growth is healthy — volume growth represents real prescription generation, price growth shows pricing power within NPPA, and new products contribute structural innovation. Compare to a hypothetical scenario where the same 9% revenue growth came from Volume +1%, Price +6%, New Products +2%. The price-led pattern would suggest the company is hitting price ceilings rather than generating new prescriptions — a quality concern. Always decompose IPM growth into Volume, Price, New Products. Companies with healthy decompositions (Cipla, Sun Pharma chronic, Mankind Pharma) are positioned for durable growth; companies with price-led patterns (some mid-cap pharma) face structural sustainability questions. AIOCD-AWACS publishes monthly data; reconcile against company-disclosed numbers in concalls.
formulas.sensitivity_note: IPM growth quality is the highest-priority diagnostic for India formulations analysis. Volume growth above 4-5% is healthy and indicates real prescription momentum. Volume growth below 2% combined with strong price growth signals price-driven optical growth that is unsustainable. Track therapy mix evolution — companies shifting toward chronic therapies (diabetes, cardio, respiratory) get stickier customer bases and longer-term durability. Companies stuck in acute therapies (anti-infectives) face higher generic substitution and pricing pressure.

formulas.name: Hospitals Sector — ARPOB and Occupancy Framework
formulas.formula: Hospital Revenue ≈ Operational Bed Days × Occupancy % × ARPOB     EBITDA Margin Driver = (Occupancy Rate − Break-even Occupancy) × Operating Leverage Coefficient

variables.meaning: Total beds × 365 days. Limits the maximum capacity for revenue generation
Percentage of operational bed days actually filled. Indian hospital industry healthy range 65-75%; below 60% is weak; above 80% is strong
Daily revenue per bed at average occupancy. Apollo Hospitals approximately 60,000 per day; Max Healthcare 50,000-55,000; tier-2 hospitals 25,000-35,000
Approximately 50-55% occupancy is typically break-even due to high fixed costs (doctors, nurses, equipment, real estate). Above this point, operating leverage kicks in

formulas.worked_example: Apollo Hospitals new facility example. New 200-bed hospital in Bengaluru. Operational bed days = 200 × 365 = 73,000. Year 1 occupancy: 45% (ramping up). Year 1 ARPOB: 45,000 (lower than mature facilities). Year 1 Revenue: 73,000 × 0.45 × 45,000 = 148 crore. Year 1 EBITDA likely negative due to fixed costs not being absorbed. Year 3 occupancy: 70%. Year 3 ARPOB: 60,000 (matured). Year 3 Revenue: 73,000 × 0.70 × 60,000 = 307 crore. Year 3 EBITDA margin: 22-25% (operating leverage on fixed costs). The ramp from year 1 to year 3 is 100% revenue growth and EBITDA going from negative to 70 crore. This explains why hospital chains take 3-4 years to fully ramp new facilities, and why margin expansion follows occupancy curves. The biggest hospital analysis errors: (1) extrapolating year 1 metrics — too pessimistic on margin; (2) extrapolating year 3 metrics on new builds — too optimistic on near-term cash flow.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Hospital sector economics are dominated by occupancy curves and fixed-cost operating leverage. Each 5 percentage points of occupancy improvement typically adds 200-300 bps to EBITDA margin. ARPOB growth comes from payer mix (private/insurance versus government schemes), specialty mix (oncology, cardiac, transplants are higher-margin), and price hikes. Track all three drivers separately. The major hospital chains (Apollo, Max, Fortis, Narayana) have very different ARPOB and payer mix profiles — treating them as homogeneous misses critical differentiation.

title: The GDP Formulas Every Analyst Must Know Cold

formulas.name: GDP Expenditure Formula
formulas.formula: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M)

variables.meaning: Private Final Consumption Expenditure (household spending)
Gross Fixed Capital Formation (business + residential + government investment)
Government Final Consumption Expenditure (government operating spending)
Exports of goods and services
Imports of goods and services

formulas.worked_example:
India FY24 (approximate, ₹ lakh crore, current prices):
C = 171.0 (58% share)
I = 91.5 (31% share)
G = 32.4 (11% share)
X - M = -9.9 (-3% share, net imports)
Total GDP = 171.0 + 91.5 + 32.4 + (-9.9) = ₹285 lakh crore

This is nominal GDP. To get real GDP, divide by the deflator (about 1.03 for FY24) → ₹276.7 lakh crore in FY12 prices.
formulas.sensitivity_note: A 1% drop in Private Consumption (C) shaves 0.58% off GDP — which is why monsoon failure, inflation shocks, or rural wage stagnation are red alerts. A 1% drop in Investment (I) shaves 0.31% off GDP — which is why capex cycles dominate market narrative. Government and net exports have smaller direct sensitivities but outsized signalling power.

formulas.name: Real GDP Growth Rate
formulas.formula: Real GDP Growth = ((Real GDP_current / Real GDP_prior) - 1) × 100

variables.meaning: Current period real GDP in constant (FY12) prices
Prior year same-quarter real GDP in constant prices

formulas.worked_example:
Q3 FY24 Real GDP = ₹43.7 lakh crore
Q3 FY23 Real GDP = ₹40.3 lakh crore
Growth = ((43.7 / 40.3) - 1) × 100 = 8.43%

This matches the headline 8.4% print that surprised markets in Feb 2024.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Always compare YoY (year-over-year), never QoQ for Indian GDP — Indian data is not seasonally adjusted at the headline level. Comparing Q3 to Q2 gives nonsense answers because of monsoon, festival, and harvest cycles.

formulas.name: GDP Deflator (Broad Inflation Measure)
formulas.formula: GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100

variables.meaning: GDP in current prices
GDP in constant base-year prices

formulas.worked_example:
FY24 Nominal GDP = ₹295 lakh crore
FY24 Real GDP = ₹172 lakh crore (FY12 prices)
Deflator = (295 / 172) × 100 = 171.5

YoY Deflator Growth = Deflator_FY24 / Deflator_FY23 - 1 = approximately 3-4%, which is the economy's aggregate price inflation.
formulas.sensitivity_note: When CPI inflation and GDP deflator diverge significantly, it signals that non-consumer prices (producer prices, asset prices) are moving differently from consumer prices — often a precursor to margin pressure in corporates.

formulas.name: Output Gap
formulas.formula: Output Gap (%) = ((Actual GDP - Potential GDP) / Potential GDP) × 100

variables.meaning: Realised real GDP in a period
Estimated maximum sustainable GDP at full employment, typically calculated via HP filter or production function

formulas.worked_example:
India FY24 Actual Real GDP growth = 8.2%
India Potential GDP growth estimate = 6.8%
Output Gap = approximately +1.4%

Positive gap → economy running hot → inflation risk → RBI unlikely to cut. This exact logic is why RBI held rates through 2024 despite growth being strong.
formulas.sensitivity_note: A positive output gap is a leading indicator of inflation and rate hikes — typically showing up in CPI with a 6-9 month lag. Professional macro analysts track the gap quarterly.

title: The Audit Signal Severity Framework and Detection Metrics

formulas.name: Audit Opinion Severity Scale
formulas.formula: Severity Score (0-10) based on opinion type and modifications

variables.meaning: Score 0 — baseline, no forensic signal
Score 2-3 — specific matter highlighted, investigate content
Score 5-6 — material issue identified, significant forensic signal
Score 9 — financial statements do not present fairly, extreme signal
Score 9 — auditor cannot form opinion, extreme signal

formulas.worked_example: Running this on three Indian coverage names. HDFC Bank FY23: Unqualified opinion from MSKA and Associates. Severity Score 0. Normal coverage treatment on audit basis alone. Manpasand Beverages FY17 (the last audit before Deloitte's May 2018 resignation): Unqualified opinion but with multiple Emphasis of Matter paragraphs regarding specific balance sheet items and related-party transactions. Severity Score 3. Forensic yellow flag warranting specific examination of the flagged matters. Note that the FY17 Unqualified opinion was Deloitte's last — within 12 months they would resign rather than sign FY18. The Emphasis of Matter paragraphs in FY17 were the specific precursor signals. CG Power FY18: Unqualified opinion with Emphasis of Matter paragraphs on specific inventory and receivables matters, plus Key Audit Matters identifying revenue recognition risks. Severity Score 4. Yellow flag that, combined with the Family 4 working capital signals and Family 6 off-balance-sheet signals from Sessions 7 and 9, produced integrated pre-collapse assessment 12 months before the August 2019 board disclosure. Interpretation framework: Severity Scores 0-2 indicate clean audit with normal coverage implications. 3-5 indicates yellow flag requiring examination of specific matters. 6-8 indicates red flag warranting substantial rating adjustment. 9-10 indicates extreme signal — Adverse, Disclaimer, or resignation — typically warranting immediate Sell rating regardless of any other consideration.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Severity interpretation should incorporate context of the specific matter identified. A qualification regarding a ₹5 crore balance sheet item in a ₹50,000 crore company is proportionally different from a qualification regarding a ₹500 crore item. Always examine materiality alongside severity.

formulas.name: Auditor Change Pattern Analysis
formulas.formula: Change Signal Strength = Base Severity + Timing Modifier + Firm Tier Transition + Explanation Clarity

variables.meaning: 0 for scheduled rotation at 5/10-year mark, 5 for year-end change at odd times, 10 for mid-engagement resignation
0 for end-of-year clean transitions, +3 for transitions with short notice or clear disruption
0 for Big Four to Big Four, +2 for Big Four to mid-tier, +5 for Big Four to smaller firm, -1 for smaller firm to Big Four
0 for clear published reasons (rotation cycle, specific business rationale), +3 for vague or minimal disclosure

formulas.worked_example: Running this on several cases. Manpasand Beverages May 2018 — Deloitte resigned mid-engagement: Base Severity 10, Timing Modifier +3 (short notice), Firm Tier Transition 0 (Deloitte to CNK Associates — mid-tier), Explanation Clarity +3 (vague letter citing 'inability to obtain information'). Total Signal Strength 16. Extreme — essentially the highest possible audit change signal. The stock collapse within weeks validated the interpretation. CG Power auditor transition during FY18 — Emphasis of Matter paragraphs precede subsequent resignation-like event: Base Severity 5 (year-end change), Timing Modifier +2, Firm Tier Transition +2 (Big Four to mid-tier replacement pattern), Explanation Clarity +1. Total Signal Strength 10. Material signal warranting substantial rating adjustment. Scheduled rotation example — Infosys rotating from Deloitte to BSR (Big Four affiliate) in 2018: Base Severity 0 (scheduled rotation), Timing Modifier 0, Firm Tier Transition 0, Explanation Clarity 0. Total Signal Strength 0. No forensic concern. Interpretation thresholds: Signal Strength 0-3 is routine, no forensic concern. 4-7 is yellow flag warranting investigation. 8-12 is material concern requiring rating adjustment. 13-20 is extreme signal often warranting immediate Sell rating.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Pattern analysis should examine multiple years to distinguish one-time events from systematic patterns. A company with Big Four auditor for 10 years that transitions to mid-tier once has different profile than a company that has transitioned through multiple auditors over 5 years.

formulas.name: Audit Firm Tier Assessment
formulas.formula: Firm Tier Classification — Big Four (Tier 1), Mid-tier Indian firms (Tier 2), Smaller firms (Tier 3)

variables.meaning: Deloitte Haskins and Sells, BSR (KPMG affiliate), Walker Chandiok (Grant Thornton/Baker Tilly), SRB and Associates (EY affiliate), Price Waterhouse (PwC), and similar
MSKA and Associates (BDO), Khimji Kunverji, MGB and Co, NGS and Co, Haribhakti, and similar established firms
Smaller Indian CA firms, often local or regional

formulas.worked_example: Classification examples: Reliance Industries FY23 — SRBC and Associates (EY affiliate), Tier 1. Wipro FY23 — Deloitte, Tier 1. TCS FY23 — BSR and Associates, Tier 1. Titan FY23 — Walker Chandiok, Tier 1. Infosys FY23 — Deloitte, Tier 1. Most large-cap Indian companies retain Tier 1 auditors due to regulatory requirements and governance norms. Mid-cap coverage shows more variability — many mid-caps use Tier 2 firms, which is not inherently a forensic concern. The issue arises when companies transition downward in tier. Manpasand Beverages FY18 transition from Deloitte (Tier 1) to CNK Associates (Tier 2 at best) — substantial tier drop combined with resignation pattern. The tier analysis supplements the change pattern analysis. Interpretation: Tier 1 auditor throughout is expected for large-caps, common for mid-caps, positive governance signal. Tier 2 auditor is acceptable for mid-caps with clear business rationale. Tier 3 auditor for listed companies requires specific investigation. Tier downward transitions are forensic signals; upward transitions suggest improving governance.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Tier classification is not a quality verdict. Some Tier 2 firms provide excellent audit quality for mid-cap clients. The forensic signal is in tier transitions and specific firm-client fit considerations, not in absolute tier levels.

formulas.name: Regulatory Action Signal Framework
formulas.formula: Regulatory Signal = NFRA Actions + ICAI Disciplinary + SEBI Actions + PCAOB Actions (if US-listed)

variables.meaning: National Financial Reporting Authority actions against specific auditors or firms — established 2018
Institute of Chartered Accountants of India disciplinary proceedings against individual auditors or firms
Securities and Exchange Board of India actions specifically related to audit failures or auditor conduct
Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (US) actions affecting Indian audit firms serving US-listed clients

formulas.worked_example: Examples of regulatory action signals. PwC debarment from auditing listed companies in India January 2018 by SEBI — following Satyam 2009 fraud, PwC was barred from conducting statutory audits of listed companies for two years. Any company switching from PwC to other firm during this period had specific context. NFRA disciplinary actions against specific auditor-firm-company combinations have been published since 2019 and should be consulted when evaluating any company's audit context. ICAI reviews and censures of individual chartered accountants or firms provide relevant context. The cumulative regulatory signal framework is informational — actions against specific firms make their future engagements subject to greater scrutiny; actions against specific individuals make their future opinions less credible. Detection technique: for any coverage name, check whether the current auditor has been subject to any material regulatory action in the prior 5 years. Check whether the auditor was connected to any major Indian audit failures. Adjust Severity Scores accordingly.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Regulatory actions provide context but should not be over-weighted. Most Big Four and mid-tier firms have clean regulatory history, and occasional actions against specific individuals do not automatically impugn firm-level capacity. The signal is cumulative and pattern-based rather than single-event.
