title: The Full Margin Walk — Revenue to PAT, Layer by Layer

formulas.name: Gross Margin
formulas.formula: Gross Margin % = (Revenue from Operations − Cost of Goods Sold) / Revenue from Operations × 100

variables.meaning: Top line excluding Other Income — always the correct denominator for operating ratios
Cost of materials consumed + purchases of stock-in-trade + changes in inventories of finished goods/WIP. For services firms, COGS is direct project-linked employee cost.

formulas.worked_example:
Asian Paints FY23:
Revenue from Operations: ₹34,489 cr
Cost of Materials Consumed: ₹20,117 cr
Purchases of Stock-in-Trade: ₹1,020 cr
Changes in Inventory: ₹(210) cr (decrease means add back)
Total COGS: ₹20,927 cr
Gross Margin = (34,489 − 20,927) / 34,489 = 39.3%

For context, Asian Paints gross margin was 44.1% in FY21 — compressed 480 bps over two years due to titanium dioxide inflation. When TiO2 eased in FY24, gross margin expanded back to ~43%. This single metric — gross margin — is the cleanest signal of raw material cycle positioning for any goods-producing business.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Gross margin compression of 100 bps on Asian Paints' revenue base of ₹34,000 cr equals ₹340 cr of lost EBITDA — roughly 15% of annual EBITDA. Raw material cycle sensitivity in paints, chemicals, FMCG can be material.

formulas.name: EBITDA and EBITDA Margin
formulas.formula: EBITDA = Revenue from Operations − COGS − Employee Benefits − Other Operating Expenses + Other Operating Income (only). EBITDA Margin % = EBITDA / Revenue from Operations × 100

variables.meaning: Salaries, wages, ESOP cost, PF, gratuity — for services firms this is the largest operating cost
SG&A, freight, advertising, power, repairs, legal, rent (where not capitalized under Ind AS 116)
Scrap sales, export incentives, operating-related recoveries — included in EBITDA. Does NOT include treasury or investment income.

formulas.worked_example:
TCS FY24:
Revenue from Operations: ₹2,40,893 cr
Employee Benefits: ₹1,39,310 cr (57.8% of revenue)
Other Operating Expenses: ₹37,383 cr (15.5% of revenue)
Total Operating Costs: ₹1,76,693 cr
EBITDA: ₹64,200 cr
EBITDA Margin: 26.7%

The insight: TCS operates at a textbook IT services cost structure — employee cost dominates at 57.8%, reflecting the people-intensive nature of the business. Contrast with Asian Paints where employee cost is 6.8% of revenue and raw materials are 58%. Entirely different businesses, entirely different cost architectures.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For IT services firms, a 100 bps wage inflation translates to approximately 60 bps of EBITDA margin compression (given employee cost is ~60% of revenue). For TCS, that's ₹1,440 cr of EBITDA at risk per 100 bps wage cycle.

formulas.name: Operating Leverage Coefficient
formulas.formula: Operating Leverage = % Change in EBITDA / % Change in Revenue

variables.meaning: A coefficient showing how much EBITDA moves for a given revenue move. Higher values mean more fixed-cost intensity.

formulas.worked_example:
UltraTech Cement FY23 → FY24:
Revenue: ₹62,760 cr → ₹72,500 cr (+15.5%)
EBITDA: ₹11,430 cr → ₹14,100 cr (+23.4%)
Operating Leverage = 23.4% / 15.5% = 1.51x

Cement companies typically run operating leverage of 1.4x to 2.0x — meaning every 1% of revenue growth drops roughly 1.5–2x to EBITDA. This is why cement earnings are so volatile — a 10% revenue decline (cement down-cycle) can produce 15–20% EBITDA decline. Compare to HUL at ~1.1x operating leverage (low fixed cost, near-variable cost structure).
formulas.sensitivity_note: Operating leverage > 1.5x is a red flag for cyclical businesses — they'll miss EBITDA estimates badly in any revenue softness quarter. Operating leverage near 1.0x (HUL, Nestlé) means earnings track revenue closely, which markets reward with multiple premium.

title: The Three Golden Integrity Equations

formulas.name: The Balance Sheet Identity
formulas.formula: Total Assets = Total Liabilities + Total Equity

variables.meaning: Everything the company owns — cash, receivables, inventory, PP&E, intangibles
Everything the company owes — payables, debt, deferred tax, provisions
Shareholders' residual claim — share capital + reserves + retained earnings

formulas.worked_example: Titan FY24: Total Assets = ₹23,512 cr. Total Liabilities = ₹14,890 cr. Total Equity = ₹8,622 cr. Check: 14,890 + 8,622 = 23,512. ✓ Balanced. In your model, you will build a cell that computes Assets − (Liabilities + Equity). If it is ever anything other than zero (or a rounding difference below ₹0.01 cr), your model is broken. This single cell, at the top of your Balance Sheet tab, is the most important formula in the entire workbook.
formulas.sensitivity_note: If the balance sheet does not balance, do not proceed. Do not forecast the next year. Do not start the DCF. Fix it first. 95% of the time the error is in the Cash Flow Statement linkage — a missing item in CFO, a sign error in capex, or a debt movement that was not flowed through.

formulas.name: The Cash Flow Reconciliation
formulas.formula: Closing Cash = Opening Cash + CFO + CFI + CFF

variables.meaning: Cash balance at the start of the period, pulled from prior year BS
Cash Flow from Operations — cash generated by running the business
Cash Flow from Investing — cash spent on capex, acquisitions, investments
Cash Flow from Financing — cash from debt issuance, equity, less dividends and repayments

formulas.worked_example: Titan FY24: Opening Cash ₹1,240 cr + CFO ₹2,860 cr + CFI (−₹1,920 cr) + CFF (−₹380 cr) = Closing Cash ₹1,800 cr. The Closing Cash figure must equal the Cash line on the Balance Sheet at year-end. If it doesn't, your statements are disconnected — which means your model is lying.
formulas.sensitivity_note: This is the second integrity check. Build a cell that computes (CFS Closing Cash − BS Cash). It must be zero. If it isn't, you have a linkage error — usually a missing item in CFO (like a non-cash expense you forgot to add back) or a double-counted item in CFF.

formulas.name: The Retained Earnings Roll
formulas.formula: Closing Retained Earnings = Opening Retained Earnings + Net Income − Dividends

variables.meaning: Prior year closing RE from the BS
Bottom line of the IS for the current year
Cash paid to shareholders, pulled from CFF

formulas.worked_example: Titan FY24: Opening RE ₹7,100 cr + Net Income ₹3,496 cr − Dividends ₹1,510 cr = Closing RE ₹9,086 cr. This closing figure flows directly into the Equity section of the current year Balance Sheet. If you break this link, retained earnings will not grow correctly, and the BS will not balance.
formulas.sensitivity_note: This is the third integrity check and the one most often broken by beginners. The mistake is usually either forgetting to link dividends from CFF into the RE roll, or linking Net Income to the wrong year. Always trace the formula: RE_current = RE_prior + NI_current − Dividends_current.

title: PED, HHI, and Lerner Index with Worked Examples

formulas.name: Price Elasticity of Demand
formulas.formula: PED = (% Change Qty Demanded) / (% Change Price)
formulas.analyst_note: Rarely calculate with formula. Observe pricing events and track volume response in next 1-2 quarters. Consistent price hikes without volume loss = demonstrated inelastic demand = strongest buy signal.
formulas.worked_example: Airtel raises recharge Rs 199 to Rs 219 (+10.1%). Subscribers drop 35.5cr to 34.8cr (-2.0%). PED = -2.0%/10.1% = -0.20. Highly inelastic -- strong pricing power.

formulas.name: Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI)
formulas.formula: HHI = Sum of (Market Share %)^2
formulas.worked_example: Indian Telecom: Jio 40%, Airtel 33%, Vi 20%, Others 7%. HHI = 1600+1089+400+49 = 3,138. Highly concentrated oligopoly. Pricing power improving as consolidation deepens.

formulas.name: Lerner Index
formulas.formula: (Price - Marginal Cost) / Price
formulas.interpretation: 0.6 = 60% of price is markup. Luxury brands and patent-protected pharma often above 0.7.

title: The Four Cash Flow Forensic Adjustments

formulas.name: Normalised CFO (Classification-Adjusted)
formulas.formula: Normalised CFO = Reported CFO − Interest Paid (if classified in financing) − Dividends Paid (if classified in financing) + Interest Received (if classified in investing) + Dividends Received (if classified in investing)

variables.meaning: Cash flow from operating activities as reported in the cash flow statement
Interest expense paid during the year, from borrowing costs note or cash flow financing section
Dividends paid to equity shareholders during the year
Interest income received during the year, from other income breakdown
Dividend income received from investments during the year

formulas.worked_example: For Reliance Industries FY23: Reported CFO ₹1,24,440 crore. Interest paid during the year (classified in financing) ₹22,520 crore. Dividends paid (classified in financing) ₹6,763 crore. Interest received (classified in investing) ₹12,450 crore. Dividends received (classified in investing) ₹2,310 crore. Normalised CFO under global IFRS convention: 1,24,440 − 22,520 − 6,763 + 12,450 + 2,310 = ₹1,09,917 crore. The classification adjustment reduces reported CFO by ₹14,523 crore, or roughly 12 percent. For valuation metrics that use CFO — EV/CFO, P/CFO, or CFO-based DCF — this difference materially changes the multiples. A stock trading at 8x reported CFO trades at 9.1x normalised CFO. When benchmarking Reliance against Exxon Mobil or Saudi Aramco (which classify interest in operating), using unadjusted CFO systematically favours Reliance's apparent cash generation versus peers. The analyst who normalises makes apples-to-apples comparisons; the analyst who does not is systematically wrong-footed. For ICICI Bank FY23: Reported CFO ₹68,450 crore. Interest paid classified in financing ₹27,890 crore. Normalised CFO: 68,450 − 27,890 = ₹40,560 crore. The adjustment is 40 percent of reported CFO for a bank. This is the magnitude that makes classification analysis non-optional for financial sector coverage.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Normalisation should be applied consistently across peer sets. If some peers classify interest in operating and others in financing, normalise all to one convention (typically operating, for comparability with global IFRS and consistency with P&L treatment). Always disclose the adjustment in research notes.

formulas.name: Adjusted Free Cash Flow
formulas.formula: Adjusted FCF = Normalised CFO − Capital Expenditure − Capitalised Interest (add back to keep consistent with expensed interest)

variables.meaning: CFO adjusted for interest and dividend classification as computed above
Cash outflow for purchase of property, plant, equipment, and intangibles from investing activities section
Interest capitalised into assets under construction during the year, disclosed in Ind AS 23 borrowing costs note

formulas.worked_example: For a hypothetical mid-cap infrastructure company FY23: Reported CFO ₹2,400 crore. Interest paid (financing) ₹1,800 crore. Capex ₹1,200 crore. Capitalised interest ₹1,500 crore. Reported FCF (by many research conventions) = 2,400 − 1,200 = ₹1,200 crore. But this overstates true cash generation dramatically. Normalised CFO = 2,400 − 1,800 = ₹600 crore. Note that the ₹1,500 crore of capitalised interest is sitting in the investing section as part of capex (not in interest paid), so we do not double-count it. Adjusted FCF = 600 − 1,200 − 0 (capitalised interest already in capex) = −₹600 crore. The company is actually burning cash, not generating it. The 3,600 crore gap between reported FCF and adjusted FCF captures the combined effect of interest classification choice plus interest capitalisation — two Family 2 and Family 6 patterns compounding. Applied to real Indian infrastructure names during FY15-FY20 construction phases, the reported FCF was consistently positive ₹500-2,000 crore while adjusted FCF was consistently negative ₹1,500-4,000 crore. Investors who used reported FCF in DCF models systematically overvalued these companies. Investors who used adjusted FCF correctly identified them as value traps.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Maintenance capex versus growth capex distinction matters here. For a steady-state business, adjusted FCF should be positive after covering maintenance capex. For a growth-phase business, some years of negative adjusted FCF are normal but must be financed by debt or equity raises — check the financing section for the funding source.

formulas.name: Quality of Earnings (QoE) Ratio
formulas.formula: QoE Ratio = CFO / Net Income (PAT) × 100

variables.meaning: Cash flow from operating activities (use reported or normalised depending on comparison purpose)
Profit after tax from the income statement, attributable to parent

formulas.worked_example: This is the Session 2 ratio revisited with forensic refinement. For HUL FY23: CFO ₹9,480 crore against PAT ₹10,120 crore = QoE Ratio of 94 percent. This is excellent — nearly every rupee of reported profit is converting to cash, consistent with a mature FMCG business with strong working capital discipline. For Titan Company FY23: CFO ₹3,890 crore against PAT ₹3,268 crore = QoE Ratio of 119 percent. Above 100 percent because working capital released during the year and non-cash charges were substantial. Also excellent. For a hypothetical mid-cap industrial company: CFO ₹240 crore against PAT ₹545 crore = QoE Ratio of 44 percent. Severely deficient — less than half of reported profit is converting to cash. The remaining ₹305 crore is being absorbed somewhere (working capital, other current assets, or classification choice). This level of QoE Ratio warrants immediate investigation. Sector benchmarks: FMCG 85-105 percent (Hindustan Unilever, Dabur, Nestle typically in this range); IT services 95-115 percent (TCS, Infosys, Wipro); pharma 85-110 percent (Sun Pharma, Cipla, Lupin); consumer durables 80-100 percent; capital goods 70-100 percent (more volatile due to project cycles); real estate N/A (inventory cycles make ratio less meaningful). Anything persistently below 70 percent for 3-plus years is a strong manipulation signal.
formulas.sensitivity_note: QoE Ratio should be computed over 3-5 year windows, not single years, because working capital timing creates natural single-year variation. The cumulative ratio is more diagnostic than any single year. Also normalise QoE using classification-adjusted CFO when comparing across companies with different interest classification conventions.

formulas.name: Cash Flow Composition Analysis
formulas.formula: Composition percentages: CFO / Total Cash Inflows from All Three Buckets × 100; Investing / Total × 100; Financing / Total × 100

variables.meaning: Sum of absolute values of all three bucket cash flows, used as a baseline

formulas.worked_example: A healthy steady-state company typically shows roughly 50-70 percent of its absolute cash flows from operating, modest negative investing (maintenance capex), and modest negative financing (debt servicing, dividends). A growth-phase company shows lower operating percentage and higher investing outflow. A distress-phase company shows weak operating, minimal investing, and high financing inflows (raising capital to survive). For Reliance Industries FY23: Operating CFO ₹1,24,440 crore, Investing −₹1,43,560 crore (heavy Jio and Retail capex), Financing ₹5,820 crore. Pattern consistent with growth-phase investment cycle funded by operating cash flow and modest financing. For a hypothetical distressed company: Operating CFO ₹180 crore, Investing ₹120 crore (asset sales generating cash), Financing ₹680 crore (raising debt). Pattern reveals operating cash flow is insufficient and the company is funding operations through asset sales and borrowing — a liquidity stress signal that P&L alone would miss. Specifically track the ratio of Financing Cash Inflows / Operating CFO — if consistently above 30 percent, the company is not self-funding and is structurally dependent on capital markets. This is a vulnerability that changes dramatically when capital markets tighten.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Cash flow composition must be analysed over multi-year windows — single years can reflect specific financing rounds or asset sales that are not representative. A company may legitimately fund growth-phase investing through financing for 3-5 years, but distress patterns show up as financing dependence combined with weak operating.

title: The PAT-CFO Reconciliation — Three Forms, One Truth

formulas.name: Cumulative Cash Conversion Ratio (CCR)
formulas.formula: CCR = Σ CFO(t-n to t) / Σ PAT(t-n to t) × 100

variables.meaning: Sum of Cash Flow from Operations (as reported in cash flow statement) over the chosen window
Sum of Profit After Tax (from consolidated P&L) over the same window
Window length — minimum 3 years, ideal 5 years, gold standard 10 years

formulas.worked_example: Running this on TCS, FY19-FY23: Cumulative PAT = ₹38,449 + 32,447 + 38,327 + 42,147 + 42,303 = ₹1,93,673 crore. Cumulative CFO = ₹36,476 + 35,335 + 41,477 + 39,545 + 42,963 = ₹1,95,796 crore. CCR = 1,95,796 / 1,93,673 = 101%. Interpretation: TCS converts every rupee of reported profit into slightly more than a rupee of cash, because non-cash depreciation adds back while working capital is tightly managed. This is world-class cash conversion. Now running the same on Manpasand Beverages, FY13-FY17: Cumulative PAT = ₹21 + 29 + 42 + 67 + 203 = ₹362 crore. Cumulative CFO = ₹13 + 18 + 26 + 8 + 19 = ₹84 crore. CCR = 84 / 362 = 23%. Interpretation: Only 23% of reported profit is converting into cash. The remaining 77% — ₹278 crore — must be sitting somewhere on the balance sheet. That is the forensic finding. Next step: drill into which working capital line absorbed it.
formulas.sensitivity_note: CCR is most reliable over 5+ year windows because short-term swings in working capital (one-off customer delays, genuine inventory build before capacity ramp) can produce misleading single-year ratios. Always look at cumulative over 5 years, not year-by-year.

formulas.name: Phantom Profit Identification
formulas.formula: Phantom Profit (approx) = Σ PAT − Σ CFO − Σ Genuine Non-Cash Items Already Added Back in CFO

variables.meaning: Cumulative reported profit over the window
Cumulative operating cash flow over the window

Since CFO (indirect method) already adds back depreciation, amortisation, and most non-cash items to PAT, the residual gap after subtracting CFO from PAT captures working capital movement + any unusual adjustments. You do not need to add back depreciation separately — the CFO figure already has.

formulas.worked_example: For Manpasand FY13-FY17: Phantom Profit = ₹362 cr − ₹84 cr = ₹278 crore. This ₹278 crore sits on the balance sheet as accumulated working capital growth. Opening this up: receivables went from ₹24 cr (FY13) to ₹269 cr (FY17) — a ₹245 cr increase, absorbing most of the gap. Inventory went from ₹21 cr to ₹86 cr, absorbing another ₹65 cr. Offset by ₹30 cr increase in payables. Net working capital absorbed ₹280 cr — matching the ₹278 cr gap within rounding. Now the forensic question crystallises: why did receivables grow 11x when revenue grew only 4x? That is the question Manpasand management could never answer in concalls.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Legitimate reasons for temporary gaps exist — rapid growth does absorb working capital, commodity cycles can swing inventory. But over 5 years, genuine businesses normalise. Gaps that persist past 5 years and keep widening are not growth-driven — they are manipulation-driven or terminal-demand-driven, and both end badly.

formulas.name: Free Cash Flow Reality Check
formulas.formula: FCF = CFO − Capex (Maintenance + Growth)

variables.meaning: Reported cash flow from operations
Cash outflow for purchase of property, plant, equipment, and intangibles (from investing section of cash flow statement)

formulas.worked_example: For Asian Paints FY23: CFO = ₹4,837 cr. Capex = ₹1,324 cr. FCF = ₹3,513 cr. Cross-check vs PAT of ₹4,168 cr: FCF/PAT = 84%, confirming healthy cash generation and genuine reinvestment. For a company with CCR below 50% AND capex exceeding CFO year after year, the math breaks — they are not generating cash and yet spending on capex, which means capex is being funded by debt or equity raises. This is the pattern visible in DHFL 2016-2018 and Reliance Communications 2014-2018 before both collapsed.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Distinguish maintenance capex (needed to keep the current business running) from growth capex (optional, for expansion). A business should cover maintenance capex from CFO even in a bad year. A business that cannot fund maintenance capex from CFO has broken economics.

title: The Classification Decision Logic — Three Tests to Place Any Stock Correctly

formulas.name: GICS Primary Sector Test (Revenue-Based Rule)
formulas.formula: Primary Sector = Sector contributing > 50% of consolidated revenue OR > 50% of consolidated EBITDA, whichever is more representative of business identity

variables.meaning: Percentage of total consolidated revenue from each business segment (use latest annual report segment disclosures)
Percentage of total consolidated EBITDA from each business segment (better for cases where revenue mix and profit mix diverge)
When neither segment crosses 50%, classify by primary EBITDA contributor, growth driver, and management commentary

formulas.worked_example: Reliance Industries FY24 segment data: O2C (Oil-to-Chemicals): Revenue ~52%, EBITDA ~37%. Digital Services (Jio): Revenue ~14%, EBITDA ~32%. Retail: Revenue ~26%, EBITDA ~17%. Oil & Gas E&P: Revenue ~3%, EBITDA ~6%. Other: ~5%/8%. Applying the 50% rule on revenue: O2C dominates at 52%, so GICS Primary Sector = Energy. But EBITDA tells a different story — O2C is only 37% of EBITDA, with Digital Services and Retail combined contributing 49%. This is why GICS classifies Reliance under Energy (revenue rule) but most analysts also track it as a Conglomerate with sum-of-parts (SOTP) valuation. The key insight: the classification rule gives you a label, but the analyst must understand the underlying mix to value it correctly. A pure Energy multiple on Reliance would dramatically undervalue the Jio and Retail businesses — which is exactly why Reliance was historically considered 'undervalued' for years until the SOTP narrative caught on.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Classification can shift over time as business mix evolves. Bajaj Finance was once classified deep in NBFC peer groups; as it scaled, it got reclassified into broader Financials and started benchmarking against private banks — its multiple expanded materially. Watch for 'reclassification triggers': segment crosses 50%, listed subsidiary spin-off, large acquisition in a different sector, or formal MSCI/Nifty index reclassification.

formulas.name: Cyclical vs Defensive Decision Rule (Earnings Volatility Test)
formulas.formula: Earnings Cyclicality = StDev(Annual EBITDA Growth, 10-year period) ÷ Mean(Annual EBITDA Growth, 10-year period). If ratio > 2.0 → Cyclical. If ratio < 0.7 → Defensive. Between → Semi-Cyclical / Structural Growth.

variables.meaning: Standard deviation of year-on-year EBITDA growth rates over a 10-year window — captures volatility
Average year-on-year EBITDA growth rate over the same window — captures trend
The ratio is technically the coefficient of variation; higher values mean earnings swing dramatically relative to their average

formulas.worked_example: Tata Steel 10-year EBITDA growth (FY15 to FY24): swings from -45% to +180%. StDev ≈ 75%, Mean ≈ 18%. Ratio = 75/18 = 4.2 → clearly Cyclical. HUL 10-year EBITDA growth: ranges from +6% to +14%. StDev ≈ 3%, Mean ≈ 9%. Ratio = 3/9 = 0.33 → clearly Defensive. TCS 10-year EBITDA growth: ranges from +8% to +22%. StDev ≈ 5%, Mean ≈ 13%. Ratio = 5/13 = 0.38 → Defensive characteristics, but with secular growth → classified as Structural Growth. The ratio gives you an objective, data-driven taxonomy beyond gut feel.
formulas.sensitivity_note: 10-year window is critical — shorter windows can mislead. Indian Banks looked Defensive on a 5-year window from 2019-2024 (post-NPA cleanup) but were extremely Cyclical on a 10-year window including the 2014-2018 NPA crisis. Always extend the window to capture at least one full cycle.

title: The Investor Decision Math — Sector Allocation, Stock Picking, and Hybrid Frameworks

formulas.name: Top-Down Sector Allocation
formulas.formula: Sector Weight = Base Weight x Macro Tilt Factor x Sector Beta

variables.meaning: Neutral sector allocation (e.g., index weight)
Adjustment based on composite leading indicator score: +1.5x for expansion, 0.5x for contraction
Sector sensitivity to leading indicators (Realty 2.5x, mid-caps 1.8x, FMCG 0.4x)

formulas.worked_example:
Example: Portfolio Construction in Different Macro Regimes

Neutral allocation (composite score 0):
- Banks: 22 percent
- Mid-caps: 18 percent
- Capital goods: 12 percent
- IT services: 12 percent
- Pharma: 10 percent
- FMCG: 12 percent
- Other: 14 percent

In an expansion regime (composite score +1.0):
Macro Tilt = +1.5x for cyclicals, 0.5x for defensives

- Banks: 22 x 1.5 = 33 percent (overweight)
- Mid-caps: 18 x 1.5 = 27 percent (overweight)
- Capital goods: 12 x 1.5 = 18 percent (overweight)
- IT services: 12 x 0.5 = 6 percent (underweight)
- Pharma: 10 x 0.7 = 7 percent (slightly underweight)
- FMCG: 12 x 0.4 = 5 percent (underweight)
- Other: 14 percent
- Adjusted total: 110 percent (must normalize to 100)

In a contraction regime (composite score -1.0):
Macro Tilt = 0.5x for cyclicals, 1.5x for defensives

- Banks: 22 x 0.5 = 11 percent (underweight)
- Mid-caps: 18 x 0.5 = 9 percent (underweight)
- Capital goods: 12 x 0.5 = 6 percent (underweight)
- IT services: 12 x 1.5 = 18 percent (overweight)
- Pharma: 10 x 1.5 = 15 percent (overweight)
- FMCG: 12 x 1.5 = 18 percent (overweight)
- Other: 14 percent
- Cash: increase to 10 percent
- Adjusted total: 90 percent equities + 10 percent cash

The top-down framework systematically tilts the portfolio based on the macro regime. In an expansion, cyclicals dominate. In a contraction, defensives dominate.

Historical performance: This systematic top-down tilt has generated 6-10 percent annual outperformance vs static (neutral) allocation across major macro regimes since 2007.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The macro tilt factor must be calibrated to current regime. During panic phases (March 2020 COVID), tilt factors should be more aggressive (2.0x for cyclicals during recovery). During calm regimes, tilt factors compress to 1.2x. Adjust based on regime intensity, not just direction.

formulas.name: Bottom-Up Stock Selection
formulas.formula: Stock Score = (DCF Upside x Confidence) + (Quality Score x Multiplier) + (Catalyst Probability x Magnitude)

variables.meaning: DCF-based intrinsic value vs current market price (percentage)
Subjective confidence in the DCF inputs (0-1 scale)
Composite of ROE, moat depth, management quality (0-10 scale)
Probability of upcoming positive catalyst (0-1 scale)
Expected stock price impact of catalyst (percentage)

formulas.worked_example:
Example: HDFC Bank Bottom-Up Analysis (October 2024)

DCF Analysis:
- Forecasted FCF growth: 14 percent CAGR for 5 years
- Terminal growth: 5 percent
- Cost of equity: 11 percent
- Implied intrinsic value: 1,950 INR
- Current price: 1,720 INR
- DCF Upside: 13 percent
- Confidence: 0.7 (high confidence — strong fundamentals)
- DCF Component: 13 percent x 0.7 = 9.1 percent

Quality Score:
- ROE: 19 percent (excellent)
- Moat: Deep (largest private bank, dominant retail franchise)
- Management quality: Excellent (consistent execution under multiple CEOs)
- Asset quality: Strong (NPAs at 1.4 percent)
- Quality Score: 9 of 10
- Multiplier: 0.5 (premium for quality)
- Quality Component: 9 x 0.5 = 4.5 percent

Catalyst Probability:
- Catalyst: Merger synergies materialization
- Probability: 0.6 (some uncertainty on integration)
- Magnitude: 8 percent (potential ROE improvement)
- Catalyst Component: 0.6 x 8 = 4.8 percent

Total Stock Score: 9.1 + 4.5 + 4.8 = 18.4 (very strong)

For a portfolio with 10 high-conviction names, HDFC Bank scores in top 3.
Position size recommendation: 8-10 percent of portfolio.

Comparison with peers:
- ICICI Bank: Score 16.2 (slightly less attractive)
- Kotak Bank: Score 14.8 (good but premium valuation)
- SBI: Score 13.5 (decent but PSU concerns)

The bottom-up framework systematically ranks stocks within a sector. It enables data-driven stock selection regardless of macro environment.
formulas.sensitivity_note: DCF inputs are the most uncertain component. Use ranges (e.g., 12-16 percent FCF growth instead of 14 percent). Calculate base, optimistic, and pessimistic scenarios. The Stock Score should reflect this range, not point estimates.

formulas.name: Hybrid Framework Position Size
formulas.formula: Position Size = Base x (Top-Down Conviction) x (Bottom-Up Conviction) x (Risk Adjustment)

variables.meaning: Neutral position size (typically 1-2 percent for individual stocks)
Confidence in macro/sector thesis (0.5x to 2x)
Confidence in stock-specific thesis (0.5x to 2x)
Volatility, liquidity, correlation considerations (0.5x to 1x)

formulas.worked_example:
Example: Position Sizing Decision Tree

Scenario A: High top-down + high bottom-up conviction (rare — 5-10 stocks)
- Macro regime favors sector strongly
- Stock has excellent fundamentals + valuation
- Example: Federal Bank in 2023 (rate-sensitive sector during pivot + private bank quality)
- Top-down conviction: 1.8x
- Bottom-up conviction: 1.7x
- Risk adjustment: 0.95x
- Position size: 1.5 percent x 1.8 x 1.7 x 0.95 = 4.4 percent (large position)

Scenario B: High top-down + medium bottom-up
- Sector favored but stock has some concerns
- Example: Cement major during real estate recovery (sector good, individual cement names mixed)
- Top-down conviction: 1.5x
- Bottom-up conviction: 1.0x
- Risk adjustment: 0.9x
- Position size: 1.5 percent x 1.5 x 1.0 x 0.9 = 2.0 percent (medium position)

Scenario C: Medium top-down + high bottom-up
- Sector neutral but excellent stock
- Example: HDFC Bank during normal banking sector regime
- Top-down conviction: 1.0x
- Bottom-up conviction: 1.6x
- Risk adjustment: 0.95x
- Position size: 1.5 percent x 1.0 x 1.6 x 0.95 = 2.3 percent (medium-strong position)

Scenario D: Low top-down + low bottom-up
- Both are neutral or weak
- Result: skip the position

Scenario E: Top-down strongly negative + bottom-up positive
- Macro headwinds but stock-specific positives
- Example: Mid-cap stock during Fed hike cycle
- Top-down conviction: 0.6x (against)
- Bottom-up conviction: 1.4x (for)
- Result: maintain small position (1.5 x 0.6 x 1.4 x 0.95 = 1.2 percent — below average)

The hybrid framework forces explicit reasoning across both dimensions. It prevents one-dimensional thinking that leads to the +85 percent vs -12 percent dispersion in the opening hook example.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Position sizing should reflect total portfolio risk. A 4.4 percent position in one stock with 4 percent positions in correlated names creates concentration risk. Always consider portfolio-level constraints. Maximum single position: 5-7 percent. Maximum sector concentration: 25-30 percent.

formulas.name: Long-Term Compounding vs Tactical Rotation
formulas.formula: Compound Return = (1 + r_macro) x (1 + r_stock) x (1 + r_compounding)

variables.meaning: Annualized return from sector rotation (top-down)
Annualized return from stock selection (bottom-up)
Annualized return from holding quality compounders

formulas.worked_example:
10-Year Return Decomposition (Indian Equity Fund):

Fund A (Pure Bottom-Up):
- Stock selection alpha: +5 percent annual
- Compounding from quality: +9 percent annual (quality compounders avg)
- Total: +14 percent annual
- 10-year compound: 270 percent total
- But experienced full 2008 (-58 percent), 2020 (-37 percent) drawdowns

Fund B (Pure Top-Down):
- Sector rotation alpha: +6 percent annual
- Stock selection alpha: 0 percent (low)
- Compounding: 0 percent (low — too much trading)
- Total: +9 percent annual (lower than benchmark)
- 10-year compound: 137 percent
- Avoided major drawdowns but missed compounding

Fund C (Hybrid):
- Sector rotation alpha: +3 percent annual
- Stock selection alpha: +3 percent annual
- Compounding from quality: +7 percent annual
- Total: +13 percent annual
- 10-year compound: 240 percent
- Avoided 50 percent of major drawdowns; captured 70 percent of compounding

The hybrid approach captures 80-90 percent of pure bottom-up returns while reducing volatility through macro positioning. The improvement in Sharpe ratio is meaningful.

For most investors, the hybrid framework is optimal:
- Avoid the 2008 GFC and 2020 COVID drawdowns of -50 percent each
- Capture the 25 percent rallies that follow
- Hold quality compounders through multiple cycles
- Generate 12-15 percent annual returns with lower volatility

The pure top-down approach often underperforms because too much trading erodes compounding. The pure bottom-up approach often underperforms because catastrophic drawdowns destroy compounding. The hybrid balances both.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Long-term compound returns depend critically on avoiding catastrophic drawdowns. A 50 percent drawdown requires 100 percent gain to recover. The hybrid framework reduces drawdowns more than it sacrifices upside, generating better risk-adjusted returns.

formulas.name: Cash Allocation Decision Math
formulas.formula: Cash Percentage = max(0, (Composite Score - threshold) x scaling factor + base)

variables.meaning: Current composite leading indicator score
Score below which cash should be added (e.g., -0.5)
How aggressively cash should be increased per unit of negative score (e.g., 8 percent per unit)
Minimum cash level (typically 3-5 percent for opportunistic capacity)

formulas.worked_example:
Cash Allocation by Composite Score:

Composite Score +1.0 to +2.0 (strong expansion):
- Cash: 5 percent (base only)
- Equity: 95 percent
- Reasoning: macro is strong; deploy fully

Composite Score 0 to +1.0 (mild expansion):
- Cash: 5-8 percent
- Equity: 92-95 percent
- Reasoning: positive but not strong; small buffer

Composite Score -0.5 to 0 (slowdown forming):
- Cash: 8-12 percent
- Equity: 88-92 percent
- Reasoning: building defensive positioning

Composite Score -1.0 to -0.5 (modest contraction):
- Cash: 12-18 percent
- Equity: 82-88 percent
- Reasoning: defensive positioning with opportunistic capacity

Composite Score -1.5 to -1.0 (significant contraction):
- Cash: 18-25 percent
- Equity: 75-82 percent
- Reasoning: aggressive defensive positioning

Composite Score below -1.5 (severe contraction):
- Cash: 25-35 percent
- Equity: 65-75 percent
- Reasoning: maximum defensive; preserve capital

The cash allocation acts as a circuit breaker preventing catastrophic drawdowns. The 2008 GFC and 2020 COVID would have caused massive losses without cash buffers. The 2023 Fed pivot recovery rewarded those who had cash to deploy.

For portfolio: integrate cash allocation with sector rotation. Together they form the top-down framework. Bottom-up determines what stocks to hold within the equity allocation; top-down determines how much equity vs cash and which sectors to overweight.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Cash allocation should respect investor mandate. A long-only fund may have maximum 10 percent cash. A balanced fund may go to 30 percent. The framework adjusts within these constraints. Also consider opportunity cost — holding cash during bull markets creates underperformance. Use cash strategically, not permanently.

title: CAPM and the Beta Levering Equations

formulas.name: Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)
formulas.formula: Ke = Rf + β × ERP

variables.meaning: Cost of equity — the annual return required by equity investors
Risk-free rate — typically the 10-year G-Sec yield in India
Beta — sensitivity of the stock's returns to the broader market
Equity risk premium = Rm - Rf, where Rm is the expected market return

formulas.worked_example: For HDFC Bank: Rf = 6.8% (current 10-year G-Sec), ERP = 7.5% (Damodaran India estimate), β = 1.0 (Bloomberg, 2-year monthly). Ke = 6.8% + 1.0 × 7.5% = 14.3%. For Asian Paints with β = 0.65: Ke = 6.8% + 0.65 × 7.5% = 11.68%. For Vedanta with β = 1.6: Ke = 6.8% + 1.6 × 7.5% = 18.8%. Notice the spread — the riskiest cyclical demands roughly 7 percentage points more than the defensive consumer staple.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Each input moves Ke roughly one-for-one. Bumping ERP from 7.5% to 8% lifts Ke by 0.5% (at β = 1) or 0.8% (at β = 1.6). Bumping beta by 0.1 lifts Ke by 0.75% (at ERP = 7.5%). Senior analysts will pressure-test each input separately, and you should be ready to defend each one independently.

formulas.name: Unlevering Beta (Removing the Effect of Financial Leverage)

variables.meaning: Unlevered beta — the beta the company would have if it had zero debt
Levered (equity) beta — the beta you observe in the market
Marginal tax rate (use 25% for most Indian companies)
Market-value debt-to-equity ratio

formulas.worked_example: Tata Motors has an observed (levered) beta of 1.4, a D/E ratio of 0.8, and a tax rate of 25%. Unlevered beta = 1.4 / [1 + (1 - 0.25) × 0.8] = 1.4 / [1 + 0.6] = 1.4 / 1.6 = 0.875. This unlevered beta represents the pure business risk of Tata Motors, stripped of financial leverage. You would unlever beta when you want to compare business risk across companies with different capital structures, or when you need to re-lever it to a target capital structure.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Higher D/E inflates observed (levered) beta. A company with the same business risk but more debt will have a higher equity beta because debt magnifies the volatility of equity returns. This is why two paint companies — one debt-free and one heavily levered — can have very different observed betas despite identical business operations.

formulas.name: Re-levering Beta (Applying a New Capital Structure)

variables.meaning: Levered beta — the beta at the target capital structure
Unlevered beta — the pure business risk beta
Marginal tax rate
Target market-value debt-to-equity ratio

formulas.worked_example: You want to value an unlisted auto company. You take Tata Motors' unlevered beta of 0.875 (assumed comparable business risk) and apply it to your target's D/E of 0.4 with T = 25%. Levered beta = 0.875 × [1 + (1 - 0.25) × 0.4] = 0.875 × 1.30 = 1.14. This is the beta you plug into CAPM for the unlisted auto company. The whole levering / unlevering exercise lets you transport business risk across different capital structures.
formulas.sensitivity_note: In practice, analysts unlever betas of multiple comparable companies, take the median of the unlevered betas, then re-lever to the subject company's capital structure. This produces a more stable estimate than relying on any single observed beta — particularly useful for IPO candidates or thinly-traded names.

title: All 6 Conditional Logic Functions

functions.name: IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false)

nested_if.syntax: =IF(condition1, result1, IF(condition2, result2, IF(condition3, result3, default)))
nested_if.three_nest_rule: If you're nesting more than 3 IFs, stop. Switch to IFS() or SWITCH() or a lookup table.

functions.description: Tests a condition. If TRUE, returns the second argument. If FALSE, returns the third.
functions.mental_model: Every IF formula is a fork in the road. The logical_test is the signpost. You go left (true) or right (false).

functions.name: AND(condition1, condition2, ...) / OR(condition1, condition2, ...)
functions.description: AND returns TRUE only if ALL conditions are true. OR returns TRUE if ANY condition is true.
functions.key_insight: AND and OR don't do anything useful alone. They return TRUE/FALSE. Their power comes from being inside an IF.

functions.name: IFERROR(value, value_if_error)
functions.trap: IFERROR catches ALL errors, including genuine bugs. If you wrap =A1/B1 in IFERROR and B1 is blank because someone forgot to enter data, you'll see 0 instead of an error — and never know the input is missing. Best practice: use IFERROR for presentation layers. In calculation layers, let errors surface.
functions.description: Tries to evaluate the first argument. If it returns ANY error (#DIV/0!, #N/A, #VALUE!, #REF!), returns the second argument instead.

errors_caught.cause: Dividing by zero or empty cell

functions.golden_pattern: Wrap every VLOOKUP, every INDEX-MATCH, and every division in IFERROR. Always. No exceptions for output layers.

functions.name: IFS(condition1, result1, condition2, result2, ..., TRUE, default)
functions.description: Tests multiple conditions in order. Returns the result for the FIRST true condition. The last pair should be TRUE, default_value as a catch-all.
functions.compatibility: IFS is available in Excel 2019, Office 365, and Google Sheets. If your firm uses Excel 2016 or earlier, fall back to nested IF.

functions.name: SWITCH(expression, value1, result1, value2, result2, ..., default)

example.explanation: If B1="Bull", returns 18%. If B1="Base", returns 12%. If B1="Bear", returns 5%. Otherwise returns 10% (default).

functions.description: Compares one expression against a list of exact values. Returns the result for the first match.
functions.when_to_use: Use SWITCH when comparing one cell against exact values (scenario name, sector code, rating). Use IFS when testing ranges or inequalities.
functions.choose_alternative: Some analysts prefer =CHOOSE(scenario_number, bull_value, base_value, bear_value) where the scenario cell contains 1, 2, or 3 instead of text. CHOOSE is older and more universally compatible.

title: Key IPO Metrics

formulas.name: Subscription Ratio
formulas.formula: Subscription Ratio = Total Shares Applied For ÷ Total Shares Offered
formulas.sensitivity: If subscription is below 1x (undersubscribed), the IPO may fail or the price may be revised downward. QIB subscription matters most — retail follows smart money.
formulas.plain_english: If 100 crore shares were offered and investors applied for 3,800 crore shares, the subscription ratio is 38x. Higher subscription = more demand than supply = likely strong listing.
formulas.worked_example: Retail portion offered ~₹3,281 crore. Retail investors applied for ~₹24,449 crore. Subscription = 24,449 / 3,281 = 7.45x.

formulas.name: Listing Day Return (Listing Gain/Loss)
formulas.formula: Listing Day Return = [(Listing Price – Issue Price) ÷ Issue Price] × 100
formulas.analysts_note: A massive listing gain doesn't mean the company is good — it means the IPO was underpriced. Consistent underpricing benefits institutional investors (who get larger allotments) at the expense of retail investors (who get lottery-based allotment and often buy more in the secondary market at inflated prices).
formulas.worked_example: Zomato issue price = ₹76, listing price = ₹115. Return = [(115 – 76) / 76] × 100 = 51.3%.

formulas.name: Cost of Equity Capital via IPO
formulas.formula: Effective Cost = Issue Expenses (BRLMs + legal + marketing) ÷ Total Funds Raised × 100
formulas.worked_example: If Zomato spent ~₹175 crore on IPO expenses to raise ₹9,375 crore, the cost = 175/9375 × 100 = 1.87%. This is found in the 'Objects of the Issue' section of the RHP.

title: The compensation metrics every analyst must compute

formulas.name: Compensation as Percentage of PAT
formulas.formula: Compensation / PAT Ratio = (Total KMP Compensation or CEO Compensation) / PAT × 100

variables.meaning: Sum of compensation paid to all Key Managerial Personnel — MD, CEO, CFO, whole-time directors, company secretary. Disclosed in the Directors Report and Report on Corporate Governance.
Total compensation paid to the MD/CEO, including fixed pay, variable pay, ESOP values, and perquisites.
Profit After Tax of the listed entity for the financial year being analysed. Use consolidated PAT for the most economically meaningful ratio.

formulas.worked_example: A mid-cap consumer products company has reported PAT of ₹240 crore for FY24. Total KMP compensation disclosed in the annual report is ₹18.4 crore, of which the MD received ₹11.2 crore. Total KMP compensation as percentage of PAT = 18.4 / 240 × 100 = 7.67 percent. CEO compensation as percentage of PAT = 11.2 / 240 × 100 = 4.67 percent. Both ratios are elevated relative to the general benchmarks (total KMP under 5 percent, CEO under 2 percent). This would warrant a downgrade to the governance score unless there is compelling context (for example, major performance outperformance that justifies elevated payouts under a disclosed formula).
formulas.sensitivity_note: Benchmarks should be applied with sector and size context. Large-cap companies with ₹5,000 crore plus PAT typically show CEO compensation at 0.1 to 0.5 percent of PAT. Mid-caps with ₹200 to 500 crore PAT typically show 1 to 3 percent. Small-caps with sub-₹100 crore PAT can show 3 to 7 percent for legitimate structural reasons. What matters most is whether the ratio has trended up or down over 3 to 5 years alongside company performance.

formulas.name: Fixed-to-Variable Split Ratio
formulas.formula: Fixed Pay Percentage = Fixed Pay / Total Compensation × 100, Variable Pay Percentage = 100 - Fixed Pay Percentage

variables.meaning: Base salary plus guaranteed allowances — the portion of compensation that will be paid regardless of company or individual performance.
Fixed Pay plus Variable Pay plus ESOP/RSU value realised in the year plus Perquisites.

formulas.worked_example: The same MD received fixed salary of ₹4.5 crore, variable bonus of ₹2.8 crore, ESOPs valued at vesting worth ₹3.2 crore, and perquisites of ₹0.7 crore. Total compensation = 4.5 + 2.8 + 3.2 + 0.7 = ₹11.2 crore. Fixed pay percentage = 4.5 / 11.2 × 100 = 40.2 percent. Variable pay (including stock) = 59.8 percent. This is a reasonable structure — majority of compensation is at risk. A package where fixed is 85 percent and everything else is tiny is the negative structure that should raise flags.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The quality of the variable pay matters as much as the split. A 60 percent variable with weak KPIs is worse than a 45 percent variable with rigorous ROE and multi-year EPS conditions. Always evaluate the structure alongside what the variable is actually measuring against.

formulas.name: Annual ESOP Dilution
formulas.formula: Annual ESOP Dilution = Shares Issued on ESOP Exercise in the Year / Total Shares Outstanding (Beginning of Year) × 100

variables.meaning: New shares issued to ESOP holders who exercised their options during the year. Disclosed in the Share Capital section of the annual report.
Total shares outstanding at the start of the financial year.

formulas.worked_example: A mid-cap IT services company had 12.0 crore shares outstanding at the start of FY24. During the year, 18 lakh shares were issued on ESOP exercise. Annual ESOP Dilution = 0.18 / 12.0 × 100 = 1.5 percent. This is slightly above the 1 percent threshold that typically warrants monitoring. Over 5 years of 1.5 percent annual dilution, the existing shareholder stake is diluted by approximately 7.2 percent cumulatively. For a ₹50,000 crore market cap company, that represents approximately ₹3,600 crore of value transferred to ESOP holders, which should be evaluated against the operational value that was delivered over that period.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Some dilution is healthy — ESOPs are a legitimate way to attract and retain talent. The question is whether dilution is proportionate to value creation. A 1.5 percent annual dilution in a company compounding EPS at 20 percent may be well justified. The same dilution in a company with flat earnings is dilutive without benefit. Always assess dilution alongside per-share value growth.

formulas.name: CEO Pay Ratio
formulas.formula: CEO Pay Ratio = CEO Compensation / Median Employee Compensation

variables.meaning: Total annual compensation of the CEO/MD including all components.
The median annual compensation of all employees in the company. Mandatory disclosure in the Directors Report for listed Indian companies.

formulas.worked_example: A mid-cap company's CEO was paid ₹11.2 crore. The median employee compensation disclosed in the Directors Report was ₹8.5 lakh. CEO Pay Ratio = 11.2 crore / 8.5 lakh = 1,120 / 8.5 = 132 times. This is within the moderate range (typically 100 to 300 times for Indian mid-caps). Ratios above 500 times are very high by Indian standards and often indicate governance concerns. Ratios above 1,000 times are typically associated with very specific structural explanations (founder-promoter with large ESOP realisation, company in capital-intensive sector with low median pay) and should be examined on their merits.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The pay ratio is most meaningful when tracked over time and compared with peers. A ratio that has risen from 80 to 250 times over 5 years while median pay has been flat is a signal that executive compensation is growing disproportionately. Compare the ratio to direct sector peers — if your company ratio is double the sector average, investigate why.

title: The Math Behind Trading Bands and Indexing

formulas.name: Mean and Standard Deviation Bands for Valuation Multiples
formulas.formula:
Upper Band = Mean(Multiple) + N × StDev(Multiple)
Lower Band = Mean(Multiple) - N × StDev(Multiple)
Where N is typically 1 (1 standard deviation)

variables.meaning: Arithmetic mean of the valuation multiple (e.g., P/B, P/E) over the historical period — typically 5 years of monthly observations = 60 data points
Standard deviation of the same series, measuring how widely the multiple has varied around its mean
Number of standard deviations for the band — usually 1 SD (covers ~68% of historical observations) or 2 SD (covers ~95%)

formulas.worked_example:
Worked Example — HDFC Bank P/B Trading Band:

Monthly P/B observations over the last 5 years (60 data points):
— Mean: 3.4x
— Standard Deviation: 0.42x

Upper Band (+1 SD) = 3.4 + (1 × 0.42) = 3.82x
Mean Line = 3.4x
Lower Band (-1 SD) = 3.4 - (1 × 0.42) = 2.98x

Current P/B: 2.7x

Interpretation: Current P/B of 2.7x is trading below the -1 SD line of 2.98x, indicating the stock is trading at a level seen less than 16% of the time over the last 5 years. Combined with an analytical thesis on ROE recovery, this becomes the visual support for a Buy call — the chart literally shows the valuation at a historical inflection point.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The width of the band is fully determined by the volatility of the multiple, not by analyst choice. A wider band means the multiple has been more volatile historically; a narrower band means it has been more stable. For stable, blue-chip names like Asian Paints or HUL, the bands are tight (StDev ~0.15-0.25x). For more cyclical names like Tata Steel or auto OEMs, the bands are wider (StDev ~0.5-1.0x). Always use 5 years of data minimum — shorter windows produce statistically noisy bands.

formulas.name: Indexing for Relative Performance Comparison
formulas.formula: Indexed Value(t) = (Price(t) / Price(t=0)) × 100

variables.meaning: Closing price of the stock or index on date t
Closing price on the start date of the chart, which becomes the indexed value of 100
The base value — every series in a relative performance chart starts at 100, allowing direct percentage comparison

formulas.worked_example:
Worked Example — Indexing TCS vs Nifty IT vs Nifty 50 from 1 Jan 2024:

Start Date: 1 Jan 2024
— TCS price: ₹3,800 → Indexed = 100
— Nifty IT price: 35,400 → Indexed = 100
— Nifty 50 price: 21,750 → Indexed = 100

End Date: 31 Mar 2026
— TCS price: ₹3,650 → Indexed = (3,650 / 3,800) × 100 = 96.05
— Nifty IT price: 38,200 → Indexed = (38,200 / 35,400) × 100 = 107.91
— Nifty 50 price: 24,800 → Indexed = (24,800 / 21,750) × 100 = 114.02

Interpretation: Over the period, TCS has underperformed both the Nifty IT index (which is up ~8%) and the Nifty 50 (up ~14%). TCS is down ~4% in absolute terms while the broader market is up. This visual gap — three lines diverging — directly supports a thesis that the stock is currently out of favour but has potential for relative recovery if the Buy thesis plays out.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The choice of start date dramatically affects the picture. Starting from a market top makes everything look bad; starting from a market bottom makes everything look good. Best practice for research: align the start date with the inception of your investment thesis or with a clear event date (results announcement, sector turning point, IPO). Always disclose the start date prominently in the chart subtitle.

title: The EV-to-Equity Bridge and the Target Price Formula

formulas.name: The Full EV-to-Equity Bridge
formulas.formula: Equity Value = EV - Net Debt - Minority Interest - Preferred Stock - Other Senior Claims + Non-Operating Assets

variables.meaning: Enterprise value from DCF (FCFF discounted at WACC)
Total interest-bearing debt minus cash and cash equivalents (use market value if listed, book value as practical approximation)
Fair value of the non-controlling stake in consolidated subsidiaries — typically estimated using a P/E or P/B multiple on the minority share of subsidiary earnings
Fair value of preferred shares — hybrid securities ranking above common equity
Pension underfunding, unfunded environmental liabilities, crystallising contingent liabilities
Fair value of investments in associates/JVs not consolidated, excess cash, investment real estate, listed equity stakes

formulas.worked_example: For Tata Motors (illustrative FY26 estimates): EV from DCF = ₹4,80,000 cr. Net Debt = ₹95,000 cr (consolidated debt minus cash). Minority Interest in JLR-related entities (fair value) = ₹15,000 cr. Investments in associates (Tata Technologies, Tata Capital — fair value of stake) = ₹35,000 cr. Equity Value = 4,80,000 - 95,000 - 15,000 + 35,000 = ₹4,05,000 cr. Notice how the four adjustments collectively moved equity value by ₹75,000 cr — about 16% of EV.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The bridge's impact varies dramatically by business. For Asian Paints (low debt, no minorities, modest investments), the bridge moves equity value by less than 5%. For Tata Motors (significant debt, complex JV/associate structure), it moves by 15-20%. For pure holding companies like Bajaj Holdings, the bridge IS the analysis — most of the value sits in non-operating stakes.

formulas.name: Target Price Per Share
formulas.formula: Target Price = Equity Value / Fully Diluted Shares Outstanding

variables.meaning: From the bridge above
Basic shares + dilution from ESOPs, warrants, convertibles, RSUs (treasury method)

formulas.worked_example: For TCS: Equity Value = ₹13,85,000 cr. Basic shares outstanding = 365 cr. Outstanding ESOPs (in-the-money) ≈ 1.2 cr shares with weighted average exercise price of ₹2,800. Treasury method dilution = 1.2 × (1 - 2,800/4,191) ≈ 0.4 cr shares. Fully Diluted Shares = 365 + 0.4 = 365.4 cr. Target Price = 13,85,000 / 365.4 = ₹3,790 per share. If junior used basic 365 cr instead, they'd get ₹3,795 — a small gap for TCS but materially larger for tech firms with bigger ESOP overhang.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Dilution can range from negligible (well-managed FMCG and industrials, <0.5% dilution) to substantial (early-stage tech, growth-phase internet companies, even some IT services with aggressive ESOP plans, 3-7% dilution). For SBC-heavy companies, ignoring dilution understates true cost to equity holders.

formulas.name: Treasury Stock Method (for ESOP Dilution)
formulas.formula: Net New Shares from Options = Outstanding Options × (1 - Strike Price / Current Market Price)

variables.meaning: In-the-money options as of the latest disclosure
Weighted average exercise price
Today's share price (or in some conventions, the target price you're computing)

formulas.worked_example: For TCS: 1.2 cr in-the-money options outstanding, weighted average strike ₹2,800. Current price ₹4,000. The treasury method assumes the exercise proceeds are used to buy back shares at the current market price. Net new shares = 1.2 × (1 - 2,800/4,000) = 1.2 × 0.30 = 0.36 cr ≈ 0.4 cr. So fully diluted share count is 365 + 0.4 = 365.4 cr.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Treasury method understates dilution for deeply in-the-money options (where strike is far below market) — in those cases, the dilution feels closer to gross outstanding options. For more conservative analysis, some practitioners simply use gross outstanding options as the dilution number, especially for high-SBC technology companies.

title: The Altman Z-Score and Piotroski F-Score Formulas with Indian Application

formulas.name: Altman Z-Score — Original Manufacturing Formula

variables.meaning: Working Capital / Total Assets = (Current Assets − Current Liabilities) / Total Assets. Captures short-term liquidity position.
Retained Earnings / Total Assets. Captures cumulative profitability and financial history — young companies have low values.
EBIT / Total Assets = Earnings Before Interest and Tax / Total Assets. Captures asset productivity — the most heavily weighted variable.
Market Value of Equity / Book Value of Total Liabilities. Market-based solvency measure. For unlisted or thinly-traded companies, use book value.
Sales / Total Assets. Asset turnover — captures operational efficiency. Excluded in non-manufacturing Z''-Score variant.

formulas.worked_example: Computing Altman Z-Score for hypothetical Indian manufacturing mid-cap FY23. Total Assets ₹1,840 crore, Current Assets ₹780 crore, Current Liabilities ₹420 crore, Retained Earnings ₹340 crore, EBIT ₹215 crore, Market Cap (equity) ₹1,280 crore, Total Liabilities ₹560 crore, Revenue ₹2,450 crore. X1 = (780-420)/1840 = 0.196. X2 = 340/1840 = 0.185. X3 = 215/1840 = 0.117. X4 = 1280/560 = 2.286. X5 = 2450/1840 = 1.332. Z = 1.2×0.196 + 1.4×0.185 + 3.3×0.117 + 0.6×2.286 + 1.0×1.332 = 0.235 + 0.259 + 0.386 + 1.372 + 1.332 = 3.584. Interpretation: Z-Score of 3.584 is above 2.99 (safe zone), indicating low bankruptcy probability. The manufacturing company has healthy financial positioning. Applied to IL&FS FY17 retroactive analysis: approximate X1 = 0.05 (low working capital), X2 = 0.08 (modest retained earnings), X3 = 0.04 (low EBIT to assets), X4 = 0.4 (high leverage), X5 = 0.12 (low sales to assets — infrastructure nature). Approximate Z-Score = 1.2×0.05 + 1.4×0.08 + 3.3×0.04 + 0.6×0.4 + 1.0×0.12 = 0.06+0.112+0.132+0.24+0.12 = 0.664. Below 1.81 distress threshold — strongly flagged. The Altman framework would have flagged IL&FS approximately 12-18 months before the September 2018 default. For Indian non-manufacturing coverage, use Z''-Score variant. Applied to same IL&FS FY17 data: Z'' = 3.25 + 6.56×0.05 + 3.26×0.08 + 6.72×0.04 + 1.05×(book equity/liabilities ratio). Computation similar severity — distress zone flagging.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For Indian companies, use the Z''-Score variant for non-manufacturing sectors (services, infrastructure, NBFC, technology). The original Z-Score was calibrated for US manufacturing and may produce less reliable signals for service-oriented or asset-light businesses. Also note that X4 (market value / liabilities) requires listed equity market cap — for private companies or thinly-traded stocks, use book value substitution with understanding of reduced reliability.

formulas.name: Altman Z''-Score — Non-Manufacturing and Emerging Markets Formula

variables.meaning: Working Capital / Total Assets (same as original)
Retained Earnings / Total Assets (same as original)
EBIT / Total Assets (same as original)
Book Value of Equity / Total Liabilities — note: uses BOOK value, not market value, making this variant applicable to private companies and robust to market volatility

formulas.worked_example: Z''-Score is preferred for Indian coverage because it excludes Sales/Total Assets (X5) which is industry-specific, and uses book equity rather than market value which is more stable. Applied to hypothetical Indian services mid-cap FY23. Total Assets ₹2,450 crore, Current Assets ₹1,140 crore, Current Liabilities ₹680 crore, Retained Earnings ₹485 crore, EBIT ₹295 crore, Book Value of Equity ₹1,560 crore, Total Liabilities ₹890 crore. X1 = (1140-680)/2450 = 0.188. X2 = 485/2450 = 0.198. X3 = 295/2450 = 0.120. X4 = 1560/890 = 1.753. Z'' = 3.25 + 6.56×0.188 + 3.26×0.198 + 6.72×0.120 + 1.05×1.753 = 3.25 + 1.233 + 0.645 + 0.806 + 1.841 = 7.775. Interpretation: Z'' of 7.775 is substantially above 2.6 safe threshold — very healthy financial positioning. Z'' thresholds: below 1.1 is distress zone; 1.1 to 2.6 is grey zone; above 2.6 is safe zone. Applied to Jet Airways FY18 retroactive: approximate Z'' of 0.8-1.0 — strongly in distress zone 12 months before April 2019 shutdown. Applied to DHFL FY18 retroactive: approximate Z'' of 1.2-1.4 — grey zone approaching distress threshold, 12 months before September 2019 default. The Z''-Score variant has been validated in multiple Indian academic studies with accuracy ranges of 85-90 percent for bankruptcy prediction 1-2 years forward.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For Indian banking and NBFC companies, standard Z-Score and Z''-Score variants may produce less reliable signals due to different business model dynamics (leverage is the business model). Specialized variants exist but require adaptation. For these sectors, integrate with NPA analysis, provision coverage ratios, and regulatory capital metrics from Session 6.

formulas.name: Piotroski F-Score — 9 Binary Signals
formulas.formula: F-Score = Sum of 9 binary signals (0 or 1 each) = 0 to 9

variables.meaning: Signal 1: Net Income > 0 (positive current year profit); Signal 2: CFO > 0 (positive operating cash flow); Signal 3: CFO > Net Income (quality earnings); Signal 4: ROA current year > prior year (improving profitability)

Signal 5: Long-Term Debt / Total Assets current year < prior year (deleveraging); Signal 6: Current Ratio current year > prior year (improving liquidity); Signal 7: No new equity issued during year (no dilution)
Signal 8: Gross Margin current year > prior year (pricing power); Signal 9: Asset Turnover current year > prior year (improving asset utilization)

formulas.worked_example: Computing Piotroski F-Score for hypothetical Indian consumer products mid-cap. FY23 Net Income ₹185 crore (positive — Signal 1 triggered, 1). FY23 CFO ₹215 crore (positive — Signal 2 triggered, 1). CFO ₹215 crore > Net Income ₹185 crore (earnings quality — Signal 3 triggered, 1). ROA FY23 9.2 percent > FY22 ROA 8.5 percent (improving — Signal 4 triggered, 1). Long-Term Debt/Total Assets FY23 0.18 < FY22 0.21 (deleveraging — Signal 5 triggered, 1). Current Ratio FY23 1.68 > FY22 1.52 (improving liquidity — Signal 6 triggered, 1). Shares outstanding FY23 equal to FY22 — no new equity issued (Signal 7 triggered, 1). Gross Margin FY23 42 percent > FY22 40 percent (pricing power — Signal 8 triggered, 1). Asset Turnover FY23 1.25 > FY22 1.18 (improving utilization — Signal 9 triggered, 1). Total F-Score = 9. Interpretation: F-Score of 9 is the maximum possible, indicating strongest fundamental financial position. This company exhibits improvement across all three categories — profitability, leverage/liquidity, and operating efficiency. Rare in practice — most strong companies score 7-8. A score of 9 combined with reasonable valuation (low P/B or P/E) represents high-conviction fundamental opportunity. Interpretation ranges: 0-3 weak financial position (concerning signals across multiple categories); 4-5 average (mixed signals); 6-9 strong (positive signals across most categories). Piotroski's original research showed that applying F-Score filter to low P/B value stocks produced approximately 7.5 percent annual outperformance — high F-Score value stocks (7-9) substantially outperformed low F-Score value stocks (0-3) over 1976-1996 period. Indian market validation studies have shown similar patterns on Nifty 500 and BSE 500 stocks.
formulas.sensitivity_note: F-Score is most powerful when combined with valuation screening. Apply F-Score as secondary filter on top of value screening (lowest 20 percent P/B in coverage universe). High F-Score among value stocks identifies genuine turnaround candidates. Low F-Score among value stocks identifies value traps where low valuation reflects genuine deterioration. The combined application is where Piotroski's original research showed the largest outperformance.

title: Key Regulatory Formulas & Thresholds

formulas.name: SAST Open Offer Price (Minimum)
formulas.formula:
Open Offer Price = Highest of:
(a) Highest price paid by acquirer for shares in the last 52 weeks
(b) VWAP of target stock on the exchange for 60 trading days before the public announcement
(c) Highest price paid under any shareholder agreement
formulas.worked_example: Company X announces an open offer. Acquirer paid ₹425 in a block deal 3 months ago (highest in 52 weeks). 60-day VWAP on NSE = ₹410. No shareholder agreement purchases. Minimum open offer price = ₹425 (highest of the three).

formulas.name: Minimum Public Shareholding (MPS)
formulas.formula:
Minimum Public Shareholding = 25% of total shares
Promoter + Promoter Group holding must not exceed 75%.
Companies violating this must reduce promoter holding via OFS, bonus on non-promoter shares, or exchange-facilitated mechanism.

formulas.name: Insider Trading — Trading Window Closure
formulas.formula:
Trading Window closes: From end of every quarter until 48 hours after board meeting approving financial results.
Typical closure: ~2–4 weeks before results + 48 hours after announcement.
Designated persons must also obtain pre-clearance and must not have a contra-trade within 6 months.

formulas.name: Research Analyst Personal Trading Restriction
formulas.formula:
No trading allowed: 30 days before publishing a research report on a stock.
No trading allowed: 5 days after publishing.
Total blackout: 35 days around each report publication.
If you cover 15 stocks and publish monthly reports, you are effectively restricted from trading in most of them most of the time.

title: Key Participant-Level Metrics

formulas.name: Net FII/DII Activity
formulas.formula:
Net FII Activity = FII Gross Purchases – FII Gross Sales
Net DII Activity = DII Gross Purchases – DII Gross Sales
Positive = net buying. Negative = net selling.
formulas.analysts_note: Look at rolling 5-day, 10-day, and 30-day net figures, not single days. One day of FII selling means nothing. Ten consecutive days of net selling is a trend. Thirty days is a regime shift.
formulas.worked_example: On a given day, FIIs buy ₹8,500 crore and sell ₹9,200 crore. Net FII = –₹700 crore (net seller). DIIs buy ₹7,800 crore and sell ₹6,900 crore. Net DII = +₹900 crore (net buyer). DIIs absorbed FII selling and then some — this is the tug-of-war in action.

formulas.name: FII Ownership Change (Quarterly)
formulas.formula:
FII Ownership Change = FII Holding (Current Quarter %) – FII Holding (Previous Quarter %)
Data source: BSE/NSE quarterly shareholding pattern filings
formulas.worked_example: HDFC Bank's FII holding drops from 55% to 52% over one quarter. That's a 3 percentage point decrease. On a ~₹12 lakh crore market cap, 3% = ~₹36,000 crore of FII selling. That's massive, and explains any price weakness during that quarter.

formulas.name: DII Absorption Ratio
formulas.formula:
DII Absorption Ratio = |Net DII Buying| / |Net FII Selling| × 100
(Only calculated when FII is net seller and DII is net buyer)
formulas.sensitivity: When the absorption ratio drops below 70%, the market typically falls 3–5%. When it exceeds 100% (DIIs buying more than FIIs are selling), the market often goes up despite FII outflows.
formulas.worked_example: In a month, FIIs sell ₹30,000 crore net and DIIs buy ₹28,000 crore net. Absorption ratio = 28,000/30,000 × 100 = 93.3%. DIIs absorbed 93% of FII selling, leaving only 7% (₹2,000 crore) to pressure prices.

formulas.name: Retail Participation Ratio
formulas.formula:
Retail Share of Turnover = (Retail Turnover / Total Market Turnover) × 100
Retail Ownership (%) from quarterly shareholding pattern filings
formulas.why_it_matters: When retail participation spikes, it often signals frothy sentiment — new entrants chasing momentum. In 2021, retail share of cash turnover reached 45%+, correlating with peak valuations in mid and small-caps. When retail retreats, it often signals capitulation and potential bottoms.

title: Decomposing Stock Returns — The Sector Attribution Formula

formulas.name: Stock Return Decomposition (Brinson Framework)
formulas.formula: R_stock = R_market + R_sector_relative + R_stock_specific

variables.meaning: Total return of the stock over the period
Return of the broad market index (e.g. Nifty 50)
Return of the sector index minus the market return (the sector premium or discount)
Return of the stock minus the sector index return (the stock-specific alpha)

formulas.worked_example: Consider Asian Paints over FY24. Asian Paints stock return: -5%. Nifty 50 return: +28%. Nifty FMCG (closest sector proxy) return: +18%. Decomposition: R_market = +28%. R_sector_relative = 18% - 28% = -10% (FMCG underperformed broader market). R_stock_specific = -5% - 18% = -23% (Asian Paints underperformed even its own sector, due to Grasim/Birla Opus entry threat). Of the -33% gap between Asian Paints and Nifty, -10% came from sector, -23% from stock-specific factors. The analyst lesson: even getting the stock call right requires getting the sector call right first.
formulas.sensitivity_note: When the sector is in a strong up-cycle (e.g. PSU banks in FY23-24, +60% sector return), even mediocre stocks deliver strong returns. When the sector is in a down-cycle (e.g. IT services in FY23, -20% sector return), even Tier-1 names struggle. This is why sector calls compound — getting the sector right gives you a 60-70% head start on the stock call.

formulas.name: Sector Multiple Premium/Discount Formula
formulas.formula: Sector Premium = (Sector P/E − Market P/E) ÷ Market P/E × 100

variables.meaning: Forward 1-year P/E ratio of the sector index
Forward 1-year P/E ratio of the broad market (Nifty 50)

formulas.worked_example: Nifty FMCG forward P/E: 42x. Nifty 50 forward P/E: 21x. Sector Premium = (42 - 21) / 21 × 100 = 100%. FMCG trades at a 100% premium to the market. This premium is the market's pricing of FMCG's structural advantages — defensive earnings, brand moats, low capital intensity. When this premium expands beyond historical bands (FMCG has historically traded at 60-90% premium), it signals overheating. When it contracts below the band, it signals a potential entry point.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Sector premiums are not static — they expand and contract with the market's appetite for defensiveness vs cyclicality. In risk-off markets (recession fears, geopolitical stress), defensive sectors like FMCG and Pharma command higher premiums. In risk-on markets (recovery, falling rates), cyclical sectors like Auto, Metals, and Real Estate close the gap and even trade at premiums to defensives.

title: The Margin Build-Up — From Revenue to EBIT in Layered Components

formulas.name: Gross Margin Calculation
formulas.formula: Gross Margin = (Revenue − COGS) / Revenue | COGS = Raw Materials + Purchases + Changes in Inventory

variables.meaning: Revenue from operations — the top line from Session 4's forecast
Cost of Goods Sold — for manufacturers this is raw materials + labour; for retailers it is purchases of inventory; varies by business model
Cost of materials consumed — directly tracked for manufacturers via input prices × usage
Goods purchased for resale — for pure retailers like DMart, this is ~90% of COGS
Negative if inventory increased (expense reduced), positive if inventory decreased (expense increased)

formulas.worked_example: Titan FY24 actuals: Revenue ₹47,100 cr, COGS (Material + Purchases + Inventory changes) ₹33,810 cr, Gross Profit ₹13,290 cr, Gross Margin = 28.2%. For the FY25E forecast, I decompose Titan's COGS into its structural drivers. Jewellery COGS is roughly 78% of Jewellery Revenue (the rest is margin on making charges, design premium, and studded mix) — this ratio moves with gold price pass-through and mix. Watches COGS is ~55% of Watches Revenue (higher brand margin). Eyewear COGS is ~45% of Eyewear Revenue (retail model). Applied to FY25E segmental revenues: Jewellery COGS = 47,772 × 78% = ₹37,262 cr; Watches COGS = 3,382 × 55% = ₹1,860 cr; Eyewear COGS = 1,040 × 45% = ₹468 cr; Other COGS = 2,136 × 70% = ₹1,495 cr. Total FY25E COGS = ₹41,085 cr. Gross Margin FY25E = (54,330 − 41,085) / 54,330 = 24.4%. Note: this is LOWER than FY24's 28.2% because the studded mix assumption is conservative. If mgmt's 37% studded mix target is achieved, COGS ratio drops to ~76% and Gross Margin rises to 26-27%. That is a live sensitivity for the model.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For Titan, every 100 bps of Jewellery COGS ratio change = ~₹478 cr of Gross Profit change on FY25E revenue. That flows directly to EBITDA. Over a 5-year forecast, persistent 100 bps of COGS-ratio change compounds to ~₹3,500 cr of cumulative EBITDA swing. Studded mix modelling is the single most important margin driver for Titan — get it wrong and your forecast is built on sand.

formulas.name: EBITDA Build from Gross Profit
formulas.formula: EBITDA = Gross Profit − Employee Cost − Other Operating Expenses | EBITDA Margin = EBITDA / Revenue

variables.meaning: Revenue − COGS, from the step above
Wages, benefits, PF, ESOP expense — semi-variable, with a fixed base and variable component
Rent, utilities, marketing, admin, travel — typically 70-80% fixed with 20-30% variable scaling

formulas.worked_example: Titan FY24: Gross Profit ₹13,290 cr, Employee Cost ₹1,985 cr, Other Opex ₹4,620 cr, EBITDA ₹6,685 cr, EBITDA Margin = 14.2%. For FY25E, I forecast Employee Cost as semi-variable: fixed base ₹1,700 cr growing at 8% inflation = ₹1,836 cr, plus variable component of ₹300 cr × (store growth 7%) = ₹321 cr. Total FY25E Employee Cost = ₹2,157 cr. Growth of 8.7% vs revenue growth of 15.4% — this is operating leverage in action. Other Opex: 75% fixed (₹3,465 cr × 7% inflation = ₹3,708 cr) + 25% variable (₹1,155 cr × revenue growth 15.4% = ₹1,333 cr) = ₹5,041 cr. FY25E EBITDA = 13,245 − 2,157 − 5,041 = ₹6,047 cr. Wait — this is LOWER than FY24 ₹6,685 cr despite higher revenue. That's because my conservative COGS assumption (78% for Jewellery vs 73% implied in FY24) crushed gross margin. If I use a more realistic 75% Jewellery COGS ratio (allowing some studded mix benefit), COGS falls to ~₹40,000 cr, Gross Profit rises to ₹14,330 cr, EBITDA = 14,330 − 2,157 − 5,041 = ₹7,132 cr. Margin = 13.1% (vs 14.2% in FY24 — some compression from mix and other-segment drag, offsetting operating leverage). This scenario feels right.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The EBITDA build makes operating leverage visible. Employee cost growing at 8.7% on revenue growth of 15.4% means every 1% incremental revenue beyond the base drops roughly 50% to EBITDA as contribution. Other Opex at 75% fixed means 75% of that line doesn't scale — also contributing to leverage. An analyst who forecasts Employee Cost and Opex as flat percentages of revenue MISSES operating leverage entirely and produces a flat-margin forecast that is structurally wrong for any scaling business.

formulas.name: EBIT from EBITDA and Depreciation
formulas.formula: EBIT = EBITDA − Depreciation & Amortisation | EBIT Margin = EBIT / Revenue

variables.meaning: From the step above — operating profit before D&A
Depreciation of tangible assets (PP&E) + Amortisation of intangibles (software, trademarks, goodwill). Non-cash but economically meaningful

formulas.worked_example: Titan FY24: EBITDA ₹6,685 cr, D&A ₹680 cr, EBIT ₹6,005 cr, EBIT Margin = 12.7%. For FY25E, D&A grows based on the capex forecast from Session 6 — but for this session, I'll use a placeholder assumption. FY25E capex is expected to be ~3.5% of revenue = ₹1,900 cr (for new stores, infrastructure, technology). Average useful life for Titan's asset base is ~10 years. Incremental depreciation from FY25E capex = ₹1,900/10 = ₹190 cr of NEW depreciation. Existing PP&E base has ₹4,800 cr of gross block with remaining average life of 7 years, contributing ₹685 cr of baseline depreciation. Total FY25E D&A = ₹685 + ₹190/2 (half-year convention for new additions) = ₹780 cr. FY25E EBIT = 7,132 − 780 = ₹6,352 cr. EBIT Margin = 11.7% (FY24: 12.7%). The slight margin contraction comes from (a) my conservative studded mix assumption on Jewellery and (b) higher depreciation from incremental capex.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For asset-light businesses (IT services, FMCG), D&A is 2-4% of revenue and EBIT margin ≈ EBITDA margin - 2-4%. For capital-intensive businesses (autos, metals, telecom), D&A is 8-15% of revenue and EBIT margin can be 8-15% lower than EBITDA. Titan is in between — at ~1.4% of revenue, D&A is a secondary margin driver but materially affects the EBIT line. In Session 6 you will rebuild the PP&E schedule properly and this placeholder becomes a rigorous forecast.
